<!-- Wave Visualizer Script -->
<script>
function changeImage(imgId, newSrc) {
    var img = document.getElementById(imgId);
    img.src = newSrc;
}

function restoreImage(imgId, originalSrc) {
    var img = document.getElementById(imgId);
    img.src = originalSrc;
}
</script>

<!-- Wave Visualizer Script -->
<script>
    const canvas = document.getElementById('visualizer');
    if (canvas) {
      const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d');
      let time = 0;
      let waveData = Array(8).fill(0).map(() => ({
          value: Math.random() * 0.5 + 0.1,
          targetValue: Math.random() * 0.15 + 0.1,
          speed: Math.random() * .02 + 0.01
      }));

      function resizeCanvas() {
          canvas.width = window.innerWidth;
          canvas.height = window.innerHeight;
      }

      function updateWaveData() {
          waveData.forEach(data => {
              if (Math.random() < 0.01) {
                  data.targetValue = Math.random() * 0.7 + 0.1;
              }
              const diff = data.targetValue - data.value;
              data.value += diff * data.speed;
          });
      }

      function draw() {
          ctx.fillStyle = 'black';
          ctx.fillRect(0, 0, canvas.width, canvas.height);

          for (let i = 0; i < 8; i++) {
              const freq = waveData[i].value * 7.0;
              ctx.beginPath();

              for (let x = 0; x < canvas.width; x += 1) {
                  const normalizedX = (x / canvas.width) * 2 - 1;
                  let px = normalizedX + i * 0.04 + freq * 0.03;
                  let py = Math.sin(px * 10 + time) * Math.cos(px * 2) * freq * 0.1 * ((i + 1) / 8);
                  const canvasY = (py + 1) * canvas.height / 2;

                  if (x === 0) {
                      ctx.moveTo(x, canvasY);
                  } else {
                      ctx.lineTo(x, canvasY);
                  }
              }

              const intensity = Math.min(1, freq * 0.3);
              const r = 255 + intensity * 100;
              const g = 243 + intensity * 130;
              const b = 197;

              ctx.lineWidth = .1 + (i * 0.3);
              ctx.strokeStyle = `rgba(${r}, ${g}, ${b}, 0.6)`;
              ctx.shadowColor = `rgba(${r}, ${g}, ${b}, 0.5)`;
              ctx.shadowBlur = 5;
              ctx.stroke();
              ctx.shadowBlur = 0;
          }
      }

      function animate() {
          time += 0.02;
          updateWaveData();
          draw();
          requestAnimationFrame(animate);
      }

      window.addEventListener('resize', resizeCanvas);
      resizeCanvas();
      animate();
    }
  </script>
  <!-- Wave Visualizer Script -->

title: "Kanvas Documentation"
url: /kanvas/index.md
description: Kanvas is a visual, collaborative tool for designing, validating, deploying, and operating Kubernetes and cloud infrastructure.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Kanvas lets you design Kubernetes and cloud infrastructure visually, validate and deploy that design to your clusters, and then operate what is running, all from one shared canvas. Teams work on the same design at the same time, so the diagram you discuss is the configuration you deploy.

## What is Kanvas?

Kanvas is a web application for creating and sharing orchestratable designs of cloud native infrastructure. A design is a declarative description of infrastructure: the components it contains, the relationships between them, their configuration, and any annotations you add to explain it. You build a design by placing components on a canvas, connecting them, and configuring each one. You can also draw shapes, lines, text, and icons to document your intent; Kanvas treats those as annotations and never deploys them.

A design does not stop at the diagram. Kanvas validates a design against the schema of every component in it, dry-runs it against your target clusters without applying anything, and deploys or undeploys it on the Kubernetes contexts you select. Every save creates a new version of the design, and multiple people can edit the same design together in real time.

This matters because one artifact carries your infrastructure from whiteboard to running cluster. Reviewers read the same design that operators deploy, and every resource Kanvas deploys carries the identity of the design that produced it, so you can trace running workloads back to their source.

## Two modes: Designer and Operator

Kanvas has two modes. You switch between them at any time; if the open design or resource has unsaved changes, Kanvas asks you to confirm before you leave.

- **[Designer]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/designer/index.md" >}})** is for authoring. You compose designs from versioned components, define relationships, configure each component, and annotate the result. Whiteboarding is a toolset inside Designer, not a separate mode. Validate, dry-run, deploy, and undeploy actions run from Designer.
- **[Operator]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/operator/index.md" >}})** is for running infrastructure. It shows the recorded state of your connected Kubernetes clusters, collected by MeshSync and served through Meshery. Operator can scope its view to the resources a single design deployed.

### Where each mode is available

Designer is available everywhere Kanvas runs, including the hosted Kanvas at [kanvas.new](https://kanvas.new). Operator mode, and every action that touches a cluster, needs a Meshery deployment that can reach your clusters.

| Capability | Hosted Kanvas (kanvas.new) | Meshery Playground or self-hosted Meshery |
|---|---|---|
| Designer: author and import designs | Available | Available |
| Share and publish designs | Requires sign-in | Requires sign-in |
| Validate, dry-run, deploy, and undeploy | Not available | Available |
| Connect clusters | Not available | Available |
| Operator mode | Not available | Available |

When you invoke a cluster-bound capability on kanvas.new, Kanvas explains that it is not available there and points you to the [Meshery Playground](https://playground.meshery.io) or a self-hosted Meshery deployment. Plan details live at [layer5.io/pricing](https://layer5.io/pricing).

### Choose your mode

<div style="display:flex;justify-content:center;">
{{< cardpane >}}
  {{< card header="Designer" >}}
    <p><a href="{{< ref "kanvas/concepts/designer/index.md" >}}">Designer</a> mode is for creating and editing designs.</p>
    <p>Compose infrastructure from a palette of versioned components, connect components with relationships, and configure each one.</p>
    <p>Validate a design, dry-run it against your clusters, and deploy it.</p>
  {{< /card >}}
  {{< card header="Operator" >}}
    <p><a href="{{< ref "kanvas/concepts/operator/index.md" >}}">Operator</a> mode is for operating your Kubernetes clusters and the infrastructure running on them.</p>
    <p>See the recorded state of the clusters you select.</p>
    <p>Filter the view to the resources that a specific design deployed.</p>
  {{< /card >}}
{{< /cardpane >}}
</div>

## How Kanvas relates to Meshery and Layer5 Cloud

Kanvas is an extension of Meshery. Its interface loads into Meshery UI, and a companion plugin runs inside Meshery Server. Meshery Server is the component that talks to your clusters: it deploys and observes infrastructure on Kanvas's behalf. [Layer5 Cloud]({{< ref "cloud/_index.md" >}}) is the remote provider behind Kanvas: it stores your designs and their versions and handles identity, sharing, the catalog, and events. [How Kanvas Works with Meshery and Layer5 Cloud]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/architecture/index.md" >}}) explains how requests move between these parts.

## Where to go next

- **[Getting Started]({{< ref "kanvas/getting-started/_index.md" >}})** - create your first design and reach a working result fast.
- **[Tutorials]({{< ref "kanvas/tutorials/_index.md" >}})** - learn Kanvas by building realistic designs end to end.
- **[How-to Guides]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/_index.md" >}})** - accomplish a specific task, such as deploying or sharing a design.
- **[Concepts]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/_index.md" >}})** - understand designs, components, relationships, and how Kanvas works.
- **[Reference]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/_index.md" >}})** - look up exact options, limits, permissions, and shortcuts.

title: "Collaborative Editing"
url: /kanvas/tutorials/collaborative-editing/index.md
description: Work on one Kanvas design with a teammate in real time, from saving and sharing it to resolving a review thread.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

In this tutorial, you and a teammate work on the same design at the same time. You save a design, share it, watch your teammate join as a live collaborator, edit together, and run a short review in a comment thread. Along the way you learn the four separate mechanisms behind collaboration in Kanvas: the live session, access, comments, and saving. Each one explains a different part of what you see.

## Before you begin

- You and a teammate each need a Layer5 account, and both of you sign in. Anonymous sessions are asked to sign in to share.
- Sharing requires the Share Design permission. Searching for people in the Share dialog and in comment mentions requires the View All Users permission. See [Permissions]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/permissions.md" >}}).
- Use [kanvas.new](https://kanvas.new). Everything in this tutorial happens in Designer and needs no cluster.

## Step 1: Save a design

Open Designer, add two or three components, give the design a name, and save it.

Saving matters before anything else. A live session is keyed to the saved design, and a new design has no identity until its first save, so it has no session and nobody can join it. From the moment the design is saved, Kanvas opens a session for it whenever the design is loaded.

You should now see the design's name in the top bar and the Share control available. Kanvas hides Share for an empty design.

## Step 2: Share the design with your teammate

Open the Share dialog, search for your teammate, and add them. Leave visibility set to Private. Copy the link and send it to your teammate.

<figure>
  <img src="../images/collaborative-editing/designer-share.png" alt="Share dialog listing people with access, visibility, and a copy-link control" />
  <figcaption>The Share dialog</figcaption>
</figure>

You should now see your teammate in the list of people with access.

This step is about **access**. A share is a grant to one person, and it carries no access level: there is no view-only or comment-only option. Your teammate can now do what you can do with the design except delete it or take ownership. They can open, edit, and save it, clone and download it, comment on it, switch it between private and public, and share it with others if their role includes Share Design. Only you as owner, or a provider administrator, can delete the design, and ownership never transfers.

The link alone does not open a private design. The grant does.

## Step 3: Open the design together

Your teammate opens the link while signed in. Keep the design open on your side.

You should now see:

- Your teammate's avatar in the action toolbar, with their first name and a ring in their color.
- Their cursor on your canvas, labeled with their first name in the same color, whenever it lies inside your visible canvas area.
- A border in their color around any component they select.

This step is about the **live session**. Your browsers connect to each other directly, peer to peer. Layer5 Cloud only introduces the two browsers; your design edits do not pass through it. People appear as live collaborators only while both of you have the saved design open. Granting access does not make anyone appear, and closing the design removes them. Colors are assigned at random for each session, so two people can share a color. A second browser tab of your own appears as another collaborator.

If no avatar appears, the session did not open. Kanvas shows no error in that case, and each of you keeps working alone. Confirm that both of you are signed in and have the saved design open. Live sync uses direct browser connections with a public relay as fallback, so a network that blocks WebRTC prevents the session.

## Step 4: Edit at the same time

Move or reconfigure one component while your teammate adds another.

You should now see each other's changes arrive without reloading. Your zoom, viewport, selection, and layout stay your own; the design itself is what syncs.

This step is about **saving**. The live session shares changes but does not store them. Each person's browser autosaves that person's own changes a few seconds after they stop editing, and each save writes the whole design, so the last save wins. Receiving a teammate's change does not trigger a save on your side. Anyone who opens the design later loads the last saved version, not the live session.

## Step 5: Start a review thread

Place a comment next to the component your teammate added, using the comment tool on the dock, Add Comment from the canvas context menu, or the <kbd>M</kbd> key. Type a question, type `@` followed by part of your teammate's name, pick them from the suggestions, and press Enter to send.

You should now see the comment appear on your teammate's canvas immediately. Your teammate receives an email because you mentioned them, unless they turned off comment notifications in their account preferences.

The Comments panel in the toolbar lists every thread that has at least one message, with filters for All, Open, Resolved, and For me. Before the first comment, it shows an empty state.

<figure>
  <img src="../images/collaborative-editing/designer-comments.png" alt="Comments panel in Designer showing the empty state" />
  <figcaption>The Comments panel before any comments exist</figcaption>
</figure>

This step is about **comments**. A comment is part of the design: it syncs live, saves with the design, and travels with clones and exports. Anyone who can edit the design can comment on it. Email follows mentions and participation: a first comment that mentions nobody emails nobody, including the owner. The mention search covers all users, and mentioning someone does not give them access to the design. Grant access through the Share dialog.

## Step 6: Reply and resolve

Your teammate replies in the same thread. Because you took part in the thread, you receive an email about the reply, unless you muted the thread with its bell or turned off the preference. A thread shows its first message until you choose to show all of them.

Resolve the thread from its own controls.

You should now see the comment leave the canvas for both of you and appear under the Resolved filter in the Comments panel. Resolving sends no notification, and neither does reopening. Adding a new message to a resolved thread reopens it.

## What you learned

- **Live session:** a peer-to-peer connection keyed to the saved design. It exists only while people have that design open, and an unsaved design has none.
- **Access:** a grant to one person with no access level. Grantees can do what the owner can do except delete the design or take ownership.
- **Comments:** part of the design itself. Mentions and thread participation decide who gets email; resolving and reopening notify no one.
- **Saving:** each person's changes autosave from their own browser, and the last save wins.

## Where to go next

- [Share a Design]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/collaborating/sharing-designs/index.md" >}}) covers visibility, grants, revokes, and share errors.
- [Review a Design with Comments]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/collaborating/reviewing-designs/index.md" >}}) covers comment placement, filters, muting, and notifications.
- [Collaboration]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/collaboration/index.md" >}}) explains how live sessions, presence, and persistence work.
- [Saving Designs]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/designs/saving-designs/index.md" >}}) explains how and when a design is saved.
- [Publishing Designs]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/designs/publishing-designs/index.md" >}}) explains publishing, which is separate from sharing.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Add and Configure Components"
url: /kanvas/guides/designing/configuring-components/index.md
description: Find and place components on the canvas, edit their configuration with the form Kanvas builds from the component definition, and lock, duplicate, copy, and paste them.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

A component is one piece of infrastructure in a design, and its configuration is what Kanvas applies when you deploy. This guide covers placing components on the canvas, editing their configuration, and moving them around by duplicating, copying, and pasting.

You need a design open in Designer mode. Designer is the only mode that allows authoring.

## Add a component

Kanvas offers several ways to place a component. All of them produce the same result: a component in the design, with its configurator open beside it.

| Method | Behavior |
|---|---|
| Drag from the component palette | The component lands where you release it. |
| Click a component in the palette or in a dock picker | The component lands at a random position near the center of the canvas. |
| Drop a component onto another component | If the pair can form a parent-child relationship, Kanvas creates it. See [Create Relationships]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/designing/creating-relationships/index.md" >}}). |
| Drop or paste a file | Image and text files become objects on the canvas. Infrastructure files (YAML, JSON, and archives such as TAR, GZ, ZIP, RAR, and 7Z) start an import. |

Text boxes, sections, and comments are annotation objects rather than infrastructure. They have their own keys: <kbd>T</kbd>, <kbd>S</kbd>, and <kbd>M</kbd>. Press <kbd>I</kbd> to pick an image file. See [Whiteboard on the Canvas]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/designing/whiteboarding/index.md" >}}).

### Find the right model and version

The palette groups models by category. Open a category to list its models, then expand a model to load its components. Each model has a version selector, sorted newest first, with the first version selected by default. The dock's compact pickers offer an "All Versions" choice and hide duplicate components, keeping the highest version.

Typing in the palette search box queries the Meshery registry after you pause for one second. Results appear in two groups, Models and Components, and an empty result reads "Sorry, no matching records found". Search matches model and component names only. It does not match labels.

The palette applies no filter of its own for deprecated or ignored models: it lists whatever the registry returns. Components whose schema is invalid appear dimmed, but you can still drag or click them.

The Kubernetes picker in the dock lists every Kubernetes component in a grid with a version filter. It hides List kinds, such as `PodList`.

### File drop limits

| File | Result | Limit |
|---|---|---|
| Image (PNG, JPG, GIF, BMP, WebP, SVG) | An image object, embedded in the design as data | 512,000 bytes (about 500 KB) |
| Text (`.txt`) | A text box holding the file text | 512,000 bytes (about 500 KB) |
| YAML, JSON, TAR, GZ, TGZ, ZIP, RAR, 7Z | An import placed at the drop position | None applied by the canvas |
| Anything else | Ignored with no message | - |

A file over the limit is rejected with an error message. The limit is fixed and identical on every plan, although the message refers to your plan.

## Edit a component's configuration

Open the configurator with any of these:

- Double-click the component (two taps within 500 ms).
- Select the component and use the Configure control in its floating style toolbar. The toolbar appears when you are zoomed in far enough to see component detail.
- Add a new component. Its configurator opens automatically.
- Select a validation warning badge on the component. The configurator opens with the offending field highlighted.

The configurator is a panel anchored to the component, on the right when there is room and on the left otherwise. The right-click menu has no Configure item.

![The component configurator showing the Config tab for a Kubernetes component](images/working-with-components/configuration-panel.png)

### The header

| Control | Behavior |
|---|---|
| Component icon | Hover to see the component version. |
| Title | The component kind, in sentence case. |
| Versions menu | Appears when the component exists in more than one model version. Choosing a version swaps the component's definition and model reference to that version. |
| Search | Narrows the form to matching fields. When nothing matches, the form says so. |
| Help | Shows the component's own description from its schema. |
| Expand and collapse | Switches the panel width between 32 rem and 45 rem. |
| Delete | Removes the component immediately, with no confirmation. |

Switching versions keeps your configuration values as they are. Kanvas does not migrate them, and validation then flags any value the new version does not accept. The switch also replaces custom styling with the new version's defaults.

### The tabs

A tab strip on the left appears when two or more tabs apply to the component. Which tabs are enabled depends on the capabilities the component's definition declares. Role permissions do not decide this. A tab that does not apply appears dimmed.

| Tab | What it holds |
|---|---|
| Config | The component's specification, as a form built from its JSON schema. |
| Labels | Key-value maps for labels and annotations. Not offered for alias components. |
| Json Schema | A read-only view of the component definition, with an Open in Registry button. |
| Relationships | The relationships this component participates in, grouped by kind, with a Show only active switch. |

Comment components open a chat thread instead of tabs.

### Required fields, defaults, and validation

- Fields are rendered from the component's schema, and defaults come from the schema. A namespaced kind shows a Namespace field that defaults to `default`.
- A red asterisk marks a required field. An empty required field shows "This field is required". Kanvas enforces first-level required fields up front, and an object whose children are all optional is not treated as required.
- The form does not validate as you type. Kanvas validates each changed component against its JSON schema after the change. Errors appear as a small red triangle beside the field label, with the messages in its tooltip, and the field is outlined.
- The component also shows a validation warning badge on the canvas, so an error you scrolled past stays visible after you close the panel. See [Component Badges]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/component-badges/index.md" >}}).

### How edits are saved

There is no Apply button. Kanvas writes an edit to the design 300 ms after you stop typing. Each write triggers three follow-ups: the design autosaves after a 3 second pause, the component is validated, and relationships are re-evaluated. Configuration that a relationship controls can therefore change shortly after you edit a related component. See [Policy Evaluation]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/relationship-evaluation/index.md" >}}).

Undo reverses configuration changes like any other edit. See [Saving Designs]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/designs/saving-designs/index.md" >}}).

### Alias components

An alias component stands for one field inside its parent component. Its form edits that field of the parent, using the field's sub-schema, and omits the Labels tab. Deleting an alias clears that field's configuration on the parent.

## Lock, duplicate, copy, and delete

Right-click a component to open its action menu. Items appear only when they apply.

| Action | Shortcut | Behavior |
|---|---|---|
| Lock and Unlock | - | Fixes the component's position so it cannot be dragged. Configuration, labels, and style stay editable. The lock is saved with the design. |
| Duplicate | <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>/<kbd>Cmd</kbd>+<kbd>D</kbd> | Creates a copy offset 50 px right and 50 px down, with a new id. Relationships between duplicated components are copied too. Names do not change. |
| Copy | <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>/<kbd>Cmd</kbd>+<kbd>C</kbd> | Copies the component. The menu item copies one component without relationships. |
| Delete | <kbd>Delete</kbd> or <kbd>Backspace</kbd> | Removes the component. Relationships that touched it are marked deleted, and the next evaluation reverses their effects on configuration. |
| Reset styles | - | Restores the model's default appearance. |
| Move Out of Parent | - | Detaches a component from the parent it sits in. |

The menu labels Delete as <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>/<kbd>Cmd</kbd>+<kbd>Delete</kbd>, but <kbd>Delete</kbd> or <kbd>Backspace</kbd> alone performs the deletion.

Other items appear in Operator mode, such as terminal, log, and performance sessions. See [Operator]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/operator/index.md" >}}).

### Style a component

A floating toolbar above a selected component offers the controls the component declares: shape (24 outlines), fill color with opacity from 0 to 1, border color, style, and thickness from 0 to 25, layer order, label, external link, image, and animation (none, blink, ripple, bounce, or pulse). Each control is shown only when the component supports it.

## Copy and paste across designs

| Task | Shortcut |
|---|---|
| Select every component | <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>/<kbd>Cmd</kbd>+<kbd>A</kbd> |
| Select several | Hold <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>/<kbd>Cmd</kbd> and drag a selection box, or <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>/<kbd>Cmd</kbd>+click each one |
| Copy the selection | <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>/<kbd>Cmd</kbd>+<kbd>C</kbd> |
| Paste | <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>/<kbd>Cmd</kbd>+<kbd>V</kbd> |
| Undo and redo | <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>/<kbd>Cmd</kbd>+<kbd>Z</kbd>, <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>/<kbd>Cmd</kbd>+<kbd>Y</kbd> or <kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>Z</kbd> |

A keyboard copy carries the selected components with their configuration, styles, and labels, plus every relationship whose two ends are both in the selection. Kanvas writes this to the system clipboard, so you can paste into another design, another browser tab, or another Kanvas session. Paste lands at the pointer when it is over the canvas and at the canvas center otherwise. The pasted group keeps its layout, and every id is regenerated.

Browsers allow clipboard access only after a user gesture. If the browser denies access, paste does nothing and shows no message. Use the keyboard shortcuts. The full list is in [Keyboard Shortcuts]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/keyboard-shortcuts.md" >}}).

## Limits and errors

- A design has a maximum number of components that depends on your plan. Layer5 Cloud enforces it when you save or import, not when you add a component. A save over the limit is rejected with a 403 response. Drawn objects such as shapes and text boxes count as components. See [Designs and Components]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/designs/index.md" >}}) for the per-plan values.
- When zoomed out, the canvas hides text, labels, and badges and prompts you to zoom in before interacting with elements.

## See also

- [Relationships]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/relationships/index.md" >}}): what the Relationships tab lists.
- [Tool Modes]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/tool-modes/index.md" >}}): every mouse interaction available on the canvas.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Create Your First Design"
url: /kanvas/getting-started/starting-scratch/index.md
description: Build a small web application design from an empty canvas, connect its components through relationships, and save it, while learning how Kanvas models and stores designs.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

In this tutorial you build a small web application design in Kanvas Designer: a Deployment that runs the application, a ConfigMap that holds its settings, and a Service that exposes it. You start from an empty canvas, connect the components, and save the result. The saved design is the starting point for [Deploy and Observe Your First Design]({{< ref "kanvas/getting-started/design-to-deployment/index.md" >}}).

Along the way you learn what a design is made of, how relationships express the way components depend on each other, and when and how Kanvas saves your work.

## Before you begin

- Open Kanvas in Designer mode, either at kanvas.new or in a Meshery you run. Either works for this tutorial. If you plan to deploy the design in the next tutorial, start in a Meshery you run so the design is already where you need it. See [Where do you want to work?]({{< ref "kanvas/getting-started/_index.md#where-do-you-want-to-work" >}}).
- Work inside a specific organization. Kanvas does not create designs while the "all organizations" scope is selected.

## Step 1: Start an empty design

Start a new design. Kanvas opens an empty canvas and names the design "Untitled Design".

That default name matters. Kanvas does not save a new design that has an empty canvas and no name of its own. A new design becomes saveable as soon as it has at least one component, or a name that is not empty and is not "Untitled Design".

Give the design a name that describes its purpose, such as `web-app`. A meaningful name makes the design easy to find later, and Kanvas also uses it to label the design's deploy steps and its Operator view.

**What you should see:** an empty canvas with your design name in place of "Untitled Design".

## Step 2: Add the application components

A **component** is one piece of infrastructure in your design: a single, typed resource such as a Kubernetes Deployment, Service, or ConfigMap, together with its configuration. Each component comes from a model, and many components exist in more than one version. Choose the version that matches the cluster you intend to deploy to.

Add three components from the Kubernetes model to the canvas:

- a **Deployment**, which will run the web application,
- a **ConfigMap**, which will hold the application's settings,
- a **Service**, which will give the application a stable network endpoint.

Kanvas renders each component on the canvas as soon as you place it. Arrange them so you can see all three.

Not everything on a canvas is infrastructure. Shapes, text, and drawings that you add for explanation are **annotation-only**: they make the design easier to read but are not resources. A connector you draw for illustration is an annotation edge for the same reason. Use annotations freely to document a design; they do not change what the design describes.

**What you should see:** three components on the canvas, each showing its kind.

## Step 3: Configure each component

Every component carries configuration based on its schema. Open a component's configuration panel to set its fields. The canvas updates as you change them.

Configure the three components so they refer to each other:

1. On the **ConfigMap**, set a name such as `web-app-config` and add one key, for example `GREETING`.
2. On the **Deployment**, set a name, a container image (for example `nginx`), and a label such as `app: web-app` on its pod template. Reference the ConfigMap by its name so the container reads its settings from it.
3. On the **Service**, add the same label (`app: web-app`) and set a port.

These references are the same ones you would write in Kubernetes manifests. Kanvas evaluates them to work out how the components relate.

**What you should see:** each component shows the name you gave it.

## Step 4: Connect the components with relationships

A **relationship** describes how two components interact or depend on each other. Kanvas draws relationships on the canvas as edges between components, or as nesting when one component contains another. Relationships fall into families:

- **Edge relationships** describe interaction between components. A Service in front of a Deployment is a network relationship. A Deployment that reads a ConfigMap is a reference relationship: one component refers to another by name.
- **Hierarchical relationships** describe containment and inheritance, such as a Namespace that must exist before the Pods inside it.

Relationships come from two sources: configuration you set, and connections you make on the canvas. Components that carry the same label form a label-match relationship automatically, so the Service and the Deployment in this design are now related. You can also drag a connection line from one component to a compatible target to create an edge relationship yourself. [Relationships]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/relationships/index.md" >}}) describes every kind and what each one means.

Check that your design shows a relationship between the Service and the Deployment, and one between the Deployment and the ConfigMap. If one is missing, compare the names and labels you set in Step 3, or drag a connection between the two components.

In large designs, Kanvas can skip drawing some relationships of one kind once that kind passes its rendering limit. When that happens it shows a warning of the form "Skipped rendering of N &lt;kind&gt; relationships due to limit of M". The relationships still belong to the design; only their drawing is skipped.

**What you should see:** the Deployment connected to both the Service and the ConfigMap.

## Step 5: Save the design

Kanvas saves for you. Once the design is saveable, Kanvas saves pending changes 3 seconds after you stop editing. If a save fails, Kanvas retries with a doubling delay (3 seconds, then 6, then 12, and so on) for up to 100 attempts.

Three things happen when a design is saved:

- **A new version is created.** Every save increments the design's version, so a design accumulates a history of versions as you work.
- **A new design starts as public.** The first save of a new design sets its visibility to public. Later saves keep whatever visibility the design has at that point. Designs can also be private or published; [Saving designs]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/designs/saving-designs/index.md" >}}) explains each.
- **Your plan's component limit is checked.** Each plan sets a maximum number of components per design, and Kanvas checks it on every save and import. A design over the limit is not saved; Kanvas reports "Design exceeds maximum limit of N components supported by your current plan". Reduce the number of components or upgrade the plan. See [Layer5 pricing](https://layer5.io/pricing) for the limit on each plan.

This three-component design is well within every plan's limit.

**What you should see:** your design saved under its new name, with no unsaved changes pending.

## Optional: Merge another design into this one

You can bring an existing design into the canvas you are working on. Kanvas merges its components and relationships into the current design and leaves the original design unchanged. Use this to assemble a larger system from designs you already have. See [Merging designs]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/designs/import-designs/index.md" >}}).

## What you built

You now have a saved design named `web-app` that describes a web application:

- three infrastructure components, each configured from its schema,
- relationships that record how the Service reaches the Deployment and how the Deployment reads the ConfigMap,
- a version history that grows with every save.

You also learned the core rules of saving: a new design needs a component or a real name before it can be saved, autosave runs 3 seconds after you stop editing, a new design starts as public, and your plan limits the number of components in a design.

## Next

Take this design to a cluster in [Deploy and Observe Your First Design]({{< ref "kanvas/getting-started/design-to-deployment/index.md" >}}). You will validate it, dry-run it, deploy it, and watch the resulting resources in Operator mode.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Designs and Components"
url: /kanvas/concepts/designs/index.md
description: What a Kanvas design is, how it is saved, versioned, and shared, what components are, and how a design maps to the resources it deploys.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

A design is the unit of work in Kanvas. It is a declarative description of infrastructure that you author on a canvas, save as a versioned document, share with others, and deploy to your clusters. Components are the building blocks of a design: some represent real infrastructure that Kanvas deploys, and others are annotations that only explain the design. Knowing which is which, and how a design behaves when you save, share, and deploy it, tells you exactly what Kanvas will do with your work.

## What a design contains

A design holds four kinds of content:

- **Components** - the infrastructure resources in the design, such as Kubernetes Deployments, Services, or cloud provider resources, each with its own configuration.
- **Relationships** - the connections between components and what those connections mean. See [Relationships]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/relationships/index.md" >}}).
- **Configuration** - the settings of each component.
- **Annotations** - shapes, arrows, text, and icons that document the design. Kanvas never deploys annotations.

## How designs are saved

### Naming and the saveability rule

A new, unsaved design is named "Untitled Design". Kanvas saves a new design only when it has at least one component, or a name that is not empty and not "Untitled Design". An empty, unnamed canvas is not saved. Once a design has been saved, it can always be saved again, even after you remove every component.

You cannot create a design while your organization scope is set to all organizations. Select a single organization first.

### Autosave

Kanvas saves pending changes automatically 3 seconds after you stop editing. If a save fails, Kanvas retries with a doubling delay (3 seconds, then 6, then 12, and so on) for up to 100 attempts.

### Versions

Every save creates a new version of the design. You never overwrite a previous version by saving.

## Who can see a design

A design has one of three visibility values:

| Visibility | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Public | Visible beyond its owner. Every newly created design starts as public. |
| Private | Visible to its owner. Other organization members need the "View Designs" permission to view private designs. |
| Published | Listed in the catalog. Unpublishing a design sets its visibility back to private. |

Saving an existing design never changes its visibility. Non-owners read private and published designs only when the design is shared with them or when they hold administrator rights.

## Components

[Components](https://docs.meshery.io/concepts/logical/components) in Kanvas fall into two categories, distinguished by whether Kanvas can orchestrate them during deployment.

### Semantic components (orchestratable)

Semantic components represent actual infrastructure resources. They map directly to real infrastructure elements, so Kanvas can create, configure, and manage their lifecycle during deployment. Examples include:

- Kubernetes resources (Pods, Services, Deployments)
- Cloud provider resources (AWS S3 buckets, Azure Functions)
- Infrastructure components (load balancers, databases)

Semantic components are either built in, like the Kubernetes components, or custom components that you [create](https://docs.meshery.io/guides/configuration-management/creating-models).

![Animation of a semantic component being styled on the Kanvas canvas](images/component_style.gif)

### Non-semantic components (annotation-only)

Non-semantic components are visual and organizational elements that document and organize your design. They do not represent deployable resources, and Kanvas ignores them during deployment. Examples include:

- Text boxes and comments
- Shapes and containers for grouping
- Arrows and lines
- Labels and tags

{{< alert title="Visual distinction rule" type="info" >}}
Semantic components have a background, which marks them as real infrastructure resources. Non-semantic components have a transparent background, which marks them as visual aids only.
{{< /alert >}}

Both kinds support visual customization. You can change a Kubernetes Pod's color, modify its shape, or replace its background logo without changing what Kanvas deploys.

### How components are organized

Kanvas draws semantic components from integration models. Kubernetes is the most common, and every integration model, such as KEDA, Prometheus, or AWS, provides components with the same orchestratable capabilities. Kanvas organizes them in a three-level hierarchy:

1. **Categories** - high-level groups, such as "Cloud Native Network" or "Database".
2. **Integration models** - specific technologies, such as Prometheus or Kubernetes.
3. **Components** - the deployable building blocks within a model.

For the full list of technologies Kanvas integrates, see the [integrations directory](https://docs.meshery.io/extensions/integrations).

### Kubernetes component conventions

Kubernetes components follow a consistent visual system, so you can identify a resource kind at a glance.

![Animation of Kubernetes components with blue backgrounds and distinct outer shapes on the Kanvas canvas](images/k8s_style.gif)

**Color and structure**

- Kubernetes component icons use a distinctive blue background.
- Every icon has the same structure: an outer shape filled with blue that encloses a white inner symbol.
- The white inner symbol identifies the specific Kubernetes kind.

**Shape as an indicator**

The outer shape identifies the component's role:

- **Triangles** mark core networking resources, such as `Service` and `APIService`.
- **Hexagons** mark foundational workload controllers, such as `StatefulSet`.
- **Unique polygons** mark specialized resources, such as `Endpoints`, `PriorityClass`, or `ValidatingWebhookConfiguration`.

### Non-semantic palettes

Kanvas provides four palettes of annotation-only components. None of them is ever deployed.

![Animation of non-semantic shapes being placed and styled on the Kanvas canvas](images/shape_style.gif)

**Generic shapes** cover general-purpose diagramming.

![The Shapes palette in Kanvas, showing generic annotation shapes](images/shapes.png)

**Arrows** show direction or create simple visual annotations. They are static shapes for illustration only. To represent a functional relationship between semantic components, such as network traffic or a dependency, use an edge instead; see the [edges shape guide](https://docs.meshery.io/extensions/edges-shape-guide).

![The Arrows palette in Kanvas, showing static arrow shapes](images/arrows.png)

**Flowchart shapes** document a design's logic and flow with standard flowchart symbols.

![The Flowchart palette in Kanvas, showing standard flowchart shapes](images/flowchart.png)

**Simple Line Icons** add icons for annotation and visual emphasis.

![The Simple Line Icons palette in Kanvas](images/simple_line_icons.png)

### One component, several representations

A semantic component looks different depending on where it appears. The Deployment component is a good example:

1. On the canvas, it has its distinctive shape and badge.

   <img src="./images/deployment-shape.png" alt="The Deployment component on the Kanvas canvas, showing its shape and badge" style="width:30%; height:auto;" />

2. In a component selection panel, it appears as an icon.

   ![The Deployment icon in a component selection panel](images/deployment-icon.png)

3. In a cluster resource overview, it appears as a resource entry.

   ![The Deployment component in a cluster resource overview](images/deployment-dashboard.png)

To practice reading designs, see [interpreting Meshery designs](https://cloud.layer5.io/academy/learning-paths/mastering-meshery/introduction-to-meshery?chapter=interpreting-meshery-designs) in the Layer5 Academy.

## Limits as shipped

The limits below describe Kanvas as it ships today. Current plans and their entitlements are listed at [layer5.io/pricing](https://layer5.io/pricing).

### Components per design

Kanvas enforces a maximum number of components per design whenever you save or import a design. The limit depends on your organization's plan and is the same for monthly and annual billing.

| Plan | Components per design |
|---|---|
| Personal | 100 |
| Team Designer | 200 |
| Team Operator | 100 |
| Enterprise | 300 |

When a design exceeds the limit, the save or import is rejected with HTTP 403 and the message "Design exceeds maximum limit of N components supported by your current plan", where N is your plan's limit. To proceed, reduce the number of components in the design or upgrade your plan.

If your organization is not entitled to add components to a design at all, the save fails with HTTP 500 and the message "Org is not entitled to adding components to a design".

### Files dropped on the canvas

You can drop files directly onto the canvas:

- **Image and text files** up to 500 KB are accepted. Larger files are rejected. The rejection message says "Your current plan allows files up to 500 KB", but the 500 KB limit is the same on every plan.
- **Infrastructure-as-code files**, such as Kubernetes manifests, are imported as a design.

## How a design maps to deployed resources

When Kanvas deploys a design, every resource it creates carries the identity of its source design:

| Metadata | Key | Value |
|---|---|---|
| Label | `design.meshery.io/id` | The id of the source design |
| Annotation | `design.meshery.io/version` | The version of the design that was deployed |
| Annotation | `component.meshery.io/id` | The id of the component in the design |

A resource that carries the design id label is managed by Meshery. Because the label is a standard Kubernetes label, you can also select a design's resources with your own tooling.

This metadata powers Operator's per-design view. A design's view is named "&lt;design name&gt;-View" and shows only the resources whose design id label matches that design, so you see exactly what one design produced across your clusters. See [Operator]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/operator/index.md" >}}).


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Explore Pods"
url: /kanvas/tutorials/kubernetes/kubernetes-pods/index.md
description: Design, deploy, expose, and inspect a standalone NGINX Pod to learn how a Kanvas component becomes a running Kubernetes object.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

In this tutorial you build a single NGINX Pod in Kanvas, deploy it to a live cluster, expose it with a NodePort Service, and inspect the running Pod in Operator: its details, a shell inside its container, and its log stream. A Pod is the smallest unit Kubernetes schedules, and every workload controller you meet later (Deployments, StatefulSets, CronJobs) exists to create and replace Pods. Working with a bare Pod first shows you exactly what those controllers automate.

The Pod in this tutorial is standalone: no controller watches it, so if it fails or is deleted, nothing recreates it. That trade-off suits learning and does not suit production.

## What you will learn

- A Pod wraps one or more containers that share a network address and are scheduled together onto one node.
- A Kanvas component is a Kubernetes object in design form: its configuration is the object's manifest, and Deploy turns it into a live object.
- Labels identify objects, and a Service's selector uses labels to find the Pods it sends traffic to.
- Deploying a design again updates the cluster in place instead of creating duplicates.
- Operator shows what actually runs in the cluster, which is the ground truth when it differs from the design.

## Before you begin

- **A cluster-backed environment.** Use Meshery Playground (https://play.meshery.io), a shared live cluster, or a self-hosted Meshery with a connected Kubernetes cluster. Hosted kanvas.new has no cluster actions; Validate, Deploy, and Undeploy there open a prompt to self-host instead.
- **An environment that holds your cluster's connection.** Deploy targets Meshery environments and the Kubernetes connections assigned to them. See [Environments](https://docs.meshery.io/concepts/logical/environments).
- **Operator mode for the inspection phases.** Operator reads the cluster through Meshery Operator and MeshSync, which must run in the cluster. Where Operator mode is turned off, its switch is disabled; the deploy summary still confirms each object.
- **A unique prefix.** Playground is shared with other users. Pick a short prefix, such as your handle, and use it in every name and label. This tutorial uses `alex`.

You need basic familiarity with containers and Kubernetes manifests. You do not need to write YAML.

## The scenario

You build two objects in one design:

```text
Service  alex-nginx-np   type NodePort, port 80, selector app=alex-nginx
    |
    |  Network relationship (traffic flows from the Service to the Pod)
    v
Pod      alex-nginx      label app=alex-nginx
    +-- container nginx  image nginx:latest, port 80
```

You deploy the Pod first, inspect it, then add the Service and deploy again.

## Build the Pod

1. Create a new design and name it `alex-pods`. Kanvas saves the design automatically as soon as it has a name or a component; there is no Save button.
2. Add a **Pod** component. The Kubernetes icon in the dock lists every Kubernetes kind, and the component palette search finds it too. The component's configurator opens as soon as the Pod lands on the canvas.
3. Set the Pod's name to `alex-nginx` and leave the namespace as `default`.
4. Add one entry to the Pod's containers: name `nginx`, image `nginx:latest`, and a container port of `80`. Containers is a list, so each entry opens in its own form.
5. In the configurator's **Labels** tab, add the label `app` with the value `alex-nginx`.

**What just happened.** The configurator form is generated from the Pod's schema in the Meshery registry, so its fields are the Kubernetes API fields. Required fields carry a red asterisk. Each edit is written to the design after a short pause; Kanvas then checks the changed component against its schema and marks problems beside the field. Those marks are warnings and never block you. The component you built is equivalent to this manifest:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: alex-nginx
  namespace: default
  labels:
    app: alex-nginx
spec:
  containers:
    - name: nginx
      image: nginx:latest
      ports:
        - containerPort: 80
```

**Check your work.** The Pod sits on the canvas without a warning badge. If a badge with an error count appears on the component, select it to see each error; it leads to the field that needs attention.

## Check the design before deploying

1. Run **Validate** from the design's **Actions** menu.
2. Run **Dry Run** from the same menu.

**What just happened.** Validate runs in your browser. It checks each component against its schema and never contacts the cluster, so it cannot catch cluster-side problems such as a missing namespace or a name already in use. Its errors are advisory. Dry Run sends each object to the cluster's API server as a server-side dry run: the API server applies its full validation and admission checks and persists nothing. Dry Run from the Actions menu targets the clusters selected in Meshery's context selector.

**Check your work.** Validate reports `No validation errors.` and Dry Run reports `No deployment errors.` A Pod without any container fails the dry run with a `Field Value Required` error on the containers field; add the container and run it again.

## Deploy and verify

1. Run **Deploy** from the **Actions** menu. The Deploy workflow has five steps: validation, choosing deployment targets, a dry run, a final review, and a summary.
2. Select the environment that holds your cluster's connection. Selecting an environment targets every Kubernetes connection assigned to it.
3. Continue past the dry run once it reports no errors, then confirm the deployment.

**What just happened.** Meshery Server turned each component into a Kubernetes object and sent it to every selected cluster. For each object it creates the object, or replaces it in place if an object of that kind and name already exists. It labels every object it applies with `design.meshery.io/id=<design id>` and records the design version and component id as annotations. That label is how Operator finds the objects that came from this design.

**Check your work.** The summary lists `Deployed Pod "alex-nginx"`, and a notification reads `Deployment completed for design 'alex-pods'.` Read the per-object rows, not only the notification: the notification reads "completed" even when individual objects failed, and failures appear only as `Failed to deploy` rows with an error card. If the summary spinner never finishes, the request failed before it reached the cluster, most often because your session expired; reload Kanvas, sign in, and deploy again.

## Inspect the Pod in Operator

1. Switch to **Operator**, either with the mode switch or with **Open In Operator** on the deploy summary. With the design open, Operator shows a view scoped to this design: only objects that carry this design's id label.
2. Select the `alex-nginx` Pod to open its details panel, and switch the panel from **Summary** to **Details** to see every field.

**What just happened.** Operator draws the objects that MeshSync reports from the cluster, not the objects in your design. For a Pod, the details panel shows its phase as a status chip, the Pod IP, the host IP of its node, its QoS class, restart count, and each container's image, ports, start time, and image pull policy. The QoS class is `BestEffort` because the container sets no resource requests or limits. The view is a snapshot: Operator loads it when you open a view, change a filter, or change the selected cluster, and it does not update on its own. To see later changes, change a filter or switch back to Operator.

**Check your work.** The status chip reads `Running`. A `Pending` Pod is not scheduled yet or is still pulling its image; load a fresh snapshot after a few seconds. If it stays `Pending`, the container status shows why, for example an image pull failure caused by a mistyped image name. If the canvas reads `No data available for the current view`, the snapshot found no objects with this design's label: MeshSync has not reported the Pod yet, or the deploy failed. If it reads `No Kubernetes context selected`, select your cluster in Meshery's context selector.

## Open a shell and stream logs

1. Start a terminal on the Pod with **Initiate Terminal Session**, which is in the Pod's right-click menu and in the details panel header. A terminal panel opens with one tab per container in the Pod.
2. Run `hostname`. It prints `alex-nginx`, because a Pod's name is the hostname of its containers.
3. Run `cat /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html` to read the page NGINX serves.
4. Start a log stream on the same Pod with **Initiate Log Session**. A log tab opens in the same panel.

**What just happened.** Kanvas asks MeshSync, inside the cluster, to open `/bin/sh` in the container through the Kubernetes exec API, the same mechanism `kubectl exec` uses. The shell runs with MeshSync's cluster permissions. The terminal sends each line when you press Enter and `Ctrl+C` sends an interrupt, so line-based commands work and full-screen programs such as `vim`, `top`, and `less` do not. Images without `/bin/sh`, such as distroless images, cannot open a shell.

The log tab shows the last 1,000 lines from every container in the Pod and then follows new output. Each line starts with `[alex-nginx:nginx]` and a Kubernetes timestamp; stdout and stderr are combined. NGINX's container entrypoint writes its startup messages here. Closing the panel hides it without ending the sessions; the trash icon on a tab ends that session.

**Check your work.** The shell prints the Pod name and the HTML page. If the terminal tab stays blank, the session did not start, and Kanvas does not display the reason. The usual causes are a container without `/bin/sh`, a Pod that is not `Running`, or MeshSync not connected. When a Pod is deleted, its log stream stops without a notice.

## Expose the Pod with a NodePort Service

1. Switch back to **Designer** and add a **Service** component named `alex-nginx-np`.
2. Set the Service type to `NodePort` and add one port with port `80` and target port `80`. Leave the node port empty so Kubernetes assigns a free one from the node port range (30000 to 32767 by default). On a shared cluster, a fixed node port that someone else holds fails the dry run.
3. Set the Service's selector to `app: alex-nginx`, the same label the Pod carries.
4. Draw a **Network** relationship from the Service to the Pod. Edge handles appear when you hover a component; choose the network option and drag to the Pod. Compatible targets show a green outline while you drag, and releasing anywhere else creates nothing.
5. Run **Deploy** again with the same environment.

**What just happened.** Kubernetes routes Service traffic by the selector alone: every `Running` Pod whose labels match the selector becomes a backend of the Service. The Network relationship records the same connection in the design so that readers of the diagram see where traffic flows, and its edge shows the port values it reads from both components. Kanvas evaluates relationships after every change, and a relationship's registry definition can copy designated fields from one component to the other. The selector you set is what Kubernetes acts on, so confirm it in the Service's configurator after you draw the edge.

Deploying the same design again creates objects that are missing and replaces objects that already exist. The Service is created; the Pod is submitted unchanged and keeps running. Kubernetes treats almost every field of a running Pod as immutable, so changing a Pod beyond its container image means deleting it and creating it again, one of the reasons real workloads use Deployments.

**Check your work.** The summary lists `Deployed Service "alex-nginx-np"`. Switch to Operator and select the Service. Its details show the service type `NodePort`, a cluster IP, the selector `app=alex-nginx`, and, under its connections, the ports including the node port Kubernetes assigned. The Service is reachable at `http://<node IP>:<node port>` from any machine that can reach the node; the Pod's host IP is one such node address. In Playground, node IPs are often not reachable from your browser. The assigned node port still confirms that Kubernetes exposed the Pod.

## Clean up

Run **Undeploy** from the **Actions** menu and select the same environment. The Undeploy workflow has the same five steps as Deploy, and its dry run checks the deletions.

Undeploy deletes each component's object by kind, name, and namespace: here, the Pod and the Service. It matches by name, not by the design label, so an object with the same kind, name, and namespace that someone else created is deleted too. That is another reason to use unique names on a shared cluster. Namespaces are removed only when the design contains a Namespace component. If an object is already gone, the dry-run step reports it as not found; select the bypass option to continue, because the real undeploy ignores missing objects.

The design itself stays in your account. Delete it from the design's file menu if you no longer need it. Deleting a design never removes objects from a cluster, so undeploy first.

## What you learned

- A Pod is one or more containers that share a hostname and network address. A standalone Pod has no controller, so nothing replaces it.
- Each Kanvas component maps to one Kubernetes object, and its configurator edits that object's manifest.
- Validate checks schemas in the browser; Dry Run asks the cluster's API server; Deploy creates or replaces each object and labels it with the design id.
- A Service finds its Pods by label selector. The Network relationship documents the connection in the design.
- Operator shows a snapshot of what runs in the cluster, and it is where you open a shell and stream logs.

## Next steps

- Continue with [Explore Deployments]({{< ref "kanvas/tutorials/kubernetes/kubernetes-deployments/index.md" >}}) to let a controller manage your Pods.
- Read [Deploying designs]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/deploying/deploying-designs/index.md" >}}) for every option in the Deploy workflow.
- Read [Operator]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/operator/index.md" >}}) to understand how Operator sees a cluster, and [Interactive terminal]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/operating/interactive-terminal/index.md" >}}) and [Log streaming]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/operating/log-streaming/index.md" >}}) for the full session behavior.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Feature Availability by Plan"
url: /kanvas/reference/feature-availability/index.md
description: Which Kanvas capabilities each Layer5 plan includes, and the role, provider, and hosting conditions that also decide whether a capability is available to you.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

This page tells you which Kanvas capabilities each Layer5 plan includes. Your plan is the first condition for using a capability, not the only one: your role, your provider, and where you run Kanvas also decide what you can do. Those conditions follow the matrix.

## Plans

The matrix has one column for each of the four Layer5 plans: Free, Team Designer, Team Operator, and Enterprise. Entitlements follow your organization's plan. Current pricing and plan details are listed at [layer5.io/pricing](https://layer5.io/pricing).

## Reading the matrix

- A check mark means the plan includes the capability.
- A dash means the plan does not include it.
- Each table covers one category of capability. The **What it does** column describes the capability in one sentence.

The matrix is refreshed automatically from the Layer5 product feature list. It lists the capabilities that have a documentation page. A capability that does not appear here is not necessarily unavailable; check the page that documents it.

## Capabilities by plan

{{< feature-tiers categories="Configuration Management|Lifecycle Management|Kanvas|Collaboration|Performance Management" >}}

## Availability depends on more than your plan

A capability is available to you only when all of the following hold: your plan includes it, your role grants it, your provider supports it, and your Kanvas deployment can reach a cluster when the capability needs one.

### Your role

Your organization assigns you roles, and each role grants a set of permissions. Kanvas checks a permission before it offers Validate, Dry run, Deploy, Undeploy, Share, and Publish. An action your role does not grant is not offered, even when your plan includes it. See [Permissions by Role]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/permissions.md" >}}) for which role holds which permission.

### Your provider

Kanvas stores designs, views, the catalog, and sharing records with a remote provider, Layer5 Cloud. Meshery can also run with a local provider, which has no remote service behind it. Under the local provider, every provider-bound feature, including views, the catalog, sharing, and support requests, returns HTTP 501 Not Implemented. Run Meshery with a remote provider to use these features.

### Where you run Kanvas

The hosted Kanvas at [kanvas.new](https://kanvas.new) is for authoring designs. Every capability that needs a cluster requires a Meshery deployment that you run: the [Meshery Playground](https://playground.meshery.io) or your own self-hosted Meshery.

| Capability | kanvas.new | Meshery you run |
|---|---|---|
| Author and edit designs | Available | Available |
| Validate | Shows a prompt | Available |
| Dry run | Shows a prompt | Available |
| Deploy | Shows a prompt | Available |
| Undeploy | Shows a prompt | Available |
| Connect clusters | Shows a prompt | Available |
| Operator mode | Shows a prompt | Available |
| Share | Requires an account | Requires an account |
| Publish | Requires an account | Requires an account |

On kanvas.new, a cluster-bound capability opens a prompt that directs you to the Meshery Playground or a self-hosted Meshery deployment. Share and Publish open a sign-in prompt when you are not signed in. For why the hosted site differs, see [How Kanvas Works with Meshery and Layer5 Cloud]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/architecture/index.md" >}}).

## Limits by plan

Each plan caps the number of components in a single design, and Kanvas enforces the cap whenever you save or import a design. The limit for each plan and the error you receive when a design exceeds it are in [Components per design]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/designs/index.md#components-per-design" >}}).

## Support by plan

The support channels and response commitments each plan includes are listed in [Support channels by plan]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/help-and-support.md#support-channels-by-plan" >}}).


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Import and Merge Designs"
url: /kanvas/guides/designs/import-designs/index.md
description: Bring Kubernetes manifests, Helm charts, Docker Compose files, Kustomize projects, and Meshery designs into Kanvas, and merge one design into another.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Import turns an existing configuration into an editable design. Kanvas identifies the format from the file content, converts it to a Meshery design, and saves it as a new design in your account. A File Upload or URL Import does not keep the original file, so exporting later produces a new file from the current design. A GitHub import is different: the design stays bound to its source, as described in [Where the imported design lands](#where-the-imported-design-lands).

Import works in Designer mode. The import action is hidden in Operator mode.

## Choose how to import

| Method | Accepts | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Import dialog, File Upload | One local file | New design, or merge into the open design |
| Import dialog, URL Import | One direct http or https URL to a single file | New design, or merge into the open design |
| Drag or paste onto the canvas | One or more files | One new design per file, or a merge prompt if the canvas is not empty |
| Catalog clone or open | A published design | Copy of the design, see [Clone a Design]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/designs/cloning-a-design/index.md" >}}) |
| GitHub integration in Layer5 Cloud | Files and folders in a connected repository | One private design per valid file |

The URL must point at a file, not a repository, a chart repository, or a directory. Folders cannot be imported directly: compress a Kustomize project or Helm chart into a single archive first.

The import dialog takes a name (1 to 255 characters, default "Untitled Design"). Names are not required to be unique. If you leave the name empty, Kanvas uses the name inside the file, and drops use the file name.

## Supported formats

Kanvas accepts `.yml`, `.yaml`, `.json`, `.tar`, `.tar.gz`, `.tgz`, `.gz`, and `.zip`. Any other extension is rejected. Archives are extracted safely and entries that try to escape the archive directory are refused.

Kanvas decides the format by content, not by the file name, and takes the first match in this order:

1. **Meshery design.** A YAML or JSON design file, or an OCI image archive (`.tar`, `.tgz`, `.zip`) whose layers contain a design file. Only the first design in an archive is taken. An OCI archive without a design file fails.
2. **Kubernetes manifest.** A `.yml` or `.yaml` file with one or more documents. Unknown resource kinds are kept as generic objects.
3. **Helm chart.** A packaged chart archive. An uncompressed `.tar` is reported as needing gzip compression. Individual chart files such as `Chart.yaml` cannot be imported, and values overrides are not an import option.
4. **Docker Compose.** Compose services are first converted to Kubernetes resources, so the design contains Kubernetes components.
5. **Kustomize.** A single kustomization file, or an archive that contains `kustomization.yaml` and every file it references.

The full matrix is in [Supported Import and Export Formats]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/supported-formats.md" >}}).

## Import a file as a new design or merge it

When the canvas is empty, import loads the new design. When a design is open, the dialog offers **Import as new** and **Merge into current**.

- **Import as new** saves the file as a design and opens it. If the open design has unsaved changes, the browser asks you to confirm before leaving. Declining cancels the load, but the imported design stays saved in your account.
- **Merge into current** saves the file as its own design, then appends its components and relationships to the open design.

Files dropped on a non-empty canvas raise a **Merge Design** prompt that names the incoming design and its component count. It offers Cancel, Open as new, and Merge into current. Cancel does not delete the design the import already saved.

Dropping several files imports each as a separate design. The import dialog processes a single file at a time.

## How a merge behaves

Merging happens in the editor and changes only the open design.

- **Identity.** Every component and relationship in the incoming design receives a new identifier. Kanvas does not match or de-duplicate against existing components, so merging the same design twice doubles its components.
- **Preserved.** Names, kinds, configuration, styles, and the internal layout of the incoming block.
- **Placement.** The block's top-left corner moves to the drop position when you dropped a file. Otherwise it lands 50 pixels right and 50 pixels down from its original coordinates, and it can overlap existing components.
- **Not carried over.** The incoming design's name, id, version, visibility, catalog data, layer preferences, and workspace. The open design keeps its own.
- **After the merge.** Relationship evaluation runs as for any edit, and autosave persists the result after three seconds. If the merged design exceeds your plan's component limit, the save fails and the merged components remain unsaved on the canvas. See [Save Designs]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/designs/saving-designs/index.md" >}}).

Merging needs no permission key, but the incoming design must be one you can read: your own, public, published, or shared with you.

## Where the imported design lands

The imported design is owned by you, placed in your selected workspace, public, at version 0.0.1, and records its detected source type. Imports from a GitHub repository are the exception: each file becomes a private design named after the file. The design records the repository and file path it came from, and the imported file itself is stored with the design. Re-importing, refreshing, and viewing that source are covered in [Connect GitHub]({{< ref "cloud/guides/integrations/github-integration/index.md" >}}#manage-imported-designs). GitHub imports read each file from the repository's default branch. The stored file is not offered for download, so exporting still produces a new file from the current design. Invalid files in a selection are reported per path and do not stop valid files from importing.

The components-per-design plan limit applies to URL imports and to every save. GitHub imports are not checked at import time. They are checked the first time the design is saved.

## URL import limits

The server fetches a URL under these limits:

- Only http and https, checked again on every redirect, with at most 5 redirects.
- 10 seconds to connect and 30 seconds for the request.
- 16 MiB maximum body.
- Destinations that resolve to loopback, private, or link-local addresses are refused.

## Failures

Every failed import shows the same message, `Failed to import design "<name>"`, whether the cause is an unrecognized format, an invalid archive, a plan limit, or an unreachable server. Nothing is saved when the server rejects the file. A failed merge shows `Failed to merge design: <reason>`.

Files dropped on the canvas follow separate rules. Images and `.txt` files become canvas objects, not designs, and files over 500 KB are rejected whatever your plan. Archive types RAR and 7Z pass the drop check but fail at import. Other file types are ignored without a message.

## Related

- [Save Designs]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/designs/saving-designs/index.md" >}}) covers plan limits and failures after an import.
- [GitHub Integration]({{< ref "cloud/guides/integrations/github-integration/index.md" >}}) covers connecting a repository.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Open an Interactive Terminal"
url: /kanvas/guides/operating/interactive-terminal/index.md
description: Open shell sessions into the containers of a running pod from the Operator canvas, and know what the terminal can and cannot do.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The interactive terminal opens a shell inside a running container without leaving the Operator canvas. Use it for last-mile diagnosis that logs and status cannot answer: testing connectivity from inside a pod, reading a mounted file, or checking an injected environment variable. It is a browser-based equivalent of `kubectl exec`, scoped to the resource you selected.

## Before you start

- **Operator mode on a Meshery you run.** The hosted kanvas.new site does not offer Operator mode. See [How Kanvas Works with Meshery and Layer5 Cloud]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/architecture/index.md" >}}).
- **A connected cluster with Meshery Operator deployed.** Meshery Operator runs MeshSync and a message broker in the cluster. MeshSync executes the shell, and Meshery Server relays input and output through the broker. If any of the three is unavailable, the terminal does not connect (see [Failure modes](#failure-modes)).
- **A running container whose image contains `/bin/sh`.** Distroless images have no shell and cannot be used.

## Open a session

The action is named **Initiate Terminal Session** and is offered on **Pod** and **Container** resources only. Right-click the resource on the canvas, or select it and use the action in the header of the Details panel. The session starts immediately and the terminal panel opens at the bottom left of the canvas. There is no separate connect step.

What opens depends on what you selected:

| You select | Sessions opened |
|---|---|
| A pod | One session per container in the pod's `containers` list, each in its own tab. Init and ephemeral containers are not included. There is no prompt to choose a container. |
| A container | One session for that container. |

A node with an active session shows a terminal badge. Selecting the badge reopens the panel.

## Work in the terminal

Each tab is one shell session. The panel is draggable, minimizable to a dock icon with a session count, and keeps its scrollback (10,000 lines). Closing the panel with the close button hides it and leaves the sessions running. The trash icon on a tab ends that tab's session and removes the tab. Leaving Operator mode closes the panel.

The terminal edits your input in the browser and sends it to the container when you press Enter:

| Key | Behavior |
|---|---|
| Printable keys, Backspace | Edit the current line locally. |
| Enter | Sends the whole line to the shell. |
| Up, Down | Walk the history of lines typed in this tab. |
| Ctrl+C | Sends an interrupt to the running command. |
| Tab | Inserts four spaces. It does not trigger shell completion. |
| Other Ctrl, Alt, and Meta combinations | Ignored. |

Because input is line-based and the remote terminal is not resized when you resize the panel, commands that take over the screen, such as `vim`, `top`, and `less`, do not work. Use commands that print and exit: `ls`, `cat`, `env`, `ps aux`, `curl`, `nslookup`.

The search icon in the panel header opens a search field with next and previous controls for finding text in the scrollback.

## Limits and scope

| Item | Behavior |
|---|---|
| Sessions per container | One live session per container per user. Starting a second session for the same container does nothing and opens no new tab. |
| Concurrent sessions overall | No limit is enforced. |
| Different users | Each user gets an independent session, even on the same container. |
| Shell | Fixed to `/bin/sh` with a terminal attached. No bash fallback and no shell selection. |
| Identity in the container | The exec call runs with MeshSync's own Kubernetes access, not a per-user Kubernetes identity. Anyone who can open a terminal has the reach of the workload's container, so treat access to this action as access to the container. |
| Idle timeout, maximum duration | None. |
| Reconnect | None. If the connection between your browser and Meshery Server drops, the tab stays on screen but is dead. Close the tab and start a new session. |

## Who can use it

Kanvas does not hide or disable the action based on role or plan. The permission model lists **View Interactive Terminal** as an Operator capability for the Team Operator plan and above. See [Permissions by Role]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/permissions.md" >}}) and [Feature Availability]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/feature-availability.md" >}}) for the current role and plan matrix.

## Failure modes

| Symptom | Cause and fix |
|---|---|
| Panel shows `Failed to create terminal session` with a reason | The Kanvas extension could not be loaded by Meshery. The reason names the cause, for example a plugin built for a different Meshery version than the one you run. Install matching versions. |
| Toast `No container found to create term session` | The selected component lists no containers. |
| Empty tab, no prompt | Meshery Server could not reach MeshSync. Confirm the cluster shows as connected and that the broker is connected. Kanvas does not display the server's error text for terminal sessions. |
| Prompt never appears, or the shell prints an error | The container has no `/bin/sh`, is not in the Running phase, or was deleted. Errors raised while MeshSync opens the shell print in the terminal itself. |
| Session goes quiet after `exit` or a pod restart | The session ended on the cluster. Kanvas shows no closed message. Close the tab and start a new session. |

For cluster connection problems, see [Troubleshoot Kanvas]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/troubleshooting.md" >}}).

## Related

- [Stream Container Logs]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/operating/log-streaming/index.md" >}}) opens in the same panel as terminal sessions.
- [Operator]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/operator/index.md" >}}) explains where this data comes from.
- [Resource Details]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/resource-details/index.md" >}}) lists the actions available for every resource kind.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Share a Design"
url: /kanvas/guides/collaborating/sharing-designs/index.md
description: Give specific people access to a design, set its visibility, share a link, and revoke access. Covers who can share, what a grant allows, and what fails.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
