In Adaptive render mode, Kanvas can suggest cost-saving changes when a design grows: disabling TagSets when there are more than 5, collapsing parents when there are more than 10, hiding unused components when there are more than 200, and using Wireframe mode when there are more than 100 relationships. Each suggestion appears at most once per 60 seconds.

## Related pages

- [Relationships]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/relationships/index.md" >}}): the kinds that evaluation applies.
- [Create Relationships]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/designing/creating-relationships/index.md" >}}): what you create by hand.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Run a Performance Test"
url: /kanvas/guides/operating/performance-testing/index.md
description: Generate load against a Service or Ingress from the Operator canvas using a performance profile, and read the results.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Operator mode shows a live picture of your clusters. A performance test adds the missing signal: how a service responds under load. You select a Service or Ingress on the canvas, Kanvas seeds a test from it, and Meshery runs the load and keeps the result as a reusable performance profile.

## Before you start

- **Operator mode on a Meshery you run.** The hosted kanvas.new site does not offer Operator mode.
- **A target Meshery Server can reach.** Meshery Server generates the load, not your browser and not the cluster. The address you test must be routable from wherever Meshery Server runs. A `ClusterIP` address is reachable from inside the cluster only.
- **Performance permissions.** The form needs **View performance profiles** to appear, and the Run Test button needs **Run test**. See [Permissions by Role]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/permissions.md" >}}).

## Start a test

The action is named **Initiate Performance Test** and is offered on **Service** and **Ingress** resources only, the kinds that expose an endpoint. It is not offered on pods, deployments, or any other kind. Right-click the resource, or select it and use the action in the header of the Details panel.

The Performance panel opens on the canvas at 400 px wide, floating and minimizable. Only one performance panel exists: starting a test from a second resource replaces the target of the open panel. The panel hosts the Meshery performance test form, so the fields, profiles, and results are the same ones Meshery provides. Opening the panel generates no load. Nothing runs until you press **Run Test**.

## What Kanvas pre-fills

| Setting | Seeded value |
|---|---|
| Profile name | `<Kind> - <component name>`, for example `Service - checkout` |
| URL to test | The first endpoint derived from the resource, or empty |
| Concurrent requests | 10 |
| Queries per second | 20 |
| Duration | 30s |
| Load generator | `fortio` |

Change any value before you run. The form also accepts request headers, cookies, content type, request body, additional load generator options as JSON, and a certificate for TLS endpoints.

### How the URL is derived

For a Service, Kanvas builds an endpoint from the service's type and ports and seeds the first one. A service with several ports yields several endpoints; edit the URL to test another port.

| Service type | Seeded URL |
|---|---|
| `ClusterIP` (also when no type is set) | `http://<clusterIP>:<port>` |
| `LoadBalancer` | `http://<ingress IP or hostname>:<port>`. Empty until the cloud assigns an address. |
| `ExternalName` | `http://<externalName>:<port>` |
| `NodePort` | Empty. Kanvas does not know node addresses. Enter `http://<node address>:<nodePort>`. |
| Headless (`clusterIP: None`) | Seeds `http://None:<port>`. Replace it with a real address. |

For an Ingress, the URL is always empty. Enter the host and path you want to test. The seeded scheme is always `http`; change it to `https` for TLS endpoints.

## Run it and read the result

1. Edit the seeded values.
2. Press **Run Test**. Meshery first saves the settings as a performance profile (the toast reads `Performance profile <name> has been created`), then submits the load test (`Load test has been submitted`).
3. A countdown runs for the test duration. The results then render in the same panel, with a way back to the form.

The same profile can be selected and re-run later, which is what makes a test repeatable before and after a change. Results are stored in Meshery's performance results history, not in Kanvas. Profiles, schedules, comparisons between runs, and how results are interpreted are covered in [Performance Management](https://docs.meshery.io/guides/performance-management) in the Meshery documentation.

## Validation and failure modes

| Message | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Please enter a valid URL along with protocol` | The URL needs a scheme such as `http://`. |
| `Please enter a valid JSON string` | The additional options field is not valid JSON. |
| Duration rejected | Duration must be positive and end in `h`, `m`, or `s`. |
| `Failed to create performance profile` | The profile could not be saved, so the test did not start. |
| `Load test did not run with msg: <message>` | The load generator reported a failure. The message names the cause, often an unreachable endpoint. |
| `Connection to the server got disconnected. Load test might be running in the background. Please check the results page in a few.` | The result stream dropped. The test may still finish; check the results page in Meshery. |
| Permission denied block or disabled Run Test | Your role lacks **View performance profiles** or **Run test**. |
| Empty panel | The host Meshery did not supply the performance form. Use a Meshery release that includes it. |

Kanvas does not pre-check that the endpoint is reachable.

## Related

- [Resource Details]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/resource-details/index.md" >}}) shows the live state of the resource you are testing.
- [Performance Limits]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/performance.md" >}}) covers the limits of Kanvas itself on large designs.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Whiteboard on the Canvas"
url: /kanvas/guides/designing/whiteboarding/index.md
description: Sketch freehand, draw annotation lines, and add shapes, text, sections, images, and comments alongside real components.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

{{< youtube id=o58hO4RDCR4 class="yt-embed-container" >}}

*[Whiteboarding in Kanvas]({{< ref "videos/features/kanvas/whiteboarding-in-kanvas.md" >}}) (3:41) follows one late-night incident from page to postmortem on a single live design. Its page has chapters and a transcript.*

Whiteboarding lets you diagram freely on the same canvas as your infrastructure. You draw shapes, text, freehand strokes, and lines to explain intent, and they sit beside real components in one design. It is on by default and available on every plan.

Drawn objects are saved with the design and shared live with collaborators. They are components marked as annotations, so they count toward your plan's components-per-design limit. See [Designs and Components]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/designs/index.md" >}}).

This guide covers the drawing tools. For per-object operations such as copying, locking, and resizing, see [Working with Canvas Objects]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/canvas-objects/index.md" >}}).

## The dock {#step-3-utilizing-whiteboard-tools}

The dock sits at the bottom of the canvas in Designer mode. Its tools, left to right:

| Tool | Shortcut | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| Select | <kbd>V</kbd> | Select, move, and configure objects. |
| Hand | <kbd>H</kbd>, or hold <kbd>Space</kbd> | Pan the canvas. |
| Components | - | Open the component palette. |
| Kubernetes | - | Open every Kubernetes component. |
| Shapes | - | Browse shape categories. |
| Comment | <kbd>M</kbd> | Drop a comment thread. |
| Image | <kbd>I</kbd> | Pick an image file and place it. |
| TextBox | <kbd>T</kbd> | Add a text box. |
| Section | <kbd>S</kbd> | Add a labeled, dashed region that holds other objects. |
| Pen | <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>/<kbd>Cmd</kbd>+<kbd>E</kbd> | Draw annotation lines. |
| Pencil | <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>/<kbd>Cmd</kbd>+<kbd>P</kbd> | Draw freehand. |
| Help Center | <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>/<kbd>Cmd</kbd>+<kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>/</kbd> | Open help. |

The Pen and Pencil icons turn green while their mode is active. Press <kbd>Esc</kbd> to leave a mode. Pinned models appear after a divider at the right end. See [Pin Models to the Dock]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/designing/pin-model-to-dock/index.md" >}}).

![The Kanvas Designer dock](images/whiteboard-dock.png)

The dock scrolls horizontally when it overflows, and it is greyed out while the app is in an error state, for example after a failed save. In Operator mode only the Select and Hand tools, Help Center, and minimized panels remain.

### Turn tools on or off

The canvas right-click menu opens an Options dialog with these toggles, all on by default:

- **Enable Dock** hides or shows the entire dock, including component pickers, not only the drawing tools.
- **Enable Pencil** and **Enable Pen** hide or show those two icons.

Each change saves to your user preferences, so it applies to all your designs and devices. The toggles hide icons only. The keyboard shortcuts for Pen, Pencil, <kbd>M</kbd>, <kbd>T</kbd>, <kbd>S</kbd>, and <kbd>I</kbd> keep working.

![The Options dialog with Enable Dock, Enable Pencil, and Enable Pen turned on](images/canvas-options.png)

No permission key gates drawing. Tier listings show Pencil, Pen, and 500 built-in shapes on Free, Team Designer, Team Operator, and Enterprise.

## Draw freehand with the Pencil

Each stroke becomes one filled shape. Defaults are caribbean green, thickness 1, and opacity 1. There is no color or thickness control before you draw. Afterward, select the stroke and use its style toolbar to change fill color, opacity, and border.

## Draw lines with the Pen

The Pen is Connector mode. Click empty canvas to place a small terminal point, then click elsewhere to place another and join them with a line. Repeated clicks draw a connected polyline. Starting from a component's edge handle also works. Cancelling mid-draw removes the dangling point.

Pen lines are annotation edges. They explain flow and do not change any component's configuration. Style them like any edge: color, line style, arrow and curve style, label, and animation.

Pan and box selection are off while you draw with the Pen or Pencil.

## Add shapes, text, sections, images, and comments

- **Shapes.** Choose from the shape categories. A shape carries no configuration and is never deployed. You can swap any object's outline for one of 24 shapes while keeping its content, position, and size.
- **Text boxes.** Double-click to edit text inline. Text options include color, weight (regular, medium, semi bold, bold, black), underline or strikethrough, alignment, and font size.
- **Sections.** A section groups the objects dropped inside it, and they move with it.
- **Images.** Images up to 512,000 bytes are embedded in the design. Larger files are rejected.
- **Comments.** A comment opens a discussion thread on the canvas. Resolved threads disappear from the canvas until reopened. See [Review a Design with Comments]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/collaborating/reviewing-designs/index.md" >}}).

![Shapes customization on the canvas](images/shapes_introduction.gif)

## Style objects and lines

Select an object to open its toolbar. Controls appear only when the object supports them.

![The style tooltip for a text box](images/text-customization.png)

| Control | Options |
|---|---|
| Fill | 13 swatches including transparent, with opacity from 0 to 1 |
| Border | Color, style (solid, dotted, dashed, double), thickness from 0 to 25 |
| Layer order | Move to front, forward, backward, to back |
| Animation | None, blink, ripple, bounce, pulse |
| Line style | Solid, dashed, or dotted; ten curve styles; eleven arrow heads |
| Line animation | Marching ants, which shows the direction of flow |

![Editing a line's style](images/line-editing.gif)

![The marching ants animation on a line](images/marching-ants.gif)

## Collaborate

Every change, including drawn objects, syncs live between everyone in the design through a shared document over a peer-to-peer session. Each collaborator appears as an avatar in the toolbar, and live cursors and selections are shared. Undo and redo cover the shared document: components, configuration, styles, relationships, drawn objects, and layer toggles.

## Limits and behavior

- Drawn objects are saved with the design. Kanvas never deploys annotations.
- Images and text files over about 500 KB are rejected, whatever your plan.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Use ConfigMaps and Secrets"
url: /kanvas/tutorials/kubernetes/kubernetes-configmaps-secrets/index.md
description: Inject configuration from a ConfigMap and a credential from a Secret into a MySQL Pod, as environment variables and as mounted files, and verify each binding in the running container.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

In this tutorial you design a MySQL Pod that takes its database name from a ConfigMap and its root password from a Secret, deploy it to a cluster, and prove from inside the container that each value arrived. Separating configuration and credentials from the container image is how one image runs unchanged in every environment, and knowing exactly how Kubernetes delivers those values tells you why a changed setting sometimes reaches a running container and sometimes does not.

## What you will learn

- How a ConfigMap and a Secret store key-value data, and why a Secret's values are base64-encoded rather than encrypted.
- The two ways a Pod consumes them: environment variables resolved once at container start, and mounted volumes that the kubelet keeps up to date.
- That a Pod refers to a ConfigMap or Secret by name and key, and that nothing checks the reference until the container starts.
- How Kanvas validates, dry-runs, and deploys a design, and what Operator shows for Secret data.

## Before you begin

- A Kanvas environment with a Kubernetes cluster connected to Meshery. Use [Meshery Playground](https://play.meshery.io), a shared live cluster, or a self-hosted Meshery with a connected cluster. Hosted kanvas.new has no cluster actions: Validate, Deploy, and Undeploy there open a self-hosted feature prompt.
- Familiarity with Pods and the Kanvas Designer. If this is your first Kanvas tutorial, complete the [Kubernetes Pods tutorial]({{< ref "kanvas/tutorials/kubernetes/kubernetes-pods/index.md" >}}) first.
- A short unique suffix for your object names and labels, such as your initials plus a number (`jd42`). Playground is shared with other users, so this tutorial writes names as `mysql-<suffix>`; replace `<suffix>` everywhere with yours.

## The scenario

You build three components and connect them by name references in the Pod spec:

```text
ConfigMap  mysql-config-<suffix>   data: database = tutorialdb
Secret     mysql-secret-<suffix>   data: root-password = <base64 of strongpassword>
    |                                   |
    |  env MYSQL_DATABASE               |  env MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD
    |  volume at /etc/app-config        |  volume at /etc/db-secret
    v                                   v
Pod        mysql-<suffix>   container mysql (image mysql:8.0)
```

The official MySQL image reads `MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD` to set the root password and `MYSQL_DATABASE` to create a database on first start, so a working login and a database named `tutorialdb` prove that both environment bindings work. The mounted files prove the volume bindings.

## Create the ConfigMap

1. Start a new design and name it, for example `configmaps-secrets-<suffix>`. Kanvas saves the design automatically a few seconds after each change; there is no Save button.
2. Add a **ConfigMap** component from the Kubernetes model. Its configurator opens beside it.
3. Set the name to `mysql-config-<suffix>`. Leave the namespace as `default`.
4. Under **Data**, add one entry with key `database` and value `tutorialdb`.
5. On the configurator's **Labels** tab, add the label `owner` with your suffix as the value. You use this label to find your objects in Operator.

**What just happened.** A ConfigMap is a plain key-value object for non-sensitive configuration. It holds strings (or binary data under `binaryData`) up to 1 MiB in total, and it does nothing on its own: a Pod has to ask for its keys. Kanvas renders the configurator from the ConfigMap's schema and checks your change against that schema in the background.

**Check your work.** The ConfigMap sits on the canvas with no warning badge. A yellow triangle badge means a schema warning; select it to jump to the field.

## Create the Secret

1. Encode the password. In any terminal, run:

    ```shell
    echo -n 'strongpassword' | base64
    ```

    The output is `c3Ryb25ncGFzc3dvcmQ=`. The `-n` matters: without it, `echo` adds a newline that becomes part of the password.

2. Add a **Secret** component. Set the name to `mysql-secret-<suffix>` and the type to `Opaque`.
3. Under **Data**, add one entry with key `root-password` and value `c3Ryb25ncGFzc3dvcmQ=`.
4. On the **Labels** tab, add the same `owner` label.

**What just happened.** A Secret has the same key-value shape as a ConfigMap, and values under `data` must be base64-encoded. **Base64 is an encoding, not encryption.** Anyone who can read the Secret object can recover the value with `echo c3Ryb25ncGFzc3dvcmQ= | base64 -d`. What protects a Secret in a cluster is RBAC on who may read Secrets, encryption at rest configured on the API server, and the kubelet keeping Secret volumes in memory instead of on disk. If you prefer not to encode values yourself, the `stringData` field accepts plain text and the API server encodes it for you.

The value is also stored in your design. Kanvas creates new designs with public visibility, so anyone who can open the design can read and decode the value. Use throwaway values like the one in this tutorial, and never put a production credential in a design.

**Check your work.** Decode the value you typed to confirm it round-trips to `strongpassword`. A value that is not valid base64 passes Validate but fails when the cluster checks the Secret in the next phase.

## Build the Pod

1. Add a **Pod** component. Set the name to `mysql-<suffix>` and add the `owner` label on the **Labels** tab.
2. Add one container with name `mysql`, image `mysql:8.0`, and a container port of `3306`.
3. Add an environment variable named `MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD`. Leave its value empty and set **Value From** to a **Secret Key Ref** with name `mysql-secret-<suffix>` and key `root-password`.
4. Add a second environment variable named `MYSQL_DATABASE`, with **Value From** set to a **Config Map Key Ref** with name `mysql-config-<suffix>` and key `database`. Use the ConfigMap reference here, not a Secret reference: each reference type looks only in its own kind of object.
5. In the Pod spec, add two volumes:
    - `app-config`, of type **Config Map**, with name `mysql-config-<suffix>`.
    - `db-secret`, of type **Secret**, with secret name `mysql-secret-<suffix>`.
6. On the `mysql` container, add two volume mounts:
    - `app-config` at mount path `/etc/app-config`, read-only.
    - `db-secret` at mount path `/etc/db-secret`, read-only.

**What just happened.** The Pod now consumes the same data in two ways:

| Delivery | What the container sees | When a changed value reaches the container |
|---|---|---|
| Environment variable (`valueFrom`) | `MYSQL_DATABASE=tutorialdb`, `MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=strongpassword` | Only when the container restarts. The kubelet resolves the values once, at start. |
| Volume | One file per key: `/etc/app-config/database`, `/etc/db-secret/root-password` | Eventually, without a restart. The kubelet refreshes mounted files periodically (not for `subPath` mounts). |

Both deliver decoded values: the container never sees base64. Each binding is a reference by object name and key. Kanvas Validate checks each component against its own schema only, and a server-side dry run of a Pod does not look up the objects it references, so a misspelled name or key surfaces only when the container tries to start.

**Check your work.** The design holds three components and no warning badges. The Pod's container shows two environment variables and two volume mounts.

## Validate, dry run, and deploy

1. Run **Validate** from the **Actions** menu. Validate runs in your browser against each component's schema and does not contact the cluster. Its findings are advisory; they never block a deploy.
2. Run **Dry Run**. Kanvas sends each component to the cluster's API server as a server-side dry run, which applies the cluster's real validation without persisting anything.
3. Run **Deploy**. Select the environment that holds your cluster connection, review the dry-run result, and deploy.

**What just happened.** Deploy creates each object, or replaces it in place if it already exists, and labels it with the design's id. Components with no declared dependency on each other are applied in parallel, so the Pod can reach the cluster before its ConfigMap and Secret do. In that case the Pod briefly reports `CreateContainerConfigError` and then starts on its own once the kubelet retries.

**Check your work.** The summary at the end of the deploy lists `Deployed ConfigMap "mysql-config-<suffix>"`, `Deployed Secret "mysql-secret-<suffix>"`, and `Deployed Pod "mysql-<suffix>"`. A `Failed to deploy` row carries an error card with the cluster's reason. A dry-run error names the component and field, for example an invalid label value or a Secret value that is not base64; select the error to open the configurator at that field.

## Verify the bindings

1. Switch to Operator. Opening Operator with the design loaded shows a view scoped to this design, which lists the objects carrying the design's id label: your ConfigMap, Secret, and Pod. Operator draws a snapshot, so if the Pod is still starting, change a filter or reopen the view to fetch fresh state.
2. Select the Pod. Its status chip reads `Running` once MySQL has started, which takes up to a minute. The container details list its environment variables and its volume mounts marked `(RO)`. For variables set from a reference, Operator shows the reference, not the value.
3. Select the Secret. Operator shows its type, `Opaque`, and does not display its data values.
4. Start a terminal session on the Pod (**Initiate Terminal Session**). Kanvas opens a `/bin/sh` shell in the container. The terminal sends one line at a time when you press Enter, so run commands one per line:

    ```shell
    printenv MYSQL_DATABASE
    cat /etc/app-config/database
    cat /etc/db-secret/root-password
    mysql -uroot -p"$MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD" -e "SHOW DATABASES;"
    ```

    With `kubectl` access to the cluster, `kubectl exec mysql-<suffix> -- printenv MYSQL_DATABASE` and the equivalent commands give the same answers.

**What just happened.** The first two commands print `tutorialdb`: the ConfigMap reached the container as a variable and as a file. The third prints `strongpassword`, decoded, which shows that anyone who can exec into a Pod can read its mounted Secrets. The last command logs in with the password from the Secret and lists `tutorialdb` among the databases, which MySQL created from the ConfigMap value on first start.

**Check your work.** If the Pod reports `CreateContainerConfigError` and stays there, a referenced name or key does not match: compare the Pod's references with the ConfigMap and Secret names and keys. If `mysql` answers `Access denied`, the stored password differs from what you expect, most often because the base64 value was encoded with a trailing newline.

Operator's **Download** action saves the complete object as JSON, and for a Secret that includes its `data`. Treat downloaded Secret files as sensitive.

## Change a value

1. Return to Designer and change the ConfigMap's `database` value to `otherdb`.
2. Deploy again. Deploy replaces the ConfigMap in place.
3. After a minute or two, run the first two commands from the previous phase again.

**What just happened.** `cat /etc/app-config/database` now prints `otherdb`, because the kubelet refreshed the mounted file. `printenv MYSQL_DATABASE` still prints `tutorialdb`, because environment variables are fixed when the container starts. MySQL also keeps its existing databases: `MYSQL_DATABASE` applies only to the first initialization. This difference is the main reason to mount configuration that must change at runtime as files.

Most fields of a running Pod, including its environment variables, cannot be changed in place. When you change the Pod itself, Deploy reports success but the running Pod keeps its old spec. To apply a Pod change, Undeploy and deploy again, or manage the Pod through a Deployment, which replaces Pods when its template changes.

## Clean up

Run **Undeploy** from the **Actions** menu in Designer. Undeploy deletes each component in the design from the cluster by kind and name: the Pod, the ConfigMap, and the Secret. It removes nothing that the design does not contain, and it deletes any object of the same kind and name in that namespace, whoever created it, which is another reason for unique names on a shared cluster.

Because the design stores the Secret value, delete the design too if you no longer need it.

## What you learned

- A ConfigMap holds configuration and a Secret holds credentials, both as key-value data. Secret values are base64-encoded, which hides nothing; access control and encryption at rest protect them.
- A Pod consumes either one through environment variables, fixed at container start, or through mounted files, which update without a restart.
- References are by name and key and are checked only when the container starts, so a typo shows up as `CreateContainerConfigError`, not as a validation error.
- Kanvas Validate checks schemas in the browser, Dry Run checks against the cluster without persisting, and Deploy creates or replaces each object. Operator shows a Secret's type but not its values.

## Next steps

- [Schedule Work with CronJobs]({{< ref "kanvas/tutorials/kubernetes/exploring-kubernetes-cronjobs/index.md" >}}) - run a container on a schedule and watch the Jobs and Pods it creates.
- [Deploy a Design]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/deploying/deploying-designs/index.md" >}}) - the full Validate, Dry Run, Deploy, and Undeploy reference for everyday use.
- [Operator]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/operator/index.md" >}}) - how Operator discovers cluster resources and what its views show.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Deploy AWS EC2 Instances"
url: /kanvas/tutorials/deploy-aws-ec2-instances-with-meshery/index.md
description: Deploy an AWS EC2 controller, a VPC network, and EC2 instances from three catalog designs to learn how Kubernetes custom resources manage real AWS infrastructure.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

In this tutorial you create a VPC network and EC2 instances in your AWS account without leaving Kanvas. You deploy three designs from the catalog, in order, to your own Kubernetes cluster: a controller that talks to AWS, a VPC network, and the EC2 instances that run inside it. Each AWS resource is a Kubernetes custom resource in the design, and a controller in the cluster turns that resource into real infrastructure.

The bridge is [AWS Controllers for Kubernetes (ACK)](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/containers/aws-controllers-for-kubernetes-ack/). ACK lets you manage AWS resources with the same declarative model you use for Pods and Services: you declare the desired state in the cluster, and the controller makes AWS match it. The trade-off is that the cluster now holds AWS credentials and creates resources that cost money, so this tutorial runs only on a cluster you control and ends with a full cleanup.

## What you will learn

- An ACK controller watches custom resources in the cluster and creates, updates, and deletes the matching AWS resources.
- A custom resource can exist only after its definition (CRD) is installed, so designs that depend on each other deploy in a deliberate order.
- Deploy applies only the ordering a design declares; it does not sort designs or install CRDs ahead of the custom resources that need them.
- A Pod reads credentials from a Secret through environment variables that reference the Secret's keys.
- Operator shows what Deploy put in the cluster, and the AWS console shows what the controller built in AWS.

## Before you begin

- **A self-hosted Meshery with a connected Kubernetes cluster.** Install Meshery by following the [Meshery installation guide](https://docs.meshery.io/installation). Minikube and Amazon EKS both work. The cluster must appear in Meshery as a connected Kubernetes connection assigned to a Meshery environment, because Deploy targets environments and the Kubernetes connections they hold. See [Environments](https://docs.meshery.io/concepts/logical/environments).
- **Not Meshery Playground, and not kanvas.new.** You put real AWS keys into a Secret in this tutorial. Meshery Playground is a shared cluster, so never deploy credentials there. Hosted kanvas.new has no cluster actions: Deploy, Undeploy, and Operator open a prompt to self-host instead.
- **Meshery Operator and MeshSync in the cluster.** Operator reads the cluster through them. Deploy works without them; only the inspection steps need them.
- **An AWS account and a dedicated IAM identity.** Create an IAM user or role for this tutorial with the minimum permissions needed to manage VPCs, subnets, gateways, elastic IPs, route tables, security groups, and EC2 instances. Do not use root or administrator keys. You need its access key ID and secret access key.
- **Budget for a short-lived bill.** The VPC design creates a NAT gateway and an elastic IP, and both incur AWS charges for as long as they exist. EC2 instances incur charges while they exist too. Plan to finish the tutorial and its cleanup in one sitting.

## The scenario

You deploy three designs. Each one depends on the one before it:

```text
1. EC2 controller design          namespace ack-system
   +-- CRDs                       teach the cluster the AWS kinds (VPC, Subnet, Instance, ...)
   +-- Service account            identity the controller Pod runs as
   +-- Secret                     AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY
   +-- Controller Pod             reads the Secret, calls the AWS API

2. VPC workflow design            region us-east-1 by default
   +-- 1 VPC
   +-- 1 internet gateway
   +-- 1 NAT gateway + 1 elastic IP
   +-- 2 route tables             public, private
   +-- 2 subnets                  public, private
   +-- 1 security group

3. EC2 instances design           instances placed in the VPC network
```

At the end, the cluster holds the controller and a set of custom resources, and your AWS account holds the matching VPC network and running instances.

## Clone the designs

The catalog holds the three designs this tutorial uses:

- [EC2 controller design](https://meshery.io/catalog/deployment/ec2-controller-design-8f7e1431-3885-4ebf-9ef7-d2ec64bd4eb5.html)
- [VPC workflow design](https://cloud.meshery.io/catalog/content/catalog/vpc-workflow-design-50cac19e-209c-4acf-b91c-4784281db033)
- [EC2 instances design](https://cloud.meshery.io/catalog/content/catalog/ec2-instances-design-a344f109-2d92-41da-8644-3bc285c3ca9e)

Clone each design into your workspace from its catalog page, then open the clone in Kanvas on your self-hosted Meshery.

**What just happened.** Only published designs can be cloned. Each clone is a new private design named `<name> (Copy)`, owned by you and placed in your selected workspace. It is independent of the catalog original: your edits never reach the source, and later changes to the source never reach your copy. That independence matters here, because you are about to put credentials into the controller design.

## Phase 1: Configure the EC2 controller

Open your copy of the EC2 controller design. Its components deploy to the `ack-system` namespace: the CRDs that define the AWS resource kinds, a service account for the controller, a Secret for your AWS credentials, and the controller Pod itself.

1. Open the Secret component's configurator by double-clicking the Secret. In its data, set exactly two keys:

    | Key | Value |
    |---|---|
    | `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` | `<base64-encoded-key>` |
    | `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` | `<base64-encoded-secret>` |

    Secret data values are base64 encoded. Encode each value locally rather than pasting keys into a website, and avoid a trailing newline:

    ```bash
    printf '%s' 'YOUR_ACCESS_KEY_ID' | base64
    printf '%s' 'YOUR_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY' | base64
    ```

2. Open the controller Pod's configurator and inspect its container's environment variables. You find two entries, `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` and `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`. Each takes its value from a `secretKeyRef` that names the credentials Secret and one of its keys. The design already contains this wiring; you change nothing here.

**What just happened.** The controller never reads the Secret directly. When the kubelet starts the controller's container, it resolves each `secretKeyRef`, decodes the matching value from the Secret, and sets it as an environment variable. The AWS SDK inside the controller reads `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` and `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` from the environment and signs every AWS API call with them. In manifest form, the wiring looks like this:

```yaml
env:
  - name: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef:
        name: <credentials-secret-name>
        key: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID
  - name: AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef:
        name: <credentials-secret-name>
        key: AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY
```

The key names in the Secret and in the `secretKeyRef` entries must match exactly. A typo leaves the variable unset or the container unable to start, and the controller cannot authenticate.

The Secret's values are now stored in your design, and Kanvas saves the design automatically. Base64 is an encoding, not encryption: anyone who can open the design can read your keys. Do not publish this design, do not share it, and do not keep it in a workspace other people use.

## Phase 2: Deploy the EC2 controller

Deploy the controller design from the **Actions** menu. The Deploy stepper validates the design, asks you to pick the environment that holds your cluster's connection, runs a dry run against that cluster, and then deploys.

On a first deploy, the dry run can report errors for objects in `ack-system`. A dry run creates nothing, including namespaces, so the cluster rejects objects aimed at a namespace that does not exist yet. If those are the only errors, tick the box that bypasses dry-run errors and continue. Deploy itself creates the missing `ack-system` namespace before it applies the objects.

The Finish step lists one row per component, such as `Deployed Secret "<name>"`, or a failure row with an error card.

**What just happened.** Meshery Server turned each component into a Kubernetes object and applied it to every cluster in the environment you picked: create the object, or replace it in place if it already exists. Deploying the same design again therefore updates the cluster instead of duplicating objects. Deploy also labeled every object it applied with the design's id, which is how Operator finds them next. The cluster now knows the AWS kinds through the new CRDs, and the controller Pod is starting with your credentials in its environment.

## Phase 3: Verify the controller in Operator

Open the design-scoped Operator view with **View in Operator** from the design's file menu. It shows only the objects this design deployed, because it filters on the design-id label that Deploy added. Confirm the Pod, the Secret, and the service account in `ack-system`, and open the controller Pod's details to check that it is running.

As an alternative, open the **Layers** panel in Operator and filter on the `ack-system` namespace and the kinds you care about. The AWS kinds that the CRDs define appear under Custom Resources once MeshSync reports them.

**What just happened.** Operator draws a snapshot of what MeshSync reports from the cluster, not a live stream. It fetches a new snapshot when a view loads, when a filter changes, or when the selected clusters change, and it draws at most 100 resources per snapshot. If the Pod was still starting when the view loaded, change a filter or reload the view to fetch a fresh snapshot.

## Phase 4: Deploy the VPC workflow

Open your copy of the VPC workflow design. It holds one custom resource per AWS networking resource: a VPC, an internet gateway, a NAT gateway, an elastic IP, a public and a private route table, a public and a private subnet, and a security group. The design targets the `us-east-1` region by default. Adjust CIDR blocks or the region in each component's configurator if your account needs different values, and keep all three designs in the same region.

Deploy the design to the same environment.

**What just happened.** This design contains no controller and no CRDs. It is a set of custom resources whose kinds exist only because Phase 2 installed their definitions. Deploy did not install those definitions for you and would not have reordered anything across designs: it applies only the ordering a design declares. Had you deployed this design first, the cluster would have rejected every component because it did not know their kinds.

Once the custom resources exist, the EC2 controller sees them and calls the AWS API to create each resource. The Finish step confirms that Kubernetes accepted the custom resources; AWS creation happens afterward, asynchronously, and can take several minutes for the NAT gateway. Open the VPC console in `us-east-1` and confirm the VPC, both subnets, both route tables, the gateways, the elastic IP, and the security group.

## Phase 5: Deploy the EC2 instances

Open your copy of the EC2 instances design and deploy it to the same environment. The design places its instances in the network you created in Phase 4.

**What just happened.** The same mechanism ran a third time. Kubernetes accepted the instance custom resources because the controller design installed their definition, and the controller created the instances in AWS inside your VPC network. The dependency chain is now complete: credentials, then controller and definitions, then network, then instances.

## Verify

- **In AWS.** Open the EC2 console in the region the designs use. Confirm that the instances are running and that they sit in the VPC and subnets from Phase 4.
- **In Operator.** Open the design-scoped view for each design to see the custom resources it deployed. Each view shows only that design's objects.
- **In the cluster.** List the AWS kinds the controller installed, then read a resource's status. ACK reports in each resource's status conditions whether it has synced with AWS:

    ```bash
    kubectl api-resources --api-group=ec2.services.k8s.aws
    kubectl describe <kind> <name> -n <namespace>
    ```

## Clean up

Remove everything in reverse order: instances, then the VPC network, then the controller. The order matters for the same reason it mattered on the way in. ACK deletes an AWS resource when its custom resource is deleted, and the controller is what makes that AWS call. If you remove the controller first, nothing is left to delete the instances, the NAT gateway, or the elastic IP, and they keep running and keep billing.

1. Undeploy the EC2 instances design, then the VPC workflow design, then the EC2 controller design, each from the **Actions** menu. Undeploy deletes each object in the design by kind and name on every cluster you select, and it ignores objects that are already gone.
2. If Undeploy reports an error, delete the custom resources with `kubectl` instead, in the same order, while the controller is still running. Use `kubectl api-resources --api-group=ec2.services.k8s.aws` to find the kinds, then `kubectl delete` the instances first and the networking resources after them. Remove the controller design only when no AWS custom resources remain.
3. Confirm in the AWS console that the instances are terminated and that the NAT gateway, the elastic IP, and the VPC are gone. The AWS console is the final word on what you are still paying for.
4. Deactivate or delete the access key you created for this tutorial, and delete your copy of the controller design or clear its Secret values.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Deploy fails with `meshery-server-1096` Kubernetes cluster is unavailable. | No cluster in the selected environment resolves to a connected Kubernetes connection. | Check that your cluster's connection status is Connected and that the connection is assigned to the environment you picked in the Deploy stepper. |
| Deploy fails with `meshery-server-1073` Unable to deploy the selected design. | This error wraps most hard deploy failures. | Read the Details section of the error card for the inner error. The most likely cause is a connection that is not assigned to the selected environment. |
| The dry run or deploy rejects the VPC or EC2 components because their kind is unknown. | The CRDs are missing: the controller design was not deployed first, or it was undeployed. | Deploy the EC2 controller design, confirm it in Operator, then deploy the dependent design again. |
| Custom resources exist, but nothing appears in AWS and their status never reports synced. | The controller cannot authenticate: wrong or badly encoded keys, a key name that does not match, or an IAM identity without the needed permissions. | Re-encode both values without a trailing newline, check the two key names in the Secret and in the Pod's `secretKeyRef` entries, check the IAM permissions, and deploy the controller design again. Read the controller Pod's log for the AWS error. |
| AWS resources appear in a region other than the one you expected. | The designs target `us-east-1` by default. | Look in `us-east-1`, or set the region in each design's configurators before you deploy. |
| Operator shows `Uh-oh. Is MeshSync healthy on the selected cluster?` | Operator received no objects for the selected cluster. | Confirm that Meshery Operator and MeshSync run in the cluster and that the cluster is selected in Operator. |
| Undeploy reports an error. | Undeploy failed for one or more objects. | Delete the custom resources with `kubectl` in reverse order while the controller still runs, then confirm in the AWS console. |

## Where to go next

- [Deploying designs]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/deploying/deploying-designs/index.md" >}}) covers the Deploy stepper, environments, and the deployment summary in full.
- [Undeploying designs]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/deploying/undeploying-designs/index.md" >}}) explains what Undeploy removes and what it leaves behind.
- [Operator]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/operator/index.md" >}}) explains how Operator builds its view of a live cluster.
- [Deploy Azure resources]({{< ref "kanvas/tutorials/deploy-azure-resources-with-meshery/index.md" >}}) applies the same controller pattern to Azure.
- [Kubernetes tutorials]({{< ref "kanvas/tutorials/kubernetes/_index.md" >}}) build the Kubernetes fundamentals this tutorial relies on.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Designer"
url: /kanvas/concepts/designer/index.md
description: How Designer mode turns a shared design document into an editable canvas, what it gates by mode and by permission, and how changes save and sync.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Designer mode is where you author a Kanvas design. You compose infrastructure from versioned components, configure each one against its schema, connect components with relationships, annotate the result, and validate or deploy it, all on one canvas that every collaborator edits at the same time. Designer works on intent: what you want to run. [Operator]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/operator/index.md" >}}) works on live state: what is running.

<figure>
  <img src="images/designer-dock.png" alt="Kanvas Designer workspace with the bottom dock of authoring tools, the Layers panel open, and the Share control in the header" />
  <figcaption>Designer: the bottom dock holds the tools for adding components and annotations, and the Layers panel controls what the canvas draws.</figcaption>
</figure>

## A design is a shared document

Everything on the canvas is an entry in one design document: every component you configure, every relationship, and every annotation you draw. The canvas draws that document. Moving a node, applying a layout, or hiding a layer writes into the design. As a result:

- Collaborators see the same canvas, including positions, locks, and layer visibility.
- Undo and redo cover every change to the document: components, configuration, styles, relationships, annotations, and layer toggles.
- Hiding a component in the Layers panel changes only what is drawn. The component stays in the design and deploys with it.

For what a design contains and how it is versioned, see [Designs]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/designs/index.md" >}}).

## Designer and Operator

| | Designer | Operator |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | Author and change a design | Inspect and act on resources running in connected clusters |
| What the canvas draws | Components, relationships, and annotations from the design document | Kubernetes resources discovered in the selected clusters |
| What you can edit | The whole design: add, configure, relate, annotate, style, lay out, delete | Nothing; live nodes are read-only |
| Actions | Validate, deploy, undeploy, share, reset design | Open a terminal, follow logs, run a performance test, open the source design |

Selection, panning, zoom, the Layers panel, and undo and redo work in both modes. Keyboard shortcuts that add or change content, such as copy, paste, duplicate, delete, Pen, and Pencil, act only in Designer.

## What you do in Designer

- **Compose from versioned components.** The palette lists models from the Meshery registry by category, and each model offers a version selector with the newest version first. Add a component by dragging or clicking, nest it by dropping it onto a compatible parent, or drop YAML, JSON, or archive files to import infrastructure as code.
- **Configure.** A new component opens its configurator, a form rendered from the component's JSON schema with the schema's defaults. Edits write to the design after a short pause and trigger validation and relationship evaluation. Switching a component to another version keeps its configuration values; validation flags any that no longer fit.
- **Relate.** Drawing an edge or nesting one component in another creates a relationship when a registry definition matches the pair. A relationship can write values from one component's configuration into another's. Kanvas re-evaluates relationships about one second after changes stop, and evaluation never blocks editing. See [Relationships]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/relationships/index.md" >}}) and [Relationship Evaluation]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/relationship-evaluation/index.md" >}}).
- **Annotate.** Shapes, text boxes, sections, images, comments, Pen connectors, and Pencil strokes explain the design without configuring infrastructure.
- **Lay out.** Six layouts rearrange the canvas: Grid, Constrained (the default), hierarchical, star, bus, and ring. A design with no saved positions is laid out automatically when it opens; otherwise Kanvas keeps the saved positions. A layout changes positions only, never configuration.
- **Validate, dry-run, deploy, and undeploy.** Kanvas checks each changed component against its schema. A badge on the component counts its validation warnings and dry-run errors. Meshery Server carries out deployment.
- **Share.** A share gives others access to the design, and anyone with a share can edit it.

## What mode gates and what permission gates

Authoring is gated by mode, not by role. Adding, configuring, duplicating, deleting, and renaming work in Designer and are blocked in Operator. Resources synced from a live cluster are read-only in every mode. Within Designer, what you can change on a component depends on that component's registry capabilities: a configurator tab or a style control appears only when the component declares it.

Only four actions are permission-gated: validate, deploy, undeploy, and share. When your role lacks one of these permissions, its control is hidden. The permission catalog also lists permissions for individual canvas gestures, such as adding shapes or resetting styles. Kanvas does not enforce those on the canvas, so withholding them has no effect. Users who are not signed in are prompted to sign in before sharing, and to sign in or run Meshery locally before validating or deploying. See [Permissions]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/permissions.md" >}}).

## How changes are stored and synchronized

Designer has no Save button. Every change to the design requests a save, and Kanvas sends it 3 seconds after the last change. A new design is not saved until it has a component or a name.

While a design is open, every change, drawn objects included, syncs live between collaborators through the shared document. Each collaborator appears as an avatar in the toolbar, and their cursor and current selection show on your canvas. Storage does not merge: each save sends the whole design, and the last save wins. Live co-editing in the open session is what reconciles concurrent edits. See [Collaboration]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/collaboration/index.md" >}}).

If a save fails, Kanvas enters an error state: the dock is disabled and edits are not applied while Kanvas retries the save with increasing delays.

## Configurable components and annotations

Every object on the canvas is a component entry in the design. Annotations carry an annotation flag; configurable components do not. The Layers panel uses that flag to split the canvas into Annotations and Configurable Components, each with a count and its own visibility toggle. Pen connectors are non-binding annotation relationships: they draw lines without changing any configuration.

The distinction does not exempt annotations from your plan. When a design is saved, Layer5 Cloud counts every component entry, annotations included, against the components-per-design limit. The limit is checked on save, not when you add an object, so a design can grow past it on the canvas and then fail to save.

## What Designer does not do

- It does not operate live workloads. Terminal sessions, log streams, and performance tests are Operator actions.
- It does not filter components by label. Label filters exist only in Operator views.
- It does not set an access level on a share. Every share can edit.
- It does not narrow relationship evaluation by layer. Evaluation always covers the whole design.

## Where to go next

- Reference: [Canvas Objects]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/canvas-objects/index.md" >}}), [Tool Modes]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/tool-modes/index.md" >}}), [Canvas Actions]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/canvas-actions/index.md" >}}), [Layout and Layers]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/layout-and-layers/index.md" >}}), [Component Badges]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/component-badges/index.md" >}}), and [Keyboard Shortcuts]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/keyboard-shortcuts.md" >}}).
- Build a design: [Configuring Components]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/designing/configuring-components/index.md" >}}), [Creating Relationships]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/designing/creating-relationships/index.md" >}}), and [Whiteboarding]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/designing/whiteboarding/index.md" >}}).
- Check and save a design: [Validating Designs]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/deploying/validating-designs/index.md" >}}) and [Saving Designs]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/designs/saving-designs/index.md" >}}).
- Give others access: [Sharing Designs]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/collaborating/sharing-designs/index.md" >}}).


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Export Designs"
url: /kanvas/guides/designs/export-designs/index.md
description: Export a design as a design file, an OCI image, a Kubernetes manifest, a Helm chart, or an embeddable script, and know what each format keeps.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Export writes a design out of Kanvas so you can back it up, move it between Meshery deployments, hand it to Helm or `kubectl`, or put it on a web page. Every export is generated from the current state of the design. You cannot export an earlier version.

Export is a File menu action, disabled on an empty design. In Operator mode, Export instead downloads the open view as `<view name>.json`.

## Choose a format

| Format | Keeps layout, annotations, and metadata | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| Design file (YAML) | Yes | Backups, moving designs, re-import into Kanvas |
| Design (OCI image) | Yes | Storing and versioning a design in a container registry |
| Kubernetes manifest | No | `kubectl apply` and pipelines that expect plain manifests |
| Helm chart | No | Helm repositories, Argo CD, Flux, Artifact Hub |
| Embed design (JavaScript) | Snapshot of the canvas | Showing a design on a web page |

Kanvas offers at least one of the first four. Which ones appear can depend on the capabilities of your Layer5 Cloud account. Per-format options and size limits are not exposed. To capture the canvas as a PNG picture, use Take Screenshot instead. See [Canvas Actions]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/canvas-actions/index.md" >}}).

## Design file (YAML) {#exporting-as-a-design-file}

A complete copy of the design, including layout, annotations, component grouping, and configuration. The download is named `<design name>.yml`. Kanvas can import it back without loss.

## Design (OCI image) {#exporting-as-an-oci-image}

The same lossless content packaged as an OCI image archive. Push it with a registry tool such as `docker push` or `oras push` to version and distribute designs alongside application artifacts. Kanvas imports the archive back, taking the design file in its layers. See [Import and Merge Designs]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/designs/import-designs/index.md" >}}).

## Source-type formats {#exporting-in-a-source-type-format}

A design can be exported as the kind of source it was built from. Both formats are lossy: layout, annotations, and comments are dropped because neither format can carry them. To keep a design fully editable, export the design file instead.

Docker Compose is an import source only. A design cannot be exported to Compose.

### Kubernetes manifest {#exporting-as-a-kubernetes-manifest}

Plain Kubernetes resource definitions, ready for `kubectl apply`.

### Helm chart {#exporting-as-a-helm-chart}

A `.tar.gz` chart archive that contains the Kubernetes resource definitions. Install it with `helm install <release> <chart>.tgz` or place it in a Helm repository.

Re-importing a manifest or chart restores the resources, but not the layout, so the graph does not reappear as you drew it.

## Embed design (JavaScript) {#exporting-as-embedding}

The Embed Design option downloads a JavaScript module and shows a two-line snippet to paste into an HTML page. The embed is a static snapshot, not a live view. See [Embed Designs]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/designs/embedding-designs/index.md" >}}).

## Access and tiers

- Exporting needs no sign-in for a public or published design. Anonymous callers can download the design file of any public or published design, not just their own. A private design is downloadable by its owner, a provider administrator, a user the design is shared with, or a user holding the View Designs permission.
- Each download of the design file writes an audit event and raises the design's download count. Anonymous downloads record as "Anonymous viewer downloaded".
- No plan tier gates export, and exporting your own design needs no permission key. Layer5 Cloud's catalog table shows its Download action to roles with the Download a Design permission.
- The browser either prompts for a save location or saves to your downloads folder. Success shows `<name> design downloaded`. Failure shows "Failed to download design".

## Keep a version you can return to

A design has a single current version, and the save history is an event log, not a set of snapshots. To keep a restorable point, export a design file or an OCI image at that moment and store it. For an OCI image, push it to a registry under a tag.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Pin Models to the Dock"
url: /kanvas/guides/designing/pin-model-to-dock/index.md
description: Keep the models you use most one step away in the dock, and remove them when you no longer need them.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Pinning a model puts its icon in the dock at the bottom of the canvas, so you can reach its components without opening the full palette. Pins belong to your account. They are not stored per design or in the browser, so they follow you across designs, browsers, and devices.

Pinning works in Designer mode. In Operator mode the dock does not show pinned models.

## Pin a model

Hover a model row in the component palette and use the pin icon. Its tooltip reads "Pin To Dock". The shape palette offers the same pin on each shape category row.

![The Pin To Dock action on a model in the component list](images/pin-to-dock.png)

Only models and shape categories can be pinned. Individual components cannot. There is no limit on how many models you pin. Kanvas matches pins by model name, so pinning the same model at a different version is the same pin.

## Use a pinned model

Pinned models appear after a divider at the right end of the dock.

![A pinned model displayed in the dock](images/pinned-model-location.png)

Select a pinned model to open a picker with its components. Click a component to add it near the center of the canvas, or drag it to a specific spot. The picker has its own search box and a version selector with an "All Versions" choice. A pinned model whose lookup returns nothing is not drawn.

![Components of a pinned model in the picker](images/use-pinned-models-components.png)

## Remove a pin

Either of these removes the pin without affecting any design:

- Select the pin icon again on the model row. Its tooltip reads "Remove From Dock".
- Hover the pinned model in the dock and select the close (X) badge.

![The Remove From Dock action](images/unpin-model-1.png)

![Unpinning with the close badge](images/unpin-model-2.png)

## Default dock

With nothing pinned the dock holds Select, Hand, Components, Kubernetes, Shapes, Comment, Image, TextBox, Section, Pen, Pencil, and Help Center. See [Whiteboard on the Canvas]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/designing/whiteboarding/index.md" >}}).


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Tool Modes"
url: /kanvas/reference/tool-modes/index.md
description: Reference for the Designer tool modes - Select, Pan, Pencil and Pen - covering how to enter and leave each, what the mouse does in each, and how wheel and zoom controls behave.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The canvas has four tool modes. The mode decides what a mouse drag does: move an object, pan the view, draw freehand or draw a connecting line. Select is the default. This page lists how to enter and leave each mode, what every mouse gesture does in it, and the wheel and zoom controls that work in all of them.

## Modes at a glance

| Mode | Purpose | Enter | Leave | Drag on empty canvas | Box selection |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Select | Select, move, configure and style objects. The default. | <kbd>V</kbd> or <kbd>Esc</kbd> | Choose another mode | Draws a selection box | On |
| Pan | Move the view without touching objects. | <kbd>H</kbd>, or hold <kbd>Space</kbd> | <kbd>V</kbd>, <kbd>Esc</kbd>, or release <kbd>Space</kbd> | Pans the view | Off |
| Pencil | Draw freehand annotations. | <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>/<kbd>Cmd</kbd> + <kbd>P</kbd>, or the Pencil tool in the dock | The same shortcut, <kbd>V</kbd> or <kbd>Esc</kbd> | Draws a stroke | Off |
| Pen | Draw connecting lines and annotation edges. | <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>/<kbd>Cmd</kbd> + <kbd>E</kbd>, or the Pen tool in the dock | The same shortcut, <kbd>V</kbd> or <kbd>Esc</kbd> | Places points and lines | Off |

The Pencil and Pen dock icons turn green while their mode is active. The mode shortcuts work in Designer mode. Select and Pan also work in Operator mode.

Releasing <kbd>Space</kbd> returns you to Select, not to the mode you held it from. If you were drawing with Pencil or Pen, re-enter that mode afterward.

Kanvas ignores single-key shortcuts while you type in a text field, so typing a label or a comment never changes the mode.

## Select mode

| Gesture | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Hover | No effect. |
| Click an object | Selects it and shows its style toolbar, resize handles and connection handles. |
| Drag an object | Moves it. Locked objects do not move. |
| Double-click a component | Opens its configurator. |
| Double-click a textbox or comment | Edits its text inline. |
| Right-click, or press and hold, on an object | Opens the object menu. |
| Right-click on empty canvas | Opens the canvas menu. See [Canvas Actions]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/canvas-actions/index.md" >}}). |
| Drag on empty canvas | Draws a selection box that selects the objects it covers. |
| <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>/<kbd>Cmd</kbd> + click | Adds an object to the selection or removes it. |

The cursor shows an arrow while hovering, a move cursor while dragging an object and a crosshair while you draw a selection box.

![Selecting several objects with a selection box in Select mode](images/select.gif)

Object actions are listed in [Canvas Objects]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/canvas-objects/index.md" >}}).

## Pan mode

Pan mode turns a drag on the canvas into a pan. The cursor is an open hand, and a closed hand while you drag. Hold <kbd>Space</kbd> to pan for as long as the key is down, or press <kbd>H</kbd> to stay in Pan mode until you leave it.

## Pencil mode

Pencil draws freehand. Each stroke you release becomes one annotation object on the canvas.

| Gesture | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Press and drag | Draws a freehand stroke. |
| Release | Completes the stroke and turns it into an object. |

A new stroke is caribbean green, with thickness 1 and full opacity. Pencil has no color or thickness control before you draw. Select the stroke afterward and change its fill, border and opacity in the style toolbar. See [Canvas Objects]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/canvas-objects/index.md" >}}).

Pencil strokes connect to nothing. They annotate. Pan and box selection are off while Pencil is active.

![Drawing a freehand stroke in Pencil mode](images/pencil.gif)

## Pen mode

Pen draws lines. Each line is an annotation edge, a non-binding relationship that carries no configuration, so it explains a design without changing it.

| Step | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Click on empty canvas | Places a small point to start from. |
| Click again elsewhere on empty canvas | Places another point and draws an edge between the two. Repeating this draws a connected line of segments. |
| Start from a component's connection handle and release on another component or a point | Draws an edge between them. |
| Cancel mid-draw | Removes the dangling point. |

Points are small borderless shapes. Edges drawn with Pen use the same style controls as every other edge: color, line style, curve, arrowhead, label and animation. See [Canvas Objects]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/canvas-objects/index.md" >}}). Pan and box selection are off while Pen is active.

Edges between registry-defined components, which configure the components they join, are drawn in Select mode from a component's connection handle. See [Relationships]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/relationships/index.md" >}}).

## Wheel and zoom controls

These are registered in Designer and Operator mode.

| Input | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Scroll wheel | Pans vertically. |
| Horizontal scroll, or <kbd>Shift</kbd> + scroll wheel | Pans horizontally. Each <kbd>Shift</kbd> step moves 50 pixels. |
| <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>/<kbd>Cmd</kbd> + scroll wheel | Zooms toward the pointer. Each step changes the zoom by 0.1. |
| <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>/<kbd>Cmd</kbd> + <kbd>+</kbd> and <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>/<kbd>Cmd</kbd> + <kbd>-</kbd> | Zooms in and out by the same step. |

The Options drawer sets the zoom range: a minimum from 0.1 to 5 (default 0.1) and a maximum from 0.1 to 30 (default 30). Zooming the page itself is left to the browser.

Object controls and badges appear only when the canvas is zoomed in far enough. When you are zoomed out, Kanvas shows a hint to zoom in to interact with elements.

## Related reading

- [Keyboard Shortcuts]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/keyboard-shortcuts.md" >}}) - every shortcut in one list.
- [Whiteboarding]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/designing/whiteboarding/index.md" >}}) - a task guide to drawing on a design.
- [Designer]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/designer/index.md" >}}) - what Designer mode is for.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Undeploy a Design"
url: /kanvas/guides/deploying/undeploying-designs/index.md
description: Remove the resources a design describes from your clusters, and understand exactly what is and is not deleted.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Undeploying deletes the Kubernetes objects that each component in a design describes, from every cluster in the environments you select. It does not touch the design itself. The design record, its versions, and its Operator view are unchanged.

## Before you start

The prerequisites match [Deploy a Design]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/deploying/deploying-designs/index.md" >}}): a Meshery you run with a connected cluster, a non-empty design, and the **Undeploy Design** permission. The hosted kanvas.new site does not run undeploy. See [Permissions by Role]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/permissions.md" >}}).

## The undeploy flow

Choose Undeploy from the design's Actions menu. The `Undeploy design "<name>"` stepper has the same five steps and gates as the deploy stepper:

1. **Validate Design.** Runs validation inline.
2. **Identify Environments.** Selects the environments, and so the clusters, to remove from.
3. **Dry Run.** An undeploy-type [dry run]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/deploying/dry-running-a-design/index.md" >}}) that deletes by name with server-side dry run. Because an absent object returns NotFound, a design that was never deployed, or is already removed, shows an error for every component here and needs the bypass checkbox to continue.
4. **Finalize.** Confirms the environments and component count. The button reads Undeploy.
5. **Finish.** Runs the removal and shows the results.

## What gets deleted

| Behavior | Detail |
|---|---|
| What is removed | One delete for each non-annotation component's object, in its namespace, on every selected cluster. |
| How it is matched | By kind and name from the design, not by label. An object with the same kind and name that was created some other way is deleted too. |
| Order | Reverse dependency order. A component whose dependent failed to delete is withheld: `Withheld <component>: <dependent> did not undeploy successfully`. |
| Objects already gone | Ignored. |
| Namespaces, custom resource definitions, volume claims, Secrets | Deleted only when the design has a component for them. |
| Dependency charts | For components of non-Kubernetes models, Meshery uninstalls the model's Helm chart: `Undeployed dependent helm chart for <component>`. This can remove custom resource definitions and operators that other designs on the cluster use. |
| Missing namespace | Created before the delete is attempted. |

Meshery always processes dependency charts on undeploy. The Include Dependencies checkbox in the dry-run step does not change this. Before you undeploy a design that uses custom resource models, check what else on the cluster depends on its definitions.

## Read the results

Success raises the event `undeployed design '<name>'.` at success severity. Failure raises `Failed to undeploy design '<name>'.` at error severity, with an error card. The error codes match those in [Deploy a Design]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/deploying/deploying-designs/index.md" >}}). The deployment count of the design is not decremented.

In Operator mode, the resources leave the live view once MeshSync reports their deletion.

## Limits

- There is no undeploy-type dry run outside the stepper.
- Deleting a design does not undeploy it. Undeploy first if you want the resources gone. See [Delete a Design]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/designs/deleting-a-design/index.md" >}}).
- As with deploy, the Finish step waits for a server event. If the request fails before the server raises one, the step keeps spinning with no error. See [Deploy a Design]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/deploying/deploying-designs/index.md" >}}).


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Canvas Actions"
url: /kanvas/reference/canvas-actions/index.md
description: Reference for the Designer canvas menu - undo and redo, paste, select all, reset, screenshot, options, shortcuts and the Help Center - with the mode in which each action is available.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Right-clicking an empty part of the canvas - anywhere no component sits - opens the **Canvas Actions** menu. Where the component context menu acts on one component, this menu acts on the canvas as a whole: undoing and redoing, pasting, selecting everything, capturing the canvas as an image, and reaching help.

The menu adapts to the mode you are in. Commenting and pasting, for example, are offered in Designer mode but not in Operator mode, where the canvas reflects discovered infrastructure rather than a design you are authoring.

## Editing actions

| Action | Shortcut | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Add Comment | <kbd>M</kbd> | Drops a comment at the point you right-clicked. Designer mode only. See [Review a Design with Comments]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/collaborating/reviewing-designs/index.md" >}}). |
| Undo | <kbd>Cmd/Ctrl</kbd> + <kbd>Z</kbd> | Reverses the last change to the design: components, configuration, styles, relationships, annotations and layer toggles. A message confirms the change was reverted, or reports that no changes remain. |
| Redo | <kbd>Cmd/Ctrl</kbd> + <kbd>Shift</kbd> + <kbd>Z</kbd> or <kbd>Cmd/Ctrl</kbd> + <kbd>Y</kbd> | Re-applies the last undone change. |
| Paste | <kbd>Cmd/Ctrl</kbd> + <kbd>V</kbd> | Pastes the clipboard contents at the cursor position. Designer mode only. |
| Select All | <kbd>Cmd/Ctrl</kbd> + <kbd>A</kbd> | Selects every component on the canvas. |
| Reset Design | | Clears every component from the canvas. Designer mode only, and destructive - see below. |

### Reset Design

Reset Design removes everything currently on the canvas. Kanvas asks you to confirm before it does, and the confirmation reminds you that undo is usually the better tool if you only want to step back a few changes. The confirmation dialog carries a "don't show this again" checkbox; ticking it stores that preference against your user settings, and the reset then happens immediately on every subsequent use.

## Screenshot Canvas

**Take Screenshot** captures the canvas as drawn - components, relationships and annotations - and downloads it to your machine as a PNG. The file is named `Kanvas-<timestamp>.png`, so repeated captures of the same design do not overwrite one another.

The capture is of the canvas, not your browser window: panels, the dock and the toolbar are not included. It records the canvas as currently viewed, so pan and zoom to frame what you want before you capture. Object controls and badges appear only when the canvas is zoomed in far enough, so zoom in first if you want them in the image.

This is the quickest way to put a design into a pull request, an incident write-up or a slide. When you need the design as data rather than as a picture - to hand to another tool, or to re-import later - use [Exporting Designs]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/designs/export-designs/index.md" >}}) instead.

## Options

**Options** opens the canvas settings drawer. Each change saves to your user preferences on the server after a short pause, applies to every design you open and shows a confirmation message. Preferences belong to you, not to a design.

| Option | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dark Theme | - | Switches the canvas between light and dark themes. |
| Snap to Grid | On | Snaps objects to the grid as you drag. |
| Hide Gridlines | On | Gridlines are hidden by default. |
| Enable Dock | On | Off hides the whole bottom dock, including the drawing tools and pickers. Keyboard shortcuts still work. |
| Show Reset Canvas Confirmation | On | Off makes Reset Design act immediately. |
| Enable Pencil | On | Shows the Pencil tool in the dock. |
| Enable Pen | On | Shows the Pen tool in the dock. |
| Auto-pan on Drag | Off | Pans the view while you drag an object past the canvas edge. Kanvas turns it off on large designs, with a limit for each render mode. See [Auto-pan on Drag]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/autopan.md" >}}). |
| Max Canvas Zoom | 30 | Upper zoom limit, from 0.1 to 30. |
| Min Canvas Zoom | 0.1 | Lower zoom limit, from 0.1 to 5. |
| Enable Debugger | Off | Shows debugging aids. |
| Relationship Evaluation Engine | Automatic (recommended) | Chooses how relationships are evaluated. |
| Show Tutorial | On | Shows the in-app tutorial. |
| Show Walkthrough | On | Shows the walkthrough. |
| Render Fidelity | - | Sets how much detail the canvas draws, from full fidelity down to a wireframe, and can adapt as a design grows. See [Render Modes]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/render-modes/index.md" >}}). |

Operator mode offers only Show Tutorial and Show Walkthrough.

## Shortcuts

**Shortcuts** (<kbd>Cmd/Ctrl</kbd> + <kbd>/</kbd>) opens the keyboard shortcut reference in the help drawer, listing the shortcuts available in both Designer and Operator modes.

## View help center

**Help Center** (<kbd>Cmd/Ctrl</kbd> + <kbd>Shift</kbd> + <kbd>/</kbd>) opens the in-app help modal. It gathers, in one place, every route by which you can learn more about Kanvas or reach someone who can help:

| Card | What it opens |
| --- | --- |
| Documentation | Guides, references and how-tos for Kanvas and Meshery. |
| Video Tutorials | Walkthroughs and demos in the Layer5 video library. |
| Quick Tips | An in-app tour of core Kanvas features, shown in a drawer beside the canvas. |
| Academy | Structured learning paths in Layer5 Cloud. |
| Discussion Forum | The Layer5 discussion forum, for questions and shared knowledge. |
| Slack | The Layer5 community Slack, for real-time conversation. |
| Keyboard Shortcuts | The same shortcut reference the Shortcuts action opens. |
| Support | A form for contacting the Kanvas team with a problem or a piece of feedback. |

Quick Tips and Keyboard Shortcuts open in a drawer alongside the canvas, so you can keep working while you read them. Support opens its form in a modal over the canvas. The remaining five cards open in a new tab. The Help Center is also reachable from the help button at the right-hand end of the dock.
