The design's creator, or any user with Approve Catalog Request, can unpublish it. The Unpublish Design permission controls the action in the Layer5 Cloud interface. Others get 403 "unauthorized to unpublish to catalog".

Unpublishing sets visibility to private (not public), starts a delete-from-catalog workflow, and records an event. Catalog data stays on the design. The earlier publish request record is not cleared, so submitting the same design again hits the existing-request rule above.

Deleting a published design also starts the delete-from-catalog workflow. See [Delete a Design]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/designs/deleting-a-design/index.md" >}}).

## Publish to Artifact Hub

Kanvas has no direct Artifact Hub publishing. To list a design there, export it as a Helm chart and publish that chart to a Helm repository, then register the repository in Artifact Hub using its own documentation. See [Export Designs]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/designs/export-designs/index.md" >}}). Exporting to a Helm chart drops layout and annotations.

## Tiers

No plan feature is checked when you publish. Publishing is governed by the permissions above. See [Permissions]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/permissions.md" >}}).


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Component Badges"
url: /kanvas/reference/component-badges/index.md
description: Reference for every badge Kanvas draws on a component - what it means, where it sits, when it appears, what a click does and how to hide it - in Designer and Operator modes.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

A badge is a small marker Kanvas draws on the edge of a component to report something about it: errors waiting to be fixed, components held inside it, a link, or where it came from. Badges are status, not decoration. A count on a badge tells you there is something to read, and clicking it shows what.

Which badges appear depends on the mode. Designer mode draws badges that help you build a valid design. Operator mode draws badges about live resources.

![A component with an error count badge and a validation summary beside it on the Designer canvas](images/example.png)

## Badges in Designer mode

| Badge | Position | Appears when | Click |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Error count | Bottom-left, red, shows a number | The component has at least one schema validation warning or deployment error. The number is the sum of both. | Opens a summary with one count per category. Each count opens the matching details: the validation results or the deployment results. |
| Inventory | Bottom-right, shows a number | The component holds other components inside it. The number is how many. | Lists the held components. Choosing one opens its configurator. |
| External Link | Top-right | You set a **Link** on the component in its style options. | Opens the URL in a new tab. |
| Parent model icon | Left edge, above the error count | The component is a parent that contains other components. | None. It shows the parent's model icon in the component color. |
| Expand and collapse | Inside the component, top-right | The component is a parent with children. | Hides the children, or shows them again. |
| Section label | Top-left, inside the section | The object is a section. | None. It carries the section name, shortened with an ellipsis when it does not fit the width. |

### Error count

The error count joins two checks into one number:

- **Validation warnings** come from checking the component's configuration against its schema, such as a missing required field or an invalid value.
- **Deployment errors** come from a dry run of the design against a cluster. See [Validating Designs]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/deploying/validating-designs/index.md" >}}).

A component with no errors shows no badge. Fix the field the warning names and the count drops, and the badge disappears at zero. Opening a validation warning from the badge takes you to the offending configuration field.

![Clicking an error badge and correcting the configuration field it reports](images/reslove-error.gif)

### Inventory

An inventory badge appears on a component that holds other components, such as a workload that holds its configuration objects. The held components are drawn inside the inventory rather than as separate nodes on the canvas. The relationship between them is created by the policy engine; see [Relationships]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/relationships/index.md" >}}).

## Badges in Operator mode

| Badge | Position | Appears when | Click |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Managed by Meshery | Top-left, green | The resource was created from a design and Kanvas knows which one. | Opens the source design in Designer mode. |
| Terminal | Bottom-right, black | The resource is a container that has a terminal session open. | Opens the terminal panel. See [Interactive Terminal]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/operating/interactive-terminal/index.md" >}}). |

Operator mode draws no health, performance or policy badge. Resource state is on the resource itself; see [Resource Details]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/resource-details/index.md" >}}).

## Showing and hiding badges

- The **Layers** panel has a **Component Badges** section with separate switches for **Validation Warnings**, **Deployment Errors** and **Inventory**. Switching one off removes its share of the error count, or the inventory badge, from the canvas without changing the design's contents. The setting is saved with the design. See [Layout and Layers]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/layout-and-layers/index.md" >}}).
- Badges draw only at Full render fidelity. In Medium and the lower fidelity modes Kanvas leaves them out to keep large designs responsive.
- Badges, like object controls, draw only when the canvas is zoomed in far enough to read them.

## Practical use

- Clear the error count on every component before you deploy. A design with no badges is a design that passes both checks.
- Use the Managed by Meshery badge to jump from a live resource to the design that produced it when you need to change its configuration.
- Hide badges before you take a screenshot for a review if you want a clean image. See [Canvas Actions]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/canvas-actions/index.md" >}}).


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Delete a Design"
url: /kanvas/guides/designs/deleting-a-design/index.md
description: Permanently delete a design you own, and understand what deletion does and does not affect.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Deleting a design removes the design record and its workspace mappings in one transaction. There is no trash and no restore. Export a copy first if you might need it. See [Export Designs]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/designs/export-designs/index.md" >}}).

## Who can delete

The server allows the design's owner or a provider administrator. Organization administrators, workspace owners, and collaborators with a share grant cannot delete a design (403 "unauthorized for the operation"). Layer5 Cloud hides its Delete action for roles without the Delete a Design permission, but the server decides by ownership, not by the key. To remove a design from a workspace without deleting it, use the workspace's remove action instead.

## Delete from Kanvas

Delete is a File menu action, disabled on an empty canvas. A confirmation reads `Delete <name> design` with the text `Are you sure you want to delete <name>?`. You confirm with a single button. There is no type-to-confirm step.

If you delete the open design, the editor resets to a new blank design. Deleting a different design from a list does not change the canvas. Kanvas shows no success message for a delete, while Layer5 Cloud shows `<name> deleted`.

## What deletion affects

| Item | Effect |
|---|---|
| Deployed resources | None. Deleting does not undeploy anything from clusters. [Undeploy]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/deploying/undeploying-designs/index.md" >}}) first if you want the resources gone. |
| Clones, Save as copies, merged-in components | Untouched. They are independent. |
| Share grants | Removed with the design. |
| Collaboration session | Ends when the canvas resets. |
| Published design | A delete-from-catalog workflow runs against the catalog repository. If it fails, the failure is logged only. The catalog request record stays. |
| Catalog clones made by others | Remain. |

An event records who deleted which design.

## Delete several designs

Layer5 Cloud's catalog designs table offers multi-select delete with the prompt `Are you sure that you want to delete <N> designs?`. It issues one delete per selected design, so a partial failure shows per-design errors. Kanvas has no multi-select delete.

## Errors

| Response | Cause |
|---|---|
| 400 "please provide a valid design ID" | The id is invalid. |
| 404 "design not found" | The design does not exist. A missing row can also surface as 500 "failed to get design from database". |
| 403 | You are not the owner or a provider administrator. |


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Render Modes"
url: /kanvas/concepts/render-modes/index.md
description: How render modes trade visual detail for canvas speed, how Adaptive mode moves between them, and how render mode interacts with size gates, Layers, Designer, and Operator.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Render mode sets how much detail Kanvas draws for a design. It works as a fidelity dial for your current session, not a property of the design. Switching modes never changes components, relationships, configuration, or layers, and the mode is not saved with the design. Every session starts in Full unless the URL sets a different mode. The switcher appears in the Options dialog and in the Designer toolbar.

## What each mode trades away

Kanvas has four render modes. Each of the first three gives up something the mode above it draws.

- **Full** draws everything: component images and gradient fills, every badge, TagSets, mount animations on new components, and animated layouts on designs that are small enough.
- **Medium** keeps component images and relationship styling but drops gradient fills, TagSets, animations, and most badges, including validation and dry-run error badges. It keeps expand and collapse badges so you can still navigate compound components.
- **Wireframe** reduces the design to its structure. Component images, all badges, and text-box overlays disappear, and edges become thin, straight, light gray lines with simple arrowheads. You can still edit everything.
- **View-only** draws as sparsely as Wireframe but keeps relationship styling on edges. It also removes interaction: components are locked, and nothing can be grabbed, dragged, selected, resized, or double-clicked.

The exact element-by-element breakdown is on [Performance Limits]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/performance.md" >}}).

## Why less detail is faster

Panning and zooming move the viewport, and every visible element must follow. In Full, that means repositioning badges, redrawing images and gradients, and tracing curved, colored edges on every frame of the gesture. Each mode below Full removes some of that per-frame work, so the same design responds faster as fidelity drops. The design's size does not change; the cost of looking at it does.

## Adaptive mode

Adaptive mode lets Kanvas turn the dial for you. Turning it on in the switcher shows an AUTO chip, and the mode you pick from then on becomes the **ceiling**: the highest fidelity Adaptive mode may use. The default ceiling is Full, and the canvas switches to the ceiling as soon as Adaptive mode turns on.

**What it measures.** While Adaptive mode is on, Kanvas measures how long the canvas takes to show the next frame after each pan or zoom. It keeps the last 20 measurements and acts on the 95th percentile, so a single slow frame does not trigger a change. It measures nothing while the canvas is idle.

**The ladder.** Adaptive mode moves one step at a time between Full, Medium, and Wireframe. It never enters or leaves View-only; that mode is always your choice.

**Down fast, up slow.** When the 95th percentile exceeds 80 ms, Kanvas drops one step, and it can drop another step 3 seconds later if the canvas is still slow. Climbing back requires 10 consecutive fast measurements (under 30 ms), at least 5 seconds since the last change, and a next mode no higher than the ceiling. The asymmetry is deliberate: lag is an immediate problem, and returning too early causes the canvas to flicker between modes.

**How it behaves today:**

- Each automatic change shows a notification, such as "Switched to Medium mode for better performance" or "Performance improved - switched to Full mode".
- The switcher shows the ceiling, not the mode currently drawn. Use the notifications to tell which mode is active.
- After a slowdown, Kanvas climbs back at most one step. It stays at that mode until the next slowdown, even when the canvas is fast again.
- Changing the ceiling while Adaptive mode is on updates the switcher, but the new ceiling takes effect the next time you turn Adaptive mode on.
- Turning Adaptive mode off leaves the canvas in whichever mode Adaptive mode last chose.

You can also start a session in a given mode or with Adaptive mode on through the URL. When a URL sets both, Adaptive mode starts with a Full ceiling and the URL's mode as the starting mode. See [URL Parameters]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/url-parameters.md" >}}).

## How render mode interacts with other features

**Size gates.** Some features turn themselves off on large designs, and render mode moves the threshold. Auto-pan on drag, which is off by default, runs only while the design's component and edge counts stay under a per-mode limit that rises as fidelity drops. Kanvas re-checks the limit whenever you add or remove elements or change modes, so the feature returns without a reload. Animated layout runs only in Full and only on small designs; in every other case, layouts apply instantly. See [Auto-pan on Drag]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/autopan.md" >}}) and [Performance Limits]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/performance.md" >}}) for the numbers.

**Zoom.** Feasibility evaluation and component style editing depend on zoom level, not render mode. They become available only once you zoom in past a fixed level, in every mode.

**Layers.** Layer visibility is saved with the design and applies in every mode. A hidden layer stays hidden in Full, and switching modes never brings it back. TagSets need both conditions: the TagSets layer must be visible and the mode must be Full. See [Layout and Layers]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/layout-and-layers/index.md" >}}).

## Designer and Operator

Render mode works the same way in [Designer]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/designer/index.md" >}}) and [Operator]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/operator/index.md" >}}). Operator's badges, which show resources managed by Meshery and terminal sessions, appear only in Full, like the other decorative badges.

## Choosing a mode

- **Full** - reviewing, presenting, or capturing a design when every badge and TagSet matters.
- **Medium** - everyday editing on a design large enough that Full feels slow.
- **Wireframe** - layout passes and heavy panning on large designs where structure matters more than appearance.
- **View-only** - showing a design to others when nobody should move anything by accident.
- **Adaptive, Full ceiling** - general work when you would rather not manage the dial. Turn it off for screenshots, recordings, and side-by-side comparisons, where a mode change in the middle would mislead.

## Related pages

- [Performance Limits]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/performance.md" >}}): render-mode matrix, size gates, and limits.
- [URL Parameters]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/url-parameters.md" >}}): set the render mode and Adaptive mode on load.
- [Auto-pan on Drag]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/autopan.md" >}}): the setting and its per-mode thresholds.
- [Layout and Layers]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/layout-and-layers/index.md" >}}): layer visibility and layout behavior.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Deploy WordPress and MySQL with Persistent Volumes"
url: /kanvas/tutorials/kubernetes/wordpress-mysql-persistentvolume/index.md
description: Build a stateful two-tier application in Kanvas with a Secret and PersistentVolumes, deploy it, and learn what persists, where, and what Undeploy leaves behind.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

In this tutorial you deploy WordPress backed by a MySQL database, and you give both tiers storage that outlives their Pods. You import the two Kubernetes example manifests into one design, add the Secret that holds the database password, and add the PersistentVolumes that the claims bind to. Stateless Pods can be replaced at any moment; a database cannot lose its files when that happens. This tutorial shows how Kubernetes separates the data from the Pod, and exactly which pieces a deploy creates and an undeploy removes.

## What you will learn

- How a PersistentVolumeClaim requests storage and how Kubernetes binds it to a PersistentVolume.
- Why data on a volume survives Pod restarts, and where it physically lives with a `hostPath` volume.
- How a Secret passes a password to containers without writing it into the Deployment, and what a Secret does not protect.
- How labels and sections organize a design without changing what it deploys.
- What Undeploy removes and what it leaves in place.

## Before you begin

- **A cluster-backed Kanvas environment.** Deploying needs a Kubernetes cluster connected to Meshery. Use [Meshery Playground](https://play.meshery.io), a shared live cluster, or a self-hosted Meshery with a connected cluster. Hosted kanvas.new does not run cluster actions: Validate, Deploy, and Undeploy there open a prompt to self-host instead. Operator views and terminal sessions also need Meshery Operator and MeshSync running in the cluster.
- **The multi-tier pattern.** You have completed [Deploy a PHP Guestbook with Redis]({{< ref "kanvas/tutorials/kubernetes/deploy-php-redis/index.md" >}}), or you already know how to import and merge manifests and how Services select Pods. [Understanding Kubernetes ConfigMaps and Secrets]({{< ref "kanvas/tutorials/kubernetes/kubernetes-configmaps-secrets/index.md" >}}) covers Secrets in more depth.
- **Unique names.** Playground is shared. Deploy replaces any object with the same kind, name, and namespace, and Undeploy deletes by kind and name. This tutorial uses the namespace `wordpress-ada` and the prefix `ada` for cluster-wide names; substitute your own.

## The scenario

You build nine objects. Two of them, the PersistentVolumes, are cluster-scoped; the rest live in your namespace.

```text
  wordpress (Service, LoadBalancer, port 80)          mysql-pass (Secret)
        |                                              /          \
  wordpress (Deployment) ---- WORDPRESS_DB_PASSWORD --'            '-- MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD
        |        \                                                       |
        |         '-- connects to host "wordpress-mysql" -->  wordpress-mysql (Service, headless, 3306)
        |                                                                |
  wp-pv-claim (PVC, 20Gi)                                  wordpress-mysql (Deployment, Recreate)
        |                                                                |
  ada-wp-pv (PV, hostPath)                                 mysql-pv-claim (PVC, 20Gi)
                                                                         |
                                                           ada-mysql-pv (PV, hostPath)
```

The two manifests, [mysql-deployment.yaml](https://kubernetes.io/examples/application/wordpress/mysql-deployment.yaml) and [wordpress-deployment.yaml](https://kubernetes.io/examples/application/wordpress/wordpress-deployment.yaml), each hold a Service, a PersistentVolumeClaim, and a Deployment. They do not include the Secret or any PersistentVolume: both Deployments expect a Secret named `mysql-pass`, and the claims expect the cluster to provide storage. You add those pieces yourself.

## Import and merge the manifests

1. On an empty canvas, import `https://kubernetes.io/examples/application/wordpress/mysql-deployment.yaml` with the **Import Design** dialog (URL Import). Name it after your design, for example `wordpress-ada`.
2. Import `https://kubernetes.io/examples/application/wordpress/wordpress-deployment.yaml` and choose **Merge into current**.
3. Set the namespace of all six components to `wordpress-ada`.

**What just happened.** Each import converted one multi-document manifest into components and saved it as its own design; merging copied the second design's components into the open one. The open design now holds six components, and your account also holds the single-manifest WordPress design, which you can delete at the end. Deploy creates the `wordpress-ada` namespace if it does not exist.

**Check your work.** The canvas shows two Deployments, two Services, and two PersistentVolumeClaims. If an import fails with `Failed to import design "<name>"`, download the file and import it with File Upload, keeping the `.yaml` extension.

## Add the Secret for the database password

Both Deployments read the password from the Secret `mysql-pass`, key `password`:

```yaml
env:
- name: MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD
  valueFrom:
    secretKeyRef:
      name: mysql-pass
      key: password
```

1. Encode a throwaway password in base64, for example `echo -n 'tutorial-only' | base64`.
2. Add a **Secret** component from the Kubernetes components in the dock.
3. Set its name to `mysql-pass`, its namespace to `wordpress-ada`, and its type to `Opaque`.
4. Add one data entry with the key `password` and your base64 value.

**What just happened.** The Deployments refer to the password by Secret name and key, so the password never appears in either Deployment, and you can change it without editing them. Base64 is an encoding, not encryption. The value is stored in your design, and new designs are saved with public visibility, so anyone who can open the design can decode it. Use a password that protects nothing else. In Operator, the details panel shows a Secret's type but not its values; the resource download from the details panel does include them.

**Check your work.** The Secret's name and key match the `secretKeyRef` exactly. A mismatch does not fail Validate or the dry run; it shows up after deployment as Pods that never start, with a status such as `CreateContainerConfigError`.

## Add PersistentVolumes and bind the claims

The claims in the manifests request 20Gi each and name no storage class, which means "use the cluster's default dynamic provisioner". Instead, you provide the volumes yourself and bind each claim to them through a storage class name of your own.

1. Add two **PersistentVolume** components. They are cluster-scoped, so they have no namespace field, and their names must be unique across the whole cluster: name them `ada-wp-pv` and `ada-mysql-pv`.
2. On both, set the storage class name to `ada-manual`, add the access mode `ReadWriteOnce`, and set the capacity to `storage: 20Gi`.
3. Give each a `hostPath` volume source with type `DirectoryOrCreate`: path `/mnt/data/ada-wp-pv` for the WordPress volume and `/mnt/data/ada-mysql-pv` for the MySQL volume.
4. Set the storage class name of both claims, `wp-pv-claim` and `mysql-pv-claim`, to `ada-manual`.

**What just happened.** A claim is a request: "20Gi, mounted read-write by one node, from class `ada-manual`." The Kubernetes control plane binds each claim to an available volume of the same class with a compatible access mode and at least the requested capacity. The class name needs no StorageClass object behind it; it only has to match. A class name unique to you keeps another reader's claim from binding your volume. A `hostPath` volume is a directory on the node where the Pod runs, so the data belongs to that node. That is acceptable for learning and wrong for production, where a node failure takes the data with it.

**Check your work.** You have two PersistentVolumes and two claims, all with the class `ada-manual`, and each volume's capacity is at least its claim's request.

## Label and group the components

1. Add the label `tutorial: wordpress-ada` to every component in its **Labels** tab.
2. Add two sections (the Section tool in the dock, or press `S`). Name one `web tier` and the other `database tier`, and drag the WordPress and MySQL components into their sections.

**What just happened.** Labels on a component become labels on the object it deploys, so you can filter for all of your objects at once in Operator, across kinds. These labels change object metadata only. They do not change any Deployment's Pod template or any Service's selector, so they do not affect traffic. Sections are annotations: a section is saved with the design, components inside it move with it, and Deploy skips it because annotations are never applied to the cluster.

**Check your work.** The design has nine Kubernetes components inside two sections, and each component lists the new label.

## Deploy and verify

1. Run **Validate**, then **Deploy**. Select the environment that holds your cluster connection.
2. At the dry-run step, expect a not-found error for each namespaced component on the first deployment: a dry run does not create namespaces, and `wordpress-ada` does not exist yet. Select **Bypass errors and initiate deployment**. Any other error names the field at fault.
3. Confirm the deployment and read the summary.

**What just happened.** Meshery Server created the namespace, then created each object, or replaced it in place if it already existed. Independent components are applied in parallel, with no ordering. Kubernetes reconciles the rest: a Pod waits for its claim to bind, a container that starts before its Secret exists retries, and WordPress restarts until MySQL accepts connections. The MySQL Deployment uses the `Recreate` strategy so that an update stops the old Pod before the new one mounts the same `ReadWriteOnce` volume.

**Check your work.** The summary lists nine `Deployed` rows. A `Failed to deploy` row carries an error card with the cause and remediation. Read the rows even when the notification says the deployment completed, since it also says so when some components failed.

## Inspect storage in Operator

1. Open the design in Operator. The view is scoped to the objects your design created.
2. In the Layers panel, open the **Storage** group and turn on PersistentVolumes and PersistentVolumeClaims, or filter by the label `tutorial=wordpress-ada`.
3. Select `ada-mysql-pv`. Its details show capacity, the bound claim and its namespace, access modes, and storage class.
4. Select the `wordpress` Service. Its type is `LoadBalancer`.
5. Optional: right-click the MySQL Pod, start a terminal session, and run `ls /var/lib/mysql` to see the database files on the mounted volume.

**What just happened.** Operator shows a snapshot of the cluster from MeshSync, refetched when you open a view, change a filter, or change clusters; it does not stream. Change a filter to see Pods that were still starting. A `LoadBalancer` Service receives an external address only when the cluster has a load balancer integration, so on Playground the load balancer field stays empty and WordPress is reachable only inside the cluster.

**Check your work.** Both claims and both volumes show `Bound`, and both Pods are Running. A claim stuck in Pending means no volume matched its class, access mode, or size; compare the claim's storage class with the volume's. A Pod stuck in Pending is usually waiting for that claim.

## What persistence means here

MySQL writes its files to `/var/lib/mysql`, which is the mounted claim, which is bound to `ada-mysql-pv`, which is the directory `/mnt/data/ada-mysql-pv` on a node. When the Pod is replaced, for a crash, an update, or a rescheduling, the new Pod mounts the same claim and finds the same files. The data's lifetime is tied to the volume and the directory, not to any Pod.

The limit of this setup is the node. A `hostPath` directory exists on one node only. If the replacement Pod lands on a different node, it gets a different, empty directory. Production clusters use a storage class backed by network or cloud storage, which can follow a Pod from node to node. The Kubernetes documentation on [Persistent Volumes](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/storage/persistent-volumes/) covers binding, reclaim policies, and dynamic provisioning in full.

## Clean up

1. Run **Undeploy** and select the same environment.
2. Delete the design and the single-manifest WordPress design if you no longer need them. See [Deleting a design]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/designs/deleting-a-design/index.md" >}}).

Undeploy deletes each component's object by kind and name. This design has a component for every object you built, so Undeploy removes both Deployments, both Services, the Secret, both claims, and both PersistentVolumes. Kubernetes holds a claim's deletion until no Pod uses it, and a volume's until no claim is bound to it, so the order resolves itself. Sections were never deployed, so there is nothing to remove for them. [Undeploying designs]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/deploying/undeploying-designs/index.md" >}}) describes removal in full.

Undeploy does not remove:

- **The data.** Deleting a manually created PersistentVolume object does not delete the files under `/mnt/data/ada-wp-pv` and `/mnt/data/ada-mysql-pv`. If you deploy again and the Pods land on the same node, MySQL starts with its old database.
- **The namespace.** `wordpress-ada` remains, empty, because the design has no Namespace component.
- **Anything not in the design.** Undeploy acts only on components it finds in the design. Had you removed the PersistentVolume components before undeploying, the volumes would stay in the cluster.

## What you learned

- A claim requests storage by class, access mode, and size; the control plane binds it to a matching volume, and a unique class name keeps the binding yours.
- Data lives on the volume, not in the Pod, so it survives Pod replacement; with `hostPath` it is also tied to one node.
- A Secret decouples a password from the Deployments that use it, but base64 is not encryption, and a Secret component stores its value in the design.
- Labels and sections organize a design. Labels also mark the deployed objects; sections never reach the cluster.
- Undeploy removes exactly the components in the design, by kind and name, and leaves volume data and unlisted objects in place.

## Next steps

- Give each replica its own identity and its own volume in [Deploy Cassandra with a StatefulSet]({{< ref "kanvas/tutorials/kubernetes/deploy-apache-cassandra-with-statefulset/index.md" >}}).
- Review every deploy option and failure mode in [Deploying designs]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/deploying/deploying-designs/index.md" >}}).
- Learn how Operator discovers and draws cluster resources in [Operator]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/operator/index.md" >}}).


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Deploy Cassandra with a StatefulSet"
url: /kanvas/tutorials/kubernetes/deploy-apache-cassandra-with-statefulset/index.md
description: Deploy a three-node Apache Cassandra ring from Kanvas and learn how a StatefulSet and a headless Service give each replica a stable name, a stable volume, and an ordered start.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

In this tutorial you deploy Apache Cassandra as a three-node ring. A Deployment treats its Pods as interchangeable; Cassandra cannot, because each node owns part of the data and other nodes must find it at a known address. A StatefulSet gives every replica a fixed ordinal, a fixed DNS name, and its own volume, and starts the replicas one at a time. You import the Kubernetes example manifests into a Kanvas design, adapt them to your cluster, deploy, and watch the ring form.

## What you will learn

- How a headless Service gives each StatefulSet Pod its own DNS name.
- Why ordinals and stable network identity let a clustered database find its peers.
- How a StatefulSet starts replicas in order and why that matters for a seed node.
- How volume claim templates give each replica its own persistent storage, and why that storage outlives the StatefulSet.

## Before you begin

- **A cluster-backed Kanvas environment.** Deploying needs a Kubernetes cluster connected to Meshery. Use [Meshery Playground](https://play.meshery.io), a shared live cluster, or a self-hosted Meshery with a connected cluster. Hosted kanvas.new does not run cluster actions: Validate, Deploy, and Undeploy there open a prompt to self-host instead. Operator views and terminal sessions also need Meshery Operator and MeshSync running in the cluster.
- **Dynamic storage.** The cluster needs a default StorageClass that provisions volumes on demand, because each Cassandra node claims its own volume.
- **Capacity.** Each Cassandra Pod requests half a CPU and 1Gi of memory, three Pods in total.
- **Persistence basics.** You have completed [Deploy WordPress and MySQL with Persistent Volumes]({{< ref "kanvas/tutorials/kubernetes/wordpress-mysql-persistentvolume/index.md" >}}), or you know how claims bind to volumes.
- **A namespace of your own.** Playground is shared, and Deploy and Undeploy act on objects by kind and name. This tutorial uses the namespace `cassandra-ada`; substitute your own.

## The scenario

```text
  cassandra (Service, clusterIP: None, port 9042)
      |  gives each Pod a DNS name: <pod>.cassandra.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local
      |
  cassandra (StatefulSet, 3 replicas, serviceName: cassandra)
      |
      +-- cassandra-0  -->  cassandra-data-cassandra-0 (PVC, 1Gi)   seed node, starts first
      +-- cassandra-1  -->  cassandra-data-cassandra-1 (PVC, 1Gi)   starts when cassandra-0 is Ready
      +-- cassandra-2  -->  cassandra-data-cassandra-2 (PVC, 1Gi)   starts when cassandra-1 is Ready
```

[cassandra-service.yaml](https://kubernetes.io/examples/application/cassandra/cassandra-service.yaml) holds the headless Service. [cassandra-statefulset.yaml](https://kubernetes.io/examples/application/cassandra/cassandra-statefulset.yaml) holds the StatefulSet and a StorageClass named `fast`. The Pods and claims in the diagram are not in either manifest: the StatefulSet controller creates them from the StatefulSet's Pod template and volume claim template.

## Import and merge the manifests

1. On an empty canvas, import `https://kubernetes.io/examples/application/cassandra/cassandra-service.yaml` with the **Import Design** dialog (URL Import), named after your design, for example `cassandra-ada`.
2. Import `https://kubernetes.io/examples/application/cassandra/cassandra-statefulset.yaml` and choose **Merge into current**.

**What just happened.** Each import converted a manifest into components and saved it as its own design in your account; the merge copied the StatefulSet manifest's components into the open design. If an import fails with `Failed to import design "<name>"`, download the file and import it with File Upload, keeping the `.yaml` extension.

**Check your work.** The canvas shows three components: a Service, a StatefulSet, and a StorageClass.

## Adapt the manifests to your cluster

The example targets a single-node minikube cluster in the `default` namespace. Three changes make it portable.

1. **Namespace.** Set the namespace of the Service and the StatefulSet to `cassandra-ada`.
2. **Seed address.** In the StatefulSet's container environment variables, change `CASSANDRA_SEEDS` from `cassandra-0.cassandra.default.svc.cluster.local` to `cassandra-0.cassandra.cassandra-ada.svc.cluster.local`.
3. **Storage.** Delete the `fast` StorageClass component, and clear the storage class name in the StatefulSet's volume claim template so each claim uses the cluster's default StorageClass.

**What just happened.** The seed address is the heart of this tutorial. A new Cassandra node joins the ring by contacting a seed, so the seed's address must be known before any Pod exists. A StatefulSet makes that possible: its Pods are named `<statefulset>-<ordinal>`, and the headless Service named in `serviceName` gives each one the DNS name `<pod>.<service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local`. `cassandra-0` therefore always answers at the same name, even after it is rescheduled to another node with a new IP address. The name includes the namespace, which is why the seed must change with it.

The `fast` StorageClass uses the minikube host-path provisioner, which provisions nothing on other clusters; claims against it stay Pending, and so do the Pods. A StorageClass is also cluster-scoped, so on a shared cluster its name can collide with another reader's. If you run minikube and keep the StorageClass, expect the dry run to report a not-found error for it even though the object is valid; bypass that error at the dry-run step.

**Check your work.** The design holds two components, both in `cassandra-ada`, and the seed address names your namespace.

## Deploy the ring

1. Run **Validate**, then **Deploy**, and select the environment that holds your cluster connection.
2. At the dry-run step, expect a not-found error for both components on the first deployment, because a dry run does not create namespaces and `cassandra-ada` does not exist yet. Select **Bypass errors and initiate deployment**.
3. Confirm the deployment and read the summary.

**What just happened.** Meshery Server created the namespace and applied both objects, in parallel and in no particular order. Kanvas applies only the two objects in your design. Everything after that is the StatefulSet controller's work: it creates `cassandra-0` and its claim, waits until that Pod is Running and Ready, then creates `cassandra-1`, then `cassandra-2`. Ordered start matters here because `cassandra-0` is the seed; the later nodes join a ring that already exists instead of racing to form separate ones. The readiness probe in the Pod template tells the controller when a node is ready.

**Check your work.** The summary lists two `Deployed` rows: Service `cassandra` and StatefulSet `cassandra`. A `Failed to deploy` row carries an error card with the cause and remediation.

## Watch ordered startup in Operator

1. Open the design in Operator, then filter by your namespace in the Layers panel so the view includes the Pods and claims the controller created.
2. Change a filter every minute or so to refresh the snapshot, and watch `cassandra-0`, `cassandra-1`, and `cassandra-2` appear in turn. Cassandra takes a few minutes to bootstrap each node.
3. Select the StatefulSet. Its details show available Pods out of replicas, the selector, the image, and the update strategy.
4. Open the **Storage** group in the Layers panel and select `cassandra-data-cassandra-0`. Its details show the requested size, storage class, and access modes.
5. Right-click `cassandra-0`, start a terminal session, and run `nodetool status`.

**What just happened.** Operator draws a snapshot from MeshSync and refetches only when you open a view, change a filter, or change clusters, which is why you refresh to follow the rollout. Each claim is named `<template>-<pod>`, so `cassandra-0` always mounts `cassandra-data-cassandra-0`. Ordinal, DNS name, and volume form one identity: if `cassandra-0` is deleted, its replacement gets the same name, the same address, and the same data.

**Check your work.** Three Pods are Running and Ready, three claims are Bound, and `nodetool status` lists three nodes with status `UN` (up, normal). If only `cassandra-0` exists after several minutes, it has not passed its readiness probe, so the controller is holding the others back; read its logs with a log session. If `cassandra-0` is Pending, its claim is Pending: the cluster has no default StorageClass, or it is out of CPU or memory.

## Clean up

1. Run **Undeploy** and select the same environment.
2. Delete the design and the single-manifest Cassandra design if you no longer need them. See [Deleting a design]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/designs/deleting-a-design/index.md" >}}).
3. Delete the claims, if you have `kubectl` access to the cluster: `kubectl delete pvc -l app=cassandra -n cassandra-ada`.

Undeploy deletes each component's object by kind and name, so it removes the Service and the StatefulSet; Kubernetes then deletes the StatefulSet's Pods. It does not remove the three claims. They are not components in the design, and Kubernetes keeps volume claims when a StatefulSet is deleted, by design, so that a database's data is never lost by accident. If you deploy the design again, the new `cassandra-0` mounts the old `cassandra-data-cassandra-0` and finds its data. The namespace also remains, because the design has no Namespace component. See [Undeploying designs]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/deploying/undeploying-designs/index.md" >}}) for the full removal behavior.

## What you learned

- A headless Service plus a StatefulSet gives every replica a DNS name built from its ordinal, so peers can be configured before they exist.
- Stable identity means name, address, and volume travel together across rescheduling.
- The StatefulSet controller starts replicas in order and waits for readiness, which lets the seed node form the ring before others join.
- Volume claim templates give each replica its own claim, and those claims outlive both the StatefulSet and Undeploy.
- Kanvas deploys and removes only the objects in the design; controllers create and own the rest.

## Next steps

- Review every deploy option and failure mode in [Deploying designs]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/deploying/deploying-designs/index.md" >}}).
- Learn how Operator discovers and draws cluster resources in [Operator]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/operator/index.md" >}}).
- Revisit storage binding and reclaim behavior in [Deploy WordPress and MySQL with Persistent Volumes]({{< ref "kanvas/tutorials/kubernetes/wordpress-mysql-persistentvolume/index.md" >}}).


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "How Kanvas Works with Meshery and Layer5 Cloud"
url: /kanvas/concepts/architecture/index.md
description: How Kanvas runs inside Meshery, where designs are stored, what talks to your clusters, and what differs between kanvas.new and self-hosted Meshery.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Kanvas is not a standalone service. It is an extension that runs inside Meshery, relies on Meshery Server to reach your clusters, and relies on a remote provider, Layer5 Cloud, to store and share designs. Knowing which part does what explains why some features need a cluster connection, why others need an account, and why the hosted Kanvas at kanvas.new offers a subset of what a self-hosted Meshery deployment offers.

<figure>
  <img src="images/kanvas-meshery-provider-architecture.webp" alt="Architecture diagram titled Meshery Architecture - Providers. On the left, a Remote Provider and a Local Provider connect to Meshery in the center. On the right, Meshery connects to Kubernetes clusters, where Meshery Operator runs MeshSync and Meshery Broker, and to adapters." />
  <figcaption>Read the diagram from left to right. Providers sit on the left: Meshery runs with either a remote provider (Layer5 Cloud for Kanvas), which stores designs and handles identity and sharing, or a local provider. Meshery sits in the middle and mediates every request. Your clusters sit on the right, where Meshery Operator runs MeshSync and Meshery Broker to report live state back to Meshery.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Kanvas is a Meshery extension

Kanvas has two parts, and both run inside Meshery:

- **The Kanvas interface** loads into Meshery UI at runtime. Designer and Operator modes are screens of Meshery UI supplied by the extension.
- **A server-side plugin** is loaded by Meshery Server and adds Kanvas behavior to it.

Because Kanvas lives inside Meshery, it inherits Meshery's connections to your clusters and Meshery's choice of provider.

## Every request goes through Meshery Server

Kanvas sends every request to Meshery Server. Meshery Server then does one of two things:

- **Answers local requests itself.** Requests about your connected clusters and their resources stay within Meshery.
- **Forwards provider-bound requests to the remote provider.** Requests for designs, views, the catalog, sharing, and support go to Layer5 Cloud, and Meshery Server relays the response back to Kanvas.

Kanvas never calls Layer5 Cloud directly, with one exception: real-time collaboration, described below.

The provider also decides which features Kanvas offers. Each provider publishes a capability document that lists the features it supports, and Kanvas enables only those features. The hosted Kanvas at kanvas.new ships its own capability document.

## Where designs live

The remote provider persists your designs. Layer5 Cloud stores each design and every version of it, records who a design is shared with, hosts the catalog of published designs, and keeps the event log. For example, when Kanvas completes a validation of a whole design, it publishes a validation event to the Layer5 Cloud event log.

## What talks to your clusters

Meshery Server, not your browser, talks to your Kubernetes clusters. It reaches them through components it deploys into each cluster:

- **Meshery Operator** runs in the cluster and deploys MeshSync and Meshery Broker there.
- **MeshSync** records the state of the cluster in Meshery Server.

Meshery Server feeds that inventory into Operator mode. Operator draws a snapshot of it each time you load a view, change a filter, or change clusters, so it reflects the cluster as of the last refresh. When you dry-run, deploy, or undeploy a design, Meshery performs the operation against the Kubernetes contexts you selected, or against all connected contexts when you select none. Meshery can also connect to adapters, which Kanvas does not require for designing or deploying.

Every resource Kanvas deploys carries a label with the id of its source design and annotations with the design version and component id. Operator's per-design view uses that label to show exactly what one design produced. See [Designs and Components]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/designs/index.md" >}}).

## Real-time collaboration: the one direct path

Real-time collaboration is the only path from your browser straight to Layer5 Cloud. When you edit a design with others, your browser connects to a signaling service hosted by Layer5 Cloud, which introduces the participants to each other. After that, edits synchronize directly between participants' browsers, peer to peer over WebRTC, rather than through Meshery Server.

## Hosted kanvas.new versus self-hosted Meshery

The hosted Kanvas at [kanvas.new](https://kanvas.new) is for authoring designs. Every capability that needs a cluster is reserved for Meshery deployments: the [Meshery Playground](https://playground.meshery.io) or your own self-hosted Meshery.

| Capability | kanvas.new, anonymous | kanvas.new, signed in | Meshery Playground or self-hosted Meshery, signed in |
|---|---|---|---|
| Author and edit designs | Available | Available | Available |
| Import designs | Available | Available | Available |
| Share and publish designs | Requires sign-in | Available | Available |
| Validate | Not available | Not available | Available |
| Dry-run | Not available | Not available | Available |
| Deploy and undeploy | Not available | Not available | Available |
| Operator mode | Not available | Not available | Available |
| Connect clusters | Not available | Not available | Available |

Every action in the table also requires the matching permission in your organization. Validate, dry-run, deploy, and undeploy are disabled while the design is empty.

What you see when you reach a boundary:

- **A cluster-bound capability on kanvas.new** opens a prompt that explains Operator mode is not available on kanvas.new and directs you to the Meshery Playground or a self-hosted Meshery deployment.
- **Sharing or publishing while anonymous** opens a "Sign in to" prompt that names the feature and offers a single Sign in action. You are anonymous when no user is signed in or the signed-in user has anonymous status.
- **Signing in** navigates the whole page to the provider and returns you to the page you started from. If the provider address is malformed, sign-in does not start and Kanvas shows the error "Sign-in could not start:" followed by the reason.

## The local provider limitation

Meshery can run with a local provider instead of a remote one. Under the local provider there is no remote service to forward requests to, so every provider-bound feature, including views, the catalog, sharing, and support requests, returns HTTP 501 Not Implemented. Use a remote provider such as Layer5 Cloud for any feature that depends on it.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Keyboard Shortcuts"
url: /kanvas/reference/keyboard-shortcuts/index.md
description: Complete list of Kanvas keyboard shortcuts for Windows, Linux and macOS, with the mode each one works in.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Kanvas binds every shortcut to both modifier keys. On Windows and Linux use <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>. On macOS use <kbd>Cmd</kbd>. The tables write the modifier as <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>/<kbd>Cmd</kbd>.

Kanvas ignores shortcuts while you type in a text field, so typing a label, a comment or a search never triggers one. Open the same list inside the app with <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>/<kbd>Cmd</kbd> + <kbd>/</kbd>.

## Modes and navigation

| Shortcut | Action | Designer | Operator |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <kbd>V</kbd> or <kbd>Esc</kbd> | Switch to the Select tool. <kbd>Esc</kbd> also closes open menus and dialogs. | Yes | Yes |
| <kbd>H</kbd> | Switch to the Pan tool. | Yes | Yes |
| <kbd>Space</kbd> (hold) | Pan while the key is down, then return to the Select tool. | Yes | Yes |
| <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>/<kbd>Cmd</kbd> + <kbd>P</kbd> | Turn the Pencil tool on or off. | Yes | No |
| <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>/<kbd>Cmd</kbd> + <kbd>E</kbd> | Turn the Pen tool on or off. | Yes | No |
| <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>/<kbd>Cmd</kbd> + <kbd>+</kbd> | Zoom in. | Yes | Yes |
| <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>/<kbd>Cmd</kbd> + <kbd>-</kbd> | Zoom out. | Yes | Yes |
| <kbd>&#92;</kbd> (backslash) | Open the Layers panel. | Yes | Yes |
| <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>/<kbd>Cmd</kbd> + <kbd>/</kbd> | Open the shortcut reference in the help drawer. | Yes | Yes |
| <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>/<kbd>Cmd</kbd> + <kbd>Shift</kbd> + <kbd>/</kbd> | Open the Help Center. | Yes | Yes |

The tools are described in [Tool Modes]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/tool-modes/index.md" >}}).

## Adding objects

| Shortcut | Action |
| --- | --- |
| <kbd>M</kbd> | Add a comment near the center of the canvas. |
| <kbd>T</kbd> | Add a textbox near the center of the canvas and start typing. |
| <kbd>S</kbd> | Add a section near the center of the canvas. |
| <kbd>I</kbd> | Open the image picker to place an image. |

Adding objects works in Designer mode only. See [Canvas Objects]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/canvas-objects/index.md" >}}).

## Editing

| Shortcut | Action |
| --- | --- |
| <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>/<kbd>Cmd</kbd> + <kbd>Z</kbd> | Undo the last change. |
| <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>/<kbd>Cmd</kbd> + <kbd>Y</kbd> or <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>/<kbd>Cmd</kbd> + <kbd>Shift</kbd> + <kbd>Z</kbd> | Redo the last undone change. |
| <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>/<kbd>Cmd</kbd> + <kbd>A</kbd> | Select all components. |
| <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>/<kbd>Cmd</kbd> + <kbd>C</kbd> | Copy the selection and the relationships between its members. |
| <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>/<kbd>Cmd</kbd> + <kbd>V</kbd> | Paste at the pointer. |
| <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>/<kbd>Cmd</kbd> + <kbd>D</kbd> | Duplicate the selection, 50 pixels right and 50 pixels down. |
| <kbd>Delete</kbd> or <kbd>Backspace</kbd> | Delete the selection. |

Undo and redo work in both modes. Copy, paste, duplicate and delete change the design, so they apply in Designer mode only. Cut has no shortcut because Kanvas has no cut action.

## Mouse and wheel

| Input | Action |
| --- | --- |
| Right-click, or press and hold | Open the object menu on an object, or the canvas menu on empty canvas. |
| Drag on empty canvas (Select tool) | Draw a selection box. |
| <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>/<kbd>Cmd</kbd> + click | Add an object to the selection or remove it. |
| Scroll wheel | Pan vertically. |
| <kbd>Shift</kbd> + scroll wheel, or horizontal scroll | Pan horizontally. |
| <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>/<kbd>Cmd</kbd> + scroll wheel | Zoom toward the pointer. |

In Operator mode, drag on empty canvas and <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>/<kbd>Cmd</kbd> + click select resources in the topology. <kbd>Esc</kbd> closes the interactive terminal while it has focus.

Zooming the page itself, rather than the canvas, is left to your browser. Kanvas binds no shortcut for it.

## Shortcuts that are not bound

The interactive terminal has no keyboard shortcut. Open it from the terminal badge on a container or from the resource's details. See [Interactive Terminal]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/operating/interactive-terminal/index.md" >}}).

Filtering resources in Operator mode is done in the view filters, not with a shortcut. See [Operator Views]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/views/index.md" >}}).


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Kubernetes Request Flow"
url: /kanvas/concepts/kubernetes-request-flow/index.md
description: How a request travels from a client through Ingress or a Service to a Pod and its containers, why labels and selectors hold the path together, how the path maps to a Kanvas design, and how to debug it layer by layer.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

A request to an application in Kubernetes passes through several objects before it reaches a process in a container, and none of those objects is wired to the next by a fixed address. Each layer finds the next one by name or by label at the moment the request arrives. Knowing that path, and what each layer is responsible for, turns "why am I not getting a response?" into a short list of places to look. This page walks the path from the client to the container, explains why labels and selectors are what hold it together, and shows how the same path appears in a Kanvas design.

## The path at a glance

The prebuilt design below models the in-cluster part of the path: a user, a ClusterIP Service, a Deployment, and a Pod running two containers. Select the image to open the design in Kanvas.

[![Kanvas design of a Kubernetes request path: a User sends a request to a ClusterIP Service, which routes it to a Deployment that manages a Pod; inside the Pod are two containers, one for application logic and one for the database layer](images/k8s-request-flow.png)](https://kanvas.new/extension/meshmap?mode=design&design=629b6039-ebb3-4bd8-9b1b-19184fade225)

The full path, including the entry layer the design leaves out, is:

| Layer | Kubernetes object | Responsibility |
|---|---|---|
| Entry | Ingress, or a Service of type LoadBalancer or NodePort | Accept traffic from outside the cluster |
| Stable address | Service (ClusterIP) | Give a changing set of Pods one name and one virtual IP |
| Routing | kube-proxy rules on every node, EndpointSlices | Translate the virtual IP to the IP of one ready Pod |
| Backends | Deployment, ReplicaSet, Pod | Keep the right number of matching Pods running |
| Process | Containers in the Pod | Listen on a port and serve the request |

## Getting into the cluster

A ClusterIP Service is reachable only from inside the cluster. Traffic from outside enters through one of three doors:

- **NodePort.** Kubernetes opens the same port, by default in the range 30000-32767, on every node. A request to any node's IP on that port is forwarded to the Service.
- **LoadBalancer.** The cluster's cloud integration provisions an external load balancer and points it at the Service's node ports. Until the provider assigns an address, the Service's external address stays pending.
- **Ingress.** An Ingress is a set of HTTP routing rules (host and path to Service). The rules do nothing on their own: an Ingress controller, itself exposed through a LoadBalancer or NodePort Service, reads them and proxies each request to the matching Service.

Every door ends in the same place: a Service.

## The Service: a stable name and address

Pods are disposable. They are replaced on every rollout, rescheduled when a node fails, and receive a new IP each time. A Service gives clients something that does not change: a DNS name (`<service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local`, or just `<service>` from the same namespace) and a virtual IP, the ClusterIP. Clients talk to the Service and never need to know which Pods exist right now.

The ClusterIP is not attached to any machine. On every node, kube-proxy (or a replacement that fills the same role) programs packet-forwarding rules that rewrite traffic sent to the ClusterIP and Service port into traffic to one backend Pod's IP and target port. The list of backends comes from EndpointSlices, which Kubernetes keeps current with the IPs of the Pods that match the Service's selector **and** report Ready. A Pod that fails its readiness probe drops out of the list and receives no new traffic until it recovers.

## Labels and selectors are the glue

No layer of this path holds a reference to a specific Pod. Each layer describes the Pods it wants with a label selector, and Kubernetes evaluates the selector continuously:

- The **Service** selector (for example `app: web`) decides which Pods receive traffic.
- The **Deployment** selector decides which Pods the Deployment, through its ReplicaSet, counts and replaces.
- The **Pod template** in the Deployment stamps labels onto every Pod it creates.

For traffic to flow, the Pod template's labels must satisfy both selectors. The Service does not route to the Deployment: it routes to whatever Pods carry matching labels, whoever created them. That design is what lets a rollout replace every Pod without touching the Service, and it is also the most common cause of a silent failure. A one-character difference between a selector and a label produces a Service with no endpoints and no error message.

The ports follow the same pattern. A Service's `targetPort` must be the port the process in the container actually listens on. The container's declared `containerPort` is informational; declaring a port does not make a process listen on it.

## Deployment, ReplicaSet, Pod: who keeps the backends alive

A Deployment does not carry traffic. It declares how many Pods you want and what they look like. The Deployment creates a ReplicaSet for each version of its Pod template, and the ReplicaSet creates and replaces Pods until the count matches. During a rolling update the old and new ReplicaSets both own Pods, and because both sets carry the labels the Service selects, the Service sends traffic to old and new Pods alike until the rollout finishes.

## Inside the Pod: one network namespace

All containers in a Pod share one network namespace. They have the same IP address and the same port space, and they reach each other on `localhost`. In the prebuilt design, the application container can reach the database-layer container at `localhost` on that container's port, and two containers in the same Pod cannot both listen on the same port. A request that arrives at the Pod's IP is delivered to whichever container listens on the target port.

## How the path maps to a Kanvas design

In a Kanvas design, each Kubernetes object on the path is a component, configured with the same fields as its manifest: the Service's type, selector, and ports; the Deployment's replicas, selector, and Pod template; each container's image and ports. The connection between a Service and the workload it fronts is a Network relationship, drawn as an edge labeled with the ports and protocols on each side. A relationship definition can also write a value from one component into the other, such as a Service port into a container port. See [Relationships]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/relationships/index.md" >}}) for the kinds of relationships and what each one changes.

The edge documents intent; the selector and labels decide behavior. When you deploy, the cluster routes traffic according to the selector and labels in the components' configuration, so check those fields whenever the edge and the running system disagree.

After a deploy, Operator shows the same objects as they exist in the cluster. Its resource details show what you need to follow the path: a Service's type, ClusterIP, and selector; a Deployment's available and desired Pods and its selector; a Pod's IP and status; and each container's status, ports, and restart count. Operator can also list EndpointSlices, open a terminal or a log session on a Pod, and filter the view by any label, which shows at once whether a selector's label matches the Pods you expect. Operator reads a snapshot of the cluster, so fetch again after a change by reopening the view or changing a filter.

## Debug a failing path layer by layer

Work from the client inward and stop at the first layer that does not behave:

| Symptom | Layer to check | What to look at |
|---|---|---|
| External clients get no answer, but requests from inside the cluster work | Entry | An Ingress controller is installed and the Ingress names its class; the LoadBalancer has an external address; the NodePort is open in the node firewall |
| The Service name does not resolve | Service | The Service exists in the namespace you are calling; use the full name `<service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local` across namespaces |
| The name resolves, but connections time out | Routing | The Service has endpoints. No endpoints means the selector matches no Pods or no matching Pod is Ready |
| The Service has no endpoints | Labels and selectors | Compare the Service selector with the Pod labels key by key, and check that the matching Pods pass their readiness probes |
| Endpoints exist, but connections are refused | Ports | `targetPort` equals the port the container process listens on, and the process listens on all interfaces, not only `127.0.0.1` |
| Fewer Pods than replicas, or Pods stuck in `Pending` | Deployment and ReplicaSet | Pod events for scheduling and image-pull failures, resource requests, and quotas |
| Pods restart repeatedly | Container | Container logs and exit codes, and liveness probe settings |
| One container cannot reach the other on `localhost` | Pod | Both containers are in the same Pod, the target container listens on the expected port, and no two containers use the same port |

## Related

- [Explore Kubernetes Services]({{< ref "kanvas/tutorials/kubernetes/kubernetes-services/index.md" >}}) - build ClusterIP, NodePort, and LoadBalancer Services and inspect them in Operator.
- [Explore Kubernetes Pods]({{< ref "kanvas/tutorials/kubernetes/kubernetes-pods/index.md" >}}) - build, deploy, and inspect a Pod.
- [Relationships]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/relationships/index.md" >}}) - what each relationship in a design means and changes.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Operator Views"
url: /kanvas/reference/views/index.md
description: What an Operator view stores, how views are saved, shared, opened, exported, and deleted, and who can do what.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

A view is to Operator mode what a design is to Designer mode: a named, saved definition you reopen later. A view stores **which resources to show**, not the resources themselves. Opening a view re-applies its filters to the current inventory of your connected clusters.

## What a view stores

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| Name | Defaults to `Untitled View`. Up to 255 characters. Not required to be unique. |
| Filters | Kinds, models, namespaces, labels, and the name search text. See [Filters](#filters). |
| Visibility | `public` or `private`. |
| Notes | Free text (Markdown) in the view's metadata, edited in View Info. |
| Owner, created, updated | Set by Layer5 Cloud. |

A view does not store layout, zoom, pan, or the selected resource. It does not store cluster selection either: the clusters selected in the Meshery context selector at the time you open the view always win. A copied link includes your current pan and zoom as URL parameters, but they are not saved in the view.

### Filters

| Filter | Matches |
|---|---|
| `kinds` | Resources of any listed Kubernetes kind. |
| `models` | Resources belonging to any listed model. |
| `namespaces` | Resources in any listed namespace, plus the Namespace objects themselves. |
| `labels` | Resources carrying any listed `key=value` label. |
| `search` | Resources whose name contains the text. |

Different filter types combine with AND. Values within one type combine with OR. A new empty view starts with kinds `Node` and `Namespace`.

### Design-scoped views

Choosing **View in Operator** from a design opens an unsaved view named `<design name>-View` whose only filter is the label `design.meshery.io/id=<design id>`. It shows exactly the resources that design deployed. The view is saved on your first filter or name change.

## Saving

Saving is automatic. Any filter change, cluster selection change, or rename saves the view after a three second pause. The first save creates the view; later saves update it. The toolbar shows `Saving...`, then `Saved`, or `Unable to save. Retrying...`. A failed save retries with doubling delays, up to 100 attempts.

Creating a view requires a concrete organization selected. Layer5 Cloud refuses creation when the organization selector is set to all organizations. Every view is created `public`, owned by the caller, and placed in the workspace you have selected for that organization (or your first workspace).

**Save as...** creates a new view with the same filters and the name `<current name>-copy` by default, owned by you, in your selected workspace, and opens it. The original is unchanged. The copy is created `public`; change its visibility afterward if you need it private. A **Clone** command and an **Import** command appear in the code but are not implemented, so Save as is the only way to duplicate a view.

## Opening and finding views

| Where | Result |
|---|---|
| File menu, **Open...** | Opens the Meshery workspace browser in Operator mode. It offers `Recents (Global)`, `My Views`, `Shared With Me`, and each workspace's Views tab. |
| Layer5 Cloud workspace | Views belong to exactly one workspace. Open the workspace and select the view. |
| Design file menu, **View in Operator** | Opens the design-scoped view. |

Non-administrators see views shared with them, public views, and their own private views. Provider administrators also see private views. Moving a view to another workspace needs the **Assign Views to Workspace** permission and is offered while browsing a workspace.

## Visibility and access

| Action | Public view | Private view |
|---|---|---|
| Open | Any user | Owner, users granted access, provider administrators |
| Edit filters, name, visibility, notes | Any signed-in user | Owner, users granted access, provider administrators |
| Share and unshare | Owner only | Owner only |
| Delete | Owner or provider administrator | Owner or provider administrator |

{{< alert type="warning" title="Public views are editable by every signed-in user" >}}
Layer5 Cloud does not check ownership or organization when a public view is updated. Anyone who can reach a public view can change its filters, name, and visibility. Keep a view private, or use **Save as...** and set the copy private, when others should not change it.
{{< /alert >}}

"Provider administrator" is the platform-level administrator role. It is not the organization administrator role.

## Sharing

The toolbar **Share** button opens the share dialog, the same one designs use. It has a **General Access** selector, a **People with Access** list, a user picker, and **Copy Link**.

| General Access setting | Visibility | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `Anyone with the link can edit` | public | Anyone with the link can open and edit. |
| `Only people with access can open with the link` | private | Only listed users can open it. |

Sharing offers a single implicit access level; there are no separate viewer and editor roles. Only the owner can change general access. Sharing sends email to new recipients, and is refused for anonymous sessions. The server requires the **Share Views** permission in the view's organization. Kanvas's own Share button checks the **Share Design** permission, so a role can see the button and still be refused by the server. See [Share a Design]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/collaborating/sharing-designs/index.md" >}}) for the dialog and its messages.

In Operator mode, the file menu's **Share...** item creates a new empty view instead of opening the dialog. Use the toolbar Share button.

## Export

**Export...** in the file menu downloads `<view name>.json`, containing the complete stored view: id, name, visibility, filters, metadata, owner, and timestamps. It is disabled for an unsaved view. Views cannot be imported back.

## View info

**Details** in the file menu (or **View Info** in a view list) shows Owner, Visibility, Notes, Created, and Updated. Everyone can read the notes. Only the owner can change visibility and notes, and only the owner sees **Save**. **Copy Link** is available to everyone.

## Delete

Delete removes the view with a soft delete. The server allows the owner and provider administrators. Anyone else receives a "no view with the requested id" error. The Meshery view list offers **Delete View** to the owner who holds the **Delete View** permission. Kanvas confirms with `Are you sure you want to delete <name>?` and shows no success or failure message afterward; the editor resets to a new empty view either way.

## Permissions and plans

The permission names for views are **View Views**, **Open view**, **Save Views**, **Clone Views**, **Share Views**, **Export views**, **Delete View**, and **Assign Views to Workspace**. Public and private views, view sharing, view export, and assigning views to workspaces are Team Operator plan features and above. Layer5 Cloud does not check most view permission names on the create, update, and delete routes; the access rules in the table above are what the server enforces. See [Permissions by Role]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/permissions.md" >}}) and [Feature Availability]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/feature-availability.md" >}}).

## Related

- [Operator]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/operator/index.md" >}}) explains where the resources a view filters come from.
- [Resource Details]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/resource-details/index.md" >}}) covers what you see when you select a resource in a view.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Troubleshoot Kanvas"
url: /kanvas/guides/troubleshooting/index.md
description: Find the symptom you see, learn what causes it, and apply the fix. Covers loading failures, missing cluster data, and failed deployments.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Kanvas separates two kinds of failure. A design action that fails, such as a dry run or a deployment, produces an event with an error code and a remediation. A Kanvas that fails to load, or an Operator view with no data, produces an in-product message. This page covers both.

{{< alert type="info" title="Ask for help from within Kanvas" >}}
The **Get Help** action opens the Help and Support form. It needs a remote provider and a signed-in identity. See [Help and Support]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/help-and-support.md" >}}).
{{< /alert >}}

## Kanvas does not load

If an unhandled error occurs, or the extension fails to load in the Meshery shell, Kanvas shows `Uh-oh! Something went wrong..` (`Uh-oh! Please pardon our mesh.` in the shell) with the error text. The screen offers:

- **Troubleshooting Guide**, a dialog with the checks below.
- **Get Help**, which opens the Help and Support form.
- **Switch To Designer**, when Designer mode is available.

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| The Kanvas bundle fails to download, or the error says the bundle has no default component | The Meshery shell downloads the Kanvas UI from the provider. A failed download, or a bundle that was built incorrectly, leaves nothing to render. | Reload. If you build Kanvas yourself, rebuild it and confirm the provider serves the new bundle. |
| Missing or stale data after an update | The browser holds a previous version. | Hard-reload the page, or open Kanvas in a private window. |
| Features missing, or errors after upgrading Meshery or Kanvas | The Kanvas version and the Meshery version are out of step. Kanvas has no version-mismatch screen. | Update Meshery, `mesheryctl`, and Kanvas together. The Help Center footer shows the installed Kanvas version. |
| Operator backend fails to start on a self-built Meshery | The server-side plugin is loaded from the provider's package path. A missing file, or dependency versions that differ from your Meshery build, make Meshery reject it. | Build the plugin from the same version as your Meshery server and place it in the provider package path. |

Designer mode does not depend on a connected cluster. Designing, saving, and validating work with none connected.

## A deployment fails

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Dry run, deploy, or undeploy fails with `meshery-server-1096` | No selected context resolved to a connected cluster. | Connect a cluster in Meshery, check that its status is Connected, and select an environment that contains it. |
| `meshery-server-1073` with a note about the environment | The connection is not assigned to the environment you selected, or it cannot reach the cluster. | Assign the connection to the environment, or upload a new kubeconfig. |
| `meshery-server-1095` | The kubeconfig is invalid. | Upload a new kubeconfig. |
| Step 2 shows `No environments found` | Your organization has no environment. | Create an environment and assign a connection to it. This needs the Create Environment and Edit Environment permissions. |
| The Finish step spins and never reports | The request failed before the server raised an event, for example when your session expired. | Sign in again and retry. Check the notification center and the server logs. |
| A prompt titled `SELF-HOSTED FEATURE` opens | You are on kanvas.new, which does not run validate, dry run, deploy, undeploy, or Operator. | Use a Meshery you run. |
| Every component fails an undeploy dry run | The objects are not on the cluster. | Check that the design was deployed, or bypass the errors. |

Error cards, codes, and remediations are described in [Deploy a Design]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/deploying/deploying-designs/index.md" >}}). The notification center's Error Docs entry opens the [Meshery error code reference](https://docs.meshery.io/reference/error-codes).

## Operator mode shows no data

Operator reads the cluster inventory that MeshSync reports through the Meshery broker. Designer keeps working when this is down.

| Message | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `No Kubernetes context selected`, `Please select one or more Kubernetes clusters.` | No cluster is selected in the context picker. | Select one or more clusters. |
| `No data available for the current view` | The view's filters or the search hide every object. | Change the filters or the search. |
| `Uh-oh. Is MeshSync healthy on the selected cluster?` or `No MeshSync data available for the selected cluster` | MeshSync has reported no objects for the cluster. The broker may be unreachable. | Check that the Meshery broker service has an external address with `kubectl get svc -n meshery`, and check firewalls and VPN software. Docker Desktop commonly fails to give the broker an address. |
| Toast `Failed to fetch resources: <reason>` | The request for cluster resources failed. | Read the reason, then check the connection and MeshSync as above. |
| Toast `No container found to create <type> session` | A terminal or log session needs a container and the object has none. | Pick an object that runs a container. |

The Troubleshooting Guide dialog repeats the data checks. It also suggests removing the local Meshery configuration folder as a last resort when stored data is corrupt. That step deletes your local Meshery configuration, so use it only when nothing else restores the data.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Resource Details"
url: /kanvas/reference/resource-details/index.md
description: The fields, actions, and capacity gauges the Details panel shows for each Kubernetes resource kind in Operator mode, and what it does not show.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Selecting a resource on the Operator canvas opens the Details panel. It shows the resource as Meshery last recorded it from the cluster, and it carries the actions that apply to that kind. Fields with no value are omitted, so each kind shows only what applies.

<div style="display:flex;justify-content:center;">
{{< cardpane >}}
  {{< card header="Node Details" >}}
    <img src="images/operator-node-details.png" alt="Details panel for a Kubernetes node" />
    <p><i>Example: Kubernetes Node details.</i></p>
  {{< /card >}}
  {{< card header="Container Details" >}}
    <img src="images/operator-container-details.png" alt="Details panel for a container in a pod" />
    <p><i>Example: Kubernetes Pod Container details.</i></p>
  {{< /card >}}
{{< /cardpane >}}
</div>

## How the panel behaves

- **Opens on a single click.** Selecting several resources does not change this: the panel always shows the last resource you clicked.
- **Not live.** The panel shows the canvas snapshot immediately, then fetches the resource's full record once. It does not update while open. Close and reselect the resource to refresh it. See [Operator]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/operator/index.md" >}}) for how the snapshot is built.
- **Two views.** **Summary** (the default) shows the key fields. **Details** adds the collapsible sections and tables, each titled with its item count, for example `Labels (4)`.
- **Status chip.** Shows the resource's phase when it has one (Running, Pending, Failed, Succeeded, Active, Terminating, Bound, Available, and so on). Otherwise it shows `Ready` whenever the resource has a Ready condition, whatever that condition's value. Do not read `Ready` as a health check.
- **Load failures.** While loading you see a loader. If the fetch fails the panel shows `Error loading instance details.`

## Fields by kind

| Kind | Fields shown |
|---|---|
| All kinds | Age (hours below 24 hours, otherwise days), kind, API version, labels, annotations, condition type names (not their True or False values), and deep links |
| Node | Kubelet version, three capacity gauges, and `Capacity` and `Allocatable` tables |
| Pod | Pod IP, host IP, QoS class, node selector, priority, container count, total restarts, init containers, containers, volumes by type, tolerations |
