--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Connect GitHub"
url: /cloud/guides/integrations/github-integration/index.md
description: Connect the Layer5 GitHub App to Layer5 Cloud, import infrastructure files from your repositories as designs, and manage or remove the connection.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The GitHub integration connects your GitHub account to Layer5 Cloud through the Layer5 GitHub App. Once connected, you can browse the repositories you granted, pick Kubernetes manifests, Helm charts, Docker Compose files, and Meshery designs, and import each file as a design. The same connection can also install a pull-request snapshot workflow in your repositories.

Use it when your infrastructure already lives in Git and you want those files on the canvas without downloading and uploading them one at a time. For a one-off file, [import it directly]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/designs/import-designs/index.md" >}}) instead.

## Before you start

- A Layer5 Cloud account.
- A GitHub account that can install a GitHub App on the user or organization that owns the repositories. For an organization, an owner may have to approve the installation.
- The View Connections permission, which shows the Integrations area in Layer5 Cloud. See [Roles and Permissions]({{< ref "cloud/reference/default-permissions.md" >}}).

### Self-hosted GitHub App requirements {#self-hosted-github-app-requirements}

The hosted service at cloud.layer5.io provides the Layer5 GitHub App. A self-hosted deployment uses its own GitHub App, and from Layer5 Cloud v1.0.287 that App must meet every item below. See the matching values in [Helm Chart Values]({{< ref "cloud/guides/self-hosted/deployment/helm-chart-values.md" >}}).

- Each Layer5 Cloud deployment has its own GitHub App. Do not share one App between deployments, such as production and staging.
- The App's first callback URL is this deployment's `https://<host>/api/integrations/github/callback`, where `<host>` is the deployment's public hostname. Layer5 Cloud sends GitHub no `redirect_uri`, so GitHub always returns to the first callback URL.
- **Request user authorization (OAuth) during installation** is enabled.
- `githubappid`, the private key, `githubAppClientId` and `githubAppClientSecret` all come from that same App.

## How the connection works

- **The connection belongs to you, not to your organization.** Each user has at most one GitHub connection. A teammate who wants to import from GitHub connects their own account.
- **GitHub confirms which installations are yours.** When you install and authorize the App, GitHub reports which installations of the Layer5 GitHub App your GitHub account can access, and only those are connected. This check ships in Layer5 Cloud v1.0.287.
- **The App sees only what you grant.** At install time GitHub asks whether the App may reach all repositories or only the ones you select. Layer5 Cloud lists exactly those repositories. Widen or narrow the grant at any time by running the setup again.
- **Cloud reads the default branch.** Scans and imports always use each repository's default branch.
- **Import is read-only.** Importing creates designs in Layer5 Cloud. It never writes to your repository. Only the optional snapshot stages commit a file.

## Connect and import

The Connect wizard has seven stages. You can start it from the Integrations area of Spaces in Layer5 Cloud, or from the Extensions page of a Meshery Server by enabling the Kanvas Snapshot GitHub Action.

| Stage | What happens | Required |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Connect GitHub App | GitHub asks you to install the Layer5 GitHub App on a personal or organization account and to choose repository access. | Yes |
| Select Repositories | Lists the repositories the App can reach. **Add Repository** reopens the GitHub installation page so you can change access or install on another account. | Yes |
| Import Designs | Lists the files in the chosen repositories. You select files or whole directories and import them. | Yes |
| Select a design for snapshots | Chooses one file per repository for pull-request snapshots. | Optional |
| Configure Secrets | Generates an API token that you add to the repository as a secret. | Optional |
| Add Workflows | Commits the snapshot workflow to the repository. | Optional |
| Finish | Summarizes what was imported and which repositories received the workflow. | Yes |

If you open the GitHub card's connection count before you have connected, the **GitHub Connections** window reads "No GitHub connections yet". Click **Connect GitHub** there to start the wizard, or follow **Learn how the GitHub integration works** to return to this guide.

The three optional stages are covered in [Visualize Pull Requests with Kanvas Snapshot]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/snapshots/kanvas-snapshot/index.md" >}}).

### What you can import

A checkbox switches the file list between every file and only the types Layer5 Cloud can import.

| Type | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| Meshery design | Becomes a design immediately. |
| Kubernetes manifest | Kept as source and converted when you open it. |
| Helm chart | Kept as source and converted when you open it. |
| Docker Compose file | Kept as source and converted when you open it. |
| Kustomize | Kept as source and converted when you open it. |

Layer5 Cloud accepts files with these extensions: `.yml`, `.yaml`, `.json`, `.tar`, `.tar.gz`, `.tar.tgz`, `.zip`, and `.gz`. A file that fails sanitizing or identification is reported as invalid or unsupported.

### What an import produces

- **One design per file.** The design is named after the file, including its extension.
- **Private by default.** The importing user owns it. Publish or share it when you are ready. See [Publish Designs]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/designs/publishing-designs/index.md" >}}).
- **Placed in your selected workspace.** From Layer5 Cloud v1.0.291, each new design is added to the workspace selected in your current organization, or to the organization's first workspace when none is selected, so it shows in My Designs.
- **Traceable to its source.** The design records its repository, path, and branch. Renaming the design does not break that link.
- **Directories import recursively.** Selecting a directory imports every supported file beneath it.
- **Failures are per file.** An unsupported or invalid file produces an error entry and does not stop the other files. The result screen lists what succeeded and what failed.

Imported designs appear in [My Designs](https://cloud.layer5.io/catalog/content/my-designs). After the import, a notification sums up the result, for example `2 designs imported, 1 updated, 3 already imported and skipped.`

### Import from a repository again

When you run the wizard again for a repository you have imported from, for example with **Reconfigure** on the GitHub card, files you already imported carry a check mark. Hover over it to see which design the file became, for example `Imported as "nginx-deployment"`. If you have nothing new to import, click **Next** without importing.

A file is matched to its design by repository, path and branch, never by name. When your selection includes files you imported before, Layer5 Cloud asks what to do with them before importing. The prompt lists the files, up to five followed by "and N more", and offers three choices:

| Choice | What happens to the previously imported files |
| --- | --- |
| **Import new files only** (default) | They are left as they are. Only files that were never imported become new designs. |
| **Update the existing designs** | Each design's content is replaced with the file's current content. The design keeps its ID, sharing and links. Edits made to it since the last import are lost. |
| **Import them again as new designs** | Additional designs are created alongside the existing ones. |

Click **Import** to proceed with your choice, or **Cancel** to change the selection. A file selected both on its own and through its directory is imported once.

### See where a design came from

In the table view of My Designs, the **Source** column shows the repository and file path of each imported design, followed by the branch when it is not the repository's default. Hover over it to see the full source, or click it to open the file on GitHub. The cell is empty for a design that was not imported from GitHub. The column appears on large screens.

An imported design's details page has a **Source** section below the left panel that lists the repository, which links to the file on GitHub, the file path and the branch ("Default branch" when the design follows the repository's default branch). The source stays with the design when you edit it, so later imports and refreshes still recognize it.

### Large repositories

Layer5 Cloud scans a repository by reading its full file tree from GitHub and keeps the result for five minutes. GitHub truncates the tree for very large repositories. When that happens, the file list is partial and Cloud answers with HTTP status 206. If a file you need is missing, select its directory or import it directly.

## Manage imported designs {#manage-imported-designs}

From Layer5 Cloud v1.0.291, your GitHub connection lists every design you have imported from GitHub, with actions to open each one or bring it up to date with its file.

1. On the Integrations area of Spaces in Layer5 Cloud, click the GitHub card's connection count to open **GitHub Connections**.
1. Click your connection to expand it. **Imported designs** lists your imported designs, newest first:

    | Column | Shows |
    | --- | --- |
    | **Design** | The design's name. |
    | **Type** | The format the design was imported from, or `-` when it is not known. |
    | **Source** | The repository, file path and, when it is not the default, branch the design was imported from. Click it to open the file on GitHub. |
    | **Last updated** | When the design last changed. |
    | **Actions** | **Open design** opens the design in My Designs. **Open source file on GitHub** opens the file in a new tab. **Refresh from source** updates the design from the file. |

The list shows only your own designs, and only you can see it on your connection. It includes every design you imported from GitHub, whatever its workspace, so designs imported before Layer5 Cloud v1.0.291 are listed here until you move them to a workspace. When you have not imported any designs yet, it reads "No imported designs yet" and offers **Import designs**, which reopens the wizard. If the list cannot be loaded, it reads "Imported designs could not be loaded"; click **Try again**.

### Refresh a design from its source

When a file changes in its repository, refresh the design instead of importing the file again:

1. In **Imported designs**, click **Refresh from source** on the design's row. The action appears only if your role holds Import Design.
1. Confirm with **Refresh**. The design's content is replaced with the file's current content on GitHub, and changes made to the design since it was imported or last refreshed are lost.

The refresh updates the same design, so it keeps its ID, owner, visibility, catalog data, workspace assignments and links. Only its content and source change. A design that was not imported as a Meshery design keeps its source file unconverted and is converted the next time you open it.

## Check or reconfigure the connection

Layer5 Cloud verifies with GitHub that the App installation the wizard opens on still exists. If you uninstalled the App from that account in GitHub, Cloud removes only that installation from the connection and opens the wizard on the next installation your connection holds. Cloud deletes the connection only once none of its installations remain. Run the wizard again to reconnect.

To change which repositories the App can read, rerun the wizard and use **Add Repository**. GitHub keeps the App installed and updates its grant. When you install the App on another account, the connection is updated with every installation your GitHub account can access, so the new installation joins the ones you already had.

### Re-authorize an existing connection

A connection created before Layer5 Cloud v1.0.287 opens the wizard on **Re-authorize your GitHub connection**, and its repositories cannot be used until GitHub confirms which installations your GitHub account can access. Click **Re-authorize**. GitHub returns you to the wizard, without asking again if you have already authorized the App, and your repository settings are kept.

## Remove the connection

Delete the GitHub connection from the Integrations area, or from the Connections page of a Meshery Server. You can delete only a connection you own, and you need the Delete a connection permission.

Deleting the connection removes it from Layer5 Cloud. It does **not** uninstall the App from GitHub, delete imported designs, or remove a workflow already committed to a repository. To revoke the App's access to your repositories, uninstall the Layer5 GitHub App in your GitHub account settings. Delete `.github/workflows/kanvas.yml` from a repository to stop its snapshots.

## Troubleshooting

| You see | Cause | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A repository is missing from the list | The App is not installed on it. | Use **Add Repository** and grant access in GitHub. |
| `invalid or unsupported file` for a file | The extension or content is not an importable type. | Check the file against the table above. |
| A partial file list | GitHub truncated the tree of a large repository. | Select the directory you need, or import the file directly. |
| `GitHub did not confirm that your GitHub account can access that installation, so it was not connected.` | The GitHub account you are signed in with cannot access the installation you chose. | Sign in to GitHub with an account that can access it, then connect GitHub again. |
| `Your GitHub account cannot access any installation of the GitHub App. Install the app on your account or organization to connect a repository.` | GitHub reports no installation of the App that your GitHub account can access. | Install the App on your account or organization, then connect GitHub again. |
| `GitHub authorization is not configured for this environment, so GitHub cannot be connected. Please contact support.` | The deployment is missing the GitHub App's OAuth client ID or client secret. | On the hosted service, contact support. On a self-hosted deployment, set `env.githubAppClientId` and `env.githubAppClientSecret`. |
| Connect, **Add Repository** or **Re-authorize** ends anywhere other than the wizard, or shows `GitHub authorization could not be completed, so GitHub was not connected. Please connect GitHub again.` or `This GitHub connection was not started from this session, took too long, or was already used, so GitHub was not connected. Please connect GitHub again.` | You declined the authorization on GitHub, took more than five minutes on GitHub, reused a return page, or are signed in to Layer5 Cloud as a different user than the one who started. Changing repository access or installing the App from GitHub's own settings or App page, instead of the wizard, returns you without the request the wizard started. On a self-hosted deployment, the GitHub App can also miss one of its requirements. | Connect GitHub again from the wizard, approve the authorization, and finish on GitHub within five minutes. Change repository access with **Add Repository**, not in GitHub's settings. On a self-hosted deployment, check every item in [Self-hosted GitHub App requirements](#self-hosted-github-app-requirements). |
| The wizard shows **Re-authorize your GitHub connection** | The connection predates installation confirmation. | Click **Re-authorize**. See [Re-authorize an existing connection](#re-authorize-an-existing-connection). |
| The connection vanished | The App was uninstalled from every account it was connected through. | Run the wizard again. |
| `unable to create JWT for GitHub integration, please uninstall app and try again` | The deployment cannot sign requests as the GitHub App. | On the hosted service, uninstall and reinstall the App. On a self-hosted deployment, check the GitHub App credentials in the deployment settings. |
| **Refresh from source** fails because the source file no longer exists | The file was moved, renamed or deleted in its repository. | Import the file from its new location. |
| **Refresh from source** fails because the file is not importable | The file is no longer a valid Helm chart, Kubernetes manifest, Docker Compose file or Meshery design. | Fix the file in its repository and refresh again. |
| **Refresh from source** fails because the App cannot reach the repository | The GitHub App no longer has access to the repository. | Reconfigure the connection with **Add Repository** and grant the App access to the repository. |
| **Refresh from source** fails because GitHub could not be reached | GitHub was unreachable, rate-limited the request or rejected the App's credentials. | Retry in a few minutes, and reconfigure the connection if the problem persists. |
| `Workflow already exists, try deleting it first at ./.github/workflows/kanvas.yml` | GitHub refused to write the snapshot workflow. | See the troubleshooting table in [Visualize Pull Requests with Kanvas Snapshot]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/snapshots/kanvas-snapshot/index.md" >}}). |

## Permissions

| Task | Requirement |
| --- | --- |
| See the Integrations area | View Connections |
| Run the wizard, scan, and import | Signed in. The server checks no permission key for these routes. |
| Refresh an imported design from its source | Own the design and hold Import Design |
| Delete the connection | Own the connection and hold Delete a connection |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Create a Learning Path"
url: /cloud/academy/creating-content/creating-your-learning-path/index.md
description: Set up your Academy content repository, structure and describe a learning path, preview it, and publish it. The repository, front matter, and publishing steps also apply to challenges and certifications.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

A learning path teaches a subject through courses and modules, with assessments that gate progress. You write it as Markdown in your organization's Academy content repository, then publish a version. This page covers the repository, layout, front matter, assets, preview, and publishing that every Academy content type shares. For the credential and assessment differences, see [Build a Challenge]({{< ref "cloud/academy/creating-content/building-challenges/index.md" >}}) and [Build a Certification]({{< ref "cloud/academy/creating-content/building-certifications/index.md" >}}).

## Prerequisites

- Git, a GitHub account, and Markdown. The Academy is built with the Hugo static site generator.
- Content registered in the [Instructor Console]({{< ref "cloud/academy/creating-content/_index.md" >}}), which gives you the content `id` and the front matter to start from.
- Your organization's ID and a personal access token from Layer5 Cloud, used when you publish. Create tokens as described in [Tokens]({{< ref "cloud/guides/security/api-tokens.md" >}}).

## Set up the content repository

Start from the `academy-example` template repository published by Layer5: [github.com/layer5io/academy-example](https://github.com/layer5io/academy-example). Fork it, clone your fork, and work on a branch.

The template's Go module path must match your fork. Change the `module` line in its module file from the template's path to `github.com/<your-username>/<your-repo-name>`, then commit and push. The publish build fails while the path still names the template.

## Directory layout

Each organization's content lives in its own directory, which is how the Academy keeps one organization's content apart from another's. Replace `<your-organization-uuid>` with your organization's ID.

| Directory | Holds |
| --- | --- |
| `content/<content-type>/<your-organization-uuid>/` | Everything you write. `<content-type>` is `learning-paths`, `challenges`, or `certifications`. The folder hierarchy defines the navigation. |
| `layouts/shortcodes/<your-organization-uuid>/` | Optional custom Hugo shortcodes for reusable components. |

### Learning path structure

A learning path contains courses. A course contains modules and can end with a test that serves as the course exam. A module contains pages and labs.

```text
learning-paths/<your-organization-uuid>
└── {learning-path-name}/
    ├── _index.md
    ├── course-1/
    │   └── _index.md
    └── course-2/
        ├── _index.md
        ├── course-exam.md
        └── module-1/
            ├── _index.md
            ├── page-1/
            │   └── _index.md
            └── test.md
```

The `_index.md` in each folder defines that level's `title`, `description`, and `type`. The remaining `.md` files are the individual activities. [Challenges]({{< ref "cloud/academy/creating-content/building-challenges/index.md#1-set-up-the-directory-structure" >}}) and [certifications]({{< ref "cloud/academy/creating-content/building-certifications/index.md#1-set-up-the-directory-structure" >}}) use a flatter layout.

## Front matter

Every `_index.md` uses the same front matter. Only `type` changes with the level.

```yaml
---
type: "learning-path"  # or "certification", "challenge", "course"
title: "Cloud Fundamentals"
description: "A learning path focused on providing the technical knowledge required for advanced topics."
weight: 5
banner: "kubernetes-icon.svg"
id: "<your-content-uuid>"
tags: [kubernetes, infrastructure]
categories: [cloud]
level: "beginner"

# Table of content covered in the test
# Each domain can have a weightage (percentage) and subdomains (items)
# Weightage should sum up to 100 across all domains ( not strictly enforced, but recommended )
competencies:
  - title: "Domain 1"
    percentage: 10 # Weightage of this domain in the test
    items: 
       -  "Subdomain 1"
       -  "Subdomain 2"

  - title: "Domain 2"
    percentage: 30
    items:
      - "Subdomain 1"
      - "Subdomain 2"

  - title: "Domain 3"
    percentage: 60
    items:
      - "Subdomain 1"
      - "Subdomain 2"



# List of resource that are recommended to complete before taking the test
# Not strictly enforced, but recommended
prerequisiteKnowledge:
  - title: "Learning Path: Cloud Computing Basics"
    link: "https://academy-domain.com/learning-paths/cloud-computing-basics"
  - title: "Basic Certification: Networking Basics"
    link: "https://academy-domain.com/certifications/networking-basics"
  - title: "Basic knowledge of Linux command line"
    link: "https://linuxcommand.org/"

# List of additional resources for further reading 
relatedResources:
  - title: "Documentation"
    link: "https://docs.example.com/"
  - title: "Instructions"
    link: "https://instructions.example.com/"
  - title: "YouTube Channel"
    link: "https://www.youtube.com/c/example" 

# Additional attributes about the test
additionalAttributes: 
  - title: "Retake Policy"
    description: "One Retake allowed after 30 days"
  - title: "Labs"
    description: "Hands-on labs included"

---
```

| Field | Applies to | Required | Behavior |
| --- | --- | :---: | --- |
| `title` | All | Yes | Display title. |
| `description` | All | Yes | Summary shown on the catalog card. |
| `type` | Path, certification, challenge | Yes | `learning-path`, `certification`, `challenge`, or `course` (singular). Plural values are rejected. |
| `id` | Path, certification, challenge | Yes | Stable UUID that learner progress is recorded against. Never change it after learners register. Two items sharing an `id` are rejected. |
| `weight` | All | No | Display order, lowest first. Without it, items sort alphabetically by title. |
| `draft` | All | No | When `true`, the page is not published. |
| `level` | Path, certification, challenge | No | `beginner`, `intermediate`, or `advanced`. Default `beginner`. |
| `banner` | Path, certification, challenge | No | Path to an image in the same folder. |
| `badge` | Path, certification, challenge | No | The awarded badge. Its `png` and `svg` fields accept a full URL or a file in the same folder. |
| `tags` | All | No | Keywords for discovery. Several allowed. |
| `categories` | All | No | The main category. Only one. |

Renaming content after publication breaks nothing as long as the `id` is unchanged. Changing the `id` orphans every existing registration.

## Assets

Place images and other files in the same folder as the Markdown that uses them (a Hugo page bundle) and reference them by file name:

```markdown
![Pod lifecycle diagram showing Pending, Running, and Succeeded states](pod-lifecycle.png)
```

Every image needs descriptive alt text. The Academy does not enforce a size limit, but large assets slow builds and can make them fail. Host large videos on an external platform and embed them with a `<video>` element that points at the hosted file. Add subtitle tracks (VTT) and a poster image to embedded video. For private videos, use signed URLs or unlisted links. The `usestatic` shortcode is deprecated; do not use it.

## Preview locally

```bash
make setup   # one time
make site    # start the local preview server
```

The preview uses a generic theme, so it shows structure and content but not your organization's branding. Branding comes from your organization settings in Layer5 Cloud. If the preview shows stale content, run `make clean` to delete the build cache and restart. To pick up theme improvements before a release, run `make theme-update`.

## Publish

Publishing sends your organization's ID and a version to Layer5 Cloud, which builds your Academy at that version.

{{< meshery-design-embed src="..//creating-your-learning-path/images/embedded-design-academy-content-publishing-workflow.js" id="embedded-design-37c37d14-be76-487a-90aa-5ada0c1c115f" size="full" >}}

### One-time setup

Store two repository secrets that the template's publish workflow reads. The names must match exactly.

| Secret | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `ACADEMY_ORG_ID` | Your organization's ID. |
| `ACADEMY_TOKEN` | Only the token string from the token JSON, beginning `eyj`. Omit the braces, the `"token":` key, and the quotes. |

### Release

Commit your changes to the default branch, then publish a GitHub release with a new version tag such as `v1.0.2`. The release starts the workflow.

- The publish request is accepted only from an organization admin or owner. The request calls Layer5 Cloud with your organization ID and the version.
- Content reaches the staging environment in about 10 minutes and production with the next Layer5 Cloud release.
- If the build fails, your previous version stays live.
- Corrections follow the same path: push, then release a new version.

### Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `401 Unauthorized` or "User must be logged in" | `ACADEMY_TOKEN` contains the whole JSON object. | Store only the token string. |
| A URL containing `//`, such as `/api/academy//update/`, | The organization ID secret is missing or misnamed. | Name the secret `ACADEMY_ORG_ID`. |
| Content missing after a release | The publish failed. | Open the audit events for your organization and filter by the Academy upsert action to see each attempt and its error. |
| Duplicate ID, invalid content type, or missing required field | Two items share an `id`, `type` is plural, or `title`, `description`, `type`, or `id` is absent. | Make IDs unique, use the singular type, and add the field. |

To see who registered for what, filter the audit events by the Academy registration action.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Create Your Layer5 Account"
url: /cloud/getting-started/getting-started-with-layer5-account/index.md
description: Create and verify a Layer5 Cloud account, sign in for the first time, and learn what Layer5 Cloud sets up for you.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Your Layer5 account is your personal identity on Layer5 Cloud. One account can belong to many organizations and teams, and it is how you import and create designs, collaborate through workspaces, and connect Meshery Servers. In this tutorial you create an account, verify it, sign in, and confirm that Layer5 Cloud has prepared an organization, a team, and a workspace for you. You do not set up any of those yourself before you can start working. The **Check your email** page and the **Import from GitHub** first-run page described below arrived in Layer5 Cloud **v1.0.278**.

## 1. Create an account

Sign up at <https://cloud.layer5.io/signup>. The registration page offers these sign-up methods:

| Method | What happens next |
|---|---|
| Email and password | You fill in one form. Layer5 Cloud signs you in right away and sends a verification email. Opening its link verifies your address and takes you back to where you started. |
| GitHub | You authorize with GitHub and are signed in straight after registration. Layer5 Cloud treats the email address GitHub reports as verified, so no verification email is sent. |
| Google | You authorize with Google and are signed in straight after registration. Layer5 Cloud treats the email address Google reports as verified, so no verification email is sent. |
| Your organization's identity provider | An organization that brings its own identity provider credentials, including a generic OIDC provider, shows that provider on its own sign-up page. |

### What the email sign-up form checks

The email sign-up form is a single screen that asks for your first name, last name, email address, and password. Layer5 Cloud validates each field and keeps what you typed when it shows an error, so you only correct the field at fault.

| Field | Rule |
|---|---|
| First and last name | 1 to 50 characters. Letters, combining marks, and spaces only. A spam filter also rejects blocked keywords in names. An invalid name shows "Invalid first name." or "Invalid last name." |
| Email address | A syntactically valid address. The spam filter also rejects disposable-email domains. An invalid or rejected address shows "Invalid email address or domain not allowed." |
| Password | At least 8 characters. Must not appear in the Have I Been Pwned breach corpus. Must not be too similar to your email address. |

When the deployment has a reCAPTCHA check enabled, the submit button stays disabled until you solve it. A field-level validation failure keeps your solved captcha. If the server rejects the whole submission after the captcha was sent, the captcha resets and asks you to "Please complete the verification again." If the network fails, the page shows "We couldn't submit your sign-up. Check your connection and try again."

GitHub and Google sign-up skip the spam filter and the captcha.

The sign-up form stays valid for 24 hours. If you leave it open longer, it restarts and you fill it in again.

## 2. Verify your email address

After an email sign-up, Layer5 Cloud signs you in and sends a verification email that contains both a verification link and a verification code. Either one completes verification. Both stay valid for 720 hours (30 days). You cannot use your account, or sign in again with your password, until you verify your address.

Opening the link verifies your address at once. You do not need to type the code or press a button. Layer5 Cloud then takes you back to the page you started signing up from, or to your dashboard if you opened the sign-up page directly. If the link has expired or was already used, the verification page says so and lets you request a new email.

Your browser lands on a **Check your email** page that says you are signed in and names the address the verification email went to. You can wait on this page:

- **Resend email** sends a new verification email without leaving the page. Once it is sent, the page also offers a form where you type the code from the new email instead of opening its link.
- **Sign out and use a different email** signs you out so you can sign up again with the correct address. Use it if you mistyped your address. An account cannot change its email address before that address is verified, so signing up again with the correct address is the fix.

The page remembers your address only in the browser tab you signed up in. If you open **Check your email** in a different tab, or your browser blocks site storage, the page shows generic text instead of your address. **Resend email** then opens the verification page, which asks for your address before it sends a new email.

If your organization uses a custom domain, the verification link, the page it opens, and the return afterward all stay on your organization's domain, with your organization's name and logo.

If your link has expired, request a new verification email and use the latest link.

## 3. Sign in {#3-signing-in-to-layer5-cloud}

Sign in at <https://cloud.layer5.io/login> with the method you signed up with. If you signed up with GitHub or Google, Layer5 Cloud sends you to that provider to authenticate. The sign-in form stays valid for 12 hours; an expired form restarts.

You are not asked to name an organization or a workspace. Layer5 Cloud creates both on your first successful sign-in, as described in the next steps.

### Where your first sign-in takes you

Your first sign-in normally opens your [dashboard](#6-dashboard). One exception applies: if you started signing up from Kanvas, or from a Meshery Server on your organization's custom domain, and you registered in this browser, your first sign-in opens the **Import from GitHub** page (titled "Get started") once. If the sign-in carries an explicit return address, Layer5 Cloud sends you there instead.

The **Import from GitHub** page holds one card. It explains that connecting GitHub lets you pick repositories and import Kubernetes manifests, Helm charts, and Docker Compose files as designs. It also names your organization and workspace: "Organizations own workspaces. You're in My Organization, working in My Workspace. Rename either anytime." From there you either start the [GitHub integration]({{< ref "cloud/guides/integrations/github-integration/index.md" >}}) wizard or skip to your dashboard.

{{< alert type="info" >}}
Layer5 Cloud remembers where you started only for the browser session you signed up in. If you sign in from a different browser, or after closing the browser you signed up in, you land on your dashboard. The **Import from GitHub** page is always available at <https://cloud.layer5.io/register/choose-start>.
{{< /alert >}}

## 4. Your default organization {#4-creating-an-organization}

Organizations are the unit of tenancy in Layer5 Cloud, and every user belongs to at least one. On your first sign-in, Layer5 Cloud creates an organization named **My Organization** (description "Default Organization"), makes you its owner, and gives you the Organization Admin role in it. You can create more organizations and join existing ones.

Layer5 Cloud also creates a team named **My Team** (description "Default Team"), attaches it to **My Organization**, and gives you the Team Admin role on it.

{{< alert type="info" >}}
For more information, see [Organizations]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/organizations/_index.md" >}}).
{{< /alert >}}

You can rename **My Organization** and change its description at any time. See [Editing your organization]({{< ref "cloud/guides/organizations/org-management/_index.md#editing-your-organization" >}}).

## 5. Your default workspace {#5-creating-a-workspace}

Workspaces are logical groups of shared resources such as environments, connections, credentials, and designs. On your first sign-in, Layer5 Cloud creates a workspace named **My Workspace** (description "Default Workspace") in **My Organization**, owned by you. You can create more workspaces and share access to their resources through teams. If any of your organizations ever has no workspace, Layer5 Cloud re-creates **My Workspace** in it.

{{< alert type="info" >}}
For more information, see [Workspaces]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/workspaces.md" >}}).
{{< /alert >}}

You can rename **My Workspace** and change its description at any time. See [Edit a Workspace]({{< ref "cloud/guides/workspaces/managing-workspaces/index.md#edit-a-workspace" >}}).

### Everything your first sign-in sets up

| Created for you | Name | Your access |
|---|---|---|
| Organization | My Organization | Owner, Organization Admin role |
| Team | My Team, attached to My Organization | Team Admin role |
| Workspace | My Workspace, in My Organization | Owner |
| Global role | Kanvas | Grants the Kanvas extension capabilities when a Meshery Server connects with your account |

Layer5 Cloud also records your primary email address so that one person signing in by a different method reuses the same account instead of creating a second one. Layer5 Cloud accepts open organization invitation links on every sign-in, not only the first.

## 6. Explore your dashboard {#6-dashboard}

The dashboard is your normal landing page after sign-in. It is a grid of widgets whose layout you can edit; Layer5 Cloud prompts you before you leave with unsaved layout changes. Available widgets include Getting Started, Workspace Activity, Explore Playground, My Academy, Learn by Video, Help Center, Meshery Instances, Kubernetes Clusters Count, Catalog Content Count, Invite Friends, Badges, My Designs, System Version, Catalog Leaderboard, and Catalog Metrics. Academy administrators see additional widgets for Academy content statistics, metrics, test analytics, and registrations.

## 7. Link GitHub or Google to your profile

Whatever method you signed up with, you can later link a GitHub or Google account to your existing profile from your profile page. Once linked, either method signs you in to the same Layer5 Cloud profile. Each provider shows **Link** or **Unlink** depending on its current state. Linking sends you to the provider and then back to your profile.

Changing a password or linking a provider is a privileged action. If your sign-in is older than the privileged-session window, Layer5 Cloud asks you to authenticate again first. The window is 24 hours on hosted Layer5 Cloud and 15 minutes by default on a self-hosted chart. For every account setting, see [Manage Your Account]({{< ref "cloud/guides/account/managing-your-account.md" >}}).

## Check your result

Your account is ready when all of the following are true:

- You can sign in at <https://cloud.layer5.io/login>. For an email account, a successful password sign-in also proves your address is verified.
- Your dashboard loads after sign-in.
- Your organization is **My Organization**, and it contains **My Workspace**.

## Next steps

- [Set Up Your Organization]({{< ref "cloud/getting-started/setting-up-your-organization.md" >}}): invite a teammate, create a team, and give it a workspace.
- [Start from a Catalog Design]({{< ref "cloud/getting-started/creating-a-design-from-template.md" >}}): clone a public design into your workspace.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Feature Availability by Plan"
url: /cloud/reference/feature-availability/index.md
description: Which Layer5 Cloud capabilities each Layer5 plan includes, the limits each plan records, and the role and deployment conditions that also decide whether a capability is available to you.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

This page tells you which Layer5 Cloud capabilities each Layer5 plan includes. Your plan is one condition for using a capability, not the only one: your role and where your Layer5 Cloud deployment runs also decide what you can do. Those conditions follow the matrix and the limits table.

## Plans

The matrix has one column for each of the four Layer5 plans: Free, Team Designer, Team Operator, and Enterprise. Each plan is offered with monthly and annual billing. The Free plan is the plan that Layer5 Cloud calls Personal in its plan records, so you see that name in subscription and entitlement data. Entitlements follow your organization's plan. Current pricing and plan details are listed at [layer5.io/pricing](https://layer5.io/pricing).

## Reading the matrix

- A check mark means the plan includes the capability.
- A dash means the plan does not include it.
- Each table covers one category of capability. The **What it does** column describes the capability in one sentence.

The matrix is refreshed automatically from the Layer5 product feature list. It lists the capabilities that have a documentation page. A capability that does not appear here is not necessarily unavailable; check the page that documents it.

This page covers the Layer5 Cloud categories. For design, deployment, collaboration, and performance capabilities, see [Kanvas Feature Availability by Plan]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/feature-availability.md" >}}).

## Capabilities by plan

{{< feature-tiers categories="Identity & Access Management|Workspaces|Catalog|Security|Managed Service Provider|Support and Deployment|Academy" >}}

## Limits by plan

Each plan records a quantity for the following entitlements.

| Entitlement | Free | Team Designer | Team Operator | Enterprise |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Components per design | 100 | 200 | 100 | 300 |
| Relationships per design | 100 | 200 | 100 | 300 |
| Image size in a design | 250 KB | 1 MiB | 1 MiB | 10 MiB |
| Designs per workspace | Unlimited | Unlimited | Unlimited | Unlimited |
| Workspaces per organization | See note | 10 | 10 | Unlimited |

For workspaces per organization on the Free plan, the plan records disagree: the monthly billing record sets 1 and the annual billing record sets 10.

### Which limits Layer5 Cloud enforces

Layer5 Cloud enforces one limit today: components per design. When you save or import a design, Layer5 Cloud compares its component count with the limit of your organization's active plan. A design that exceeds the limit is refused with the error `Design exeeds maximum limit of N components supported by your current plan`, where N is the limit. To proceed, reduce the number of components in the design or upgrade the plan. When an organization holds more than one active subscription, the highest component limit among them applies. An organization with no active subscription cannot save or import a design; the request fails with HTTP 500 and the error `Org is not entitled to adding components to a design`.

Layer5 Cloud records every other quantity in the table and lists it through the entitlements API (`GET /api/entitlement/features`), but it does not refuse an action because of any of them. For the API's base URL and authentication, see the [API Reference]({{< ref "cloud/reference/api-reference/_index.md" >}}).

## Availability depends on more than your plan

### Your role

Authorization in Layer5 Cloud is by permission key. Each role you hold grants a set of keys, and your effective permissions are the union of the keys from every role you hold in the organization you are working in. An action your role does not grant is refused with HTTP 403, even when your plan includes the capability. See [Roles and Permissions]({{< ref "cloud/reference/default-permissions.md" >}}) for which role holds which permission.

### Where your deployment runs

Layer5 Cloud runs either as the hosted service that Layer5 operates or as a [self-hosted deployment]({{< ref "cloud/guides/self-hosted/_index.md" >}}) that you operate. Self-hosted Deployment is listed under the Enterprise plan in the **Support and Deployment** table. The difference that matters most for availability is provider administration. The Provider Admin role administers the deployment and passes every permission check; on a self-hosted deployment, your operators assign it.

### Custom roles

Only Provider Admins create custom roles. Layer5 Cloud refuses a role creation request from anyone else with HTTP 403. On hosted Layer5 Cloud, an organization therefore cannot create a custom role itself; on a self-hosted deployment, the operator's Provider Admins can. Roles are defined for the whole deployment, not per organization, so a role change applies in every organization where the role is held.

The **Custom Roles** and **User-defined Roles** rows in the **Identity & Access Management** table describe how those capabilities are packaged into plans. Layer5 Cloud does not check your plan when a custom role is created.

### Plan rows and enforcement

The component limit is the only entitlement Layer5 Cloud enforces by plan. The capability rows in the matrix describe how Layer5 packages its plans. When an action is unavailable and the plan is not the component limit, check your role and your deployment first.

## Support by plan

The support channels and response commitments each plan includes are listed in [Support]({{< ref "cloud/reference/support.md" >}}).


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Helm Chart Values"
url: /cloud/guides/self-hosted/deployment/helm-chart-values/index.md
description: Reference for the layer5-cloud Helm chart: every value you set, its default, what it controls, and whether it lands in a ConfigMap or a Secret.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The `layer5-cloud` chart installs the Layer5 Cloud server and, as subcharts from the Ory repository, Kratos and Hydra. The defaults below are those of chart version 0.2.0, which ships with Layer5 Cloud v1.0.278. Run `helm show values layer5/layer5-cloud` to print the defaults of the version you install. For the install procedure, see [Deploy Layer5 Cloud]({{< ref "cloud/guides/self-hosted/deployment/_index.md" >}}).

## How values reach the server

The chart writes `env.*` values into one ConfigMap and one Secret, and the server pod reads both as environment variables. Sensitive values go to the Secret. Any change to either rolls the server pods, because the pod template carries a checksum of both.

| Where it lands | Values |
| --- | --- |
| Secret | `env.githubappkeypath` (the key file content), `env.githubAppClientSecret`, `env.stripeWebhookSecret`, `env.githubWebhookSecret`, `env.kratosWebhookApiKey`, `env.cloudCredentialEncryptionKey`, `env.cloudOidcStateHmacKey`, `env.providerOrgGithubSecret`, `env.providerOrgGoogleSecret`, and all four `smtp.*` values |
| ConfigMap | Every other `env.*` value |

Both the Secret and the Helm release still hold your values in plaintext, so protect the release history and your values file.

## Workload

| Key | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `replicaCount` | `1` | Server replicas. Ignored when autoscaling is on. |
| `image.repository` | `layer5/meshery-cloud` | Server image. |
| `image.tag` | `latest` | Image tag. Pin it to a release such as `v1.0.278`. When empty, the chart uses its own `appVersion`. |
| `image.pullPolicy` | `Always` | Image pull policy. |
| `imagePullSecrets` | `[]` | Pull secrets for a private registry. |
| `updateStrategy` | RollingUpdate, 25% unavailable, 25% surge | Deployment update strategy. |
| `resources.requests` | `256Mi` memory, `250m` CPU | Requested resources. |
| `resources.limits` | `{}` | No limits by default. |
| `autoscaling.enabled` | `false` | Enables a HorizontalPodAutoscaler. |
| `autoscaling.minReplicas`, `.maxReplicas` | `1`, `100` | Autoscaler bounds. |
| `autoscaling.targetCPUUtilizationPercentage` | `80` | Autoscaler target. |
| `nodeSelector`, `tolerations`, `affinity` | `{}`, `[]`, `{}` | Pod scheduling. |
| `podAnnotations`, `podSecurityContext`, `securityContext` | `{}` | Pod and container settings. |
| `serviceAccount.create`, `.name`, `.annotations` | `true`, `meshery-cloud`, `{}` | Service account. |
| `nameOverride`, `fullnameOverride` | `""`, `meshery-cloud` | Resource naming. The Deployment, Service, ConfigMap, and Secret derive their names from `fullnameOverride`. |

The container has a liveness probe on `/healthz` and readiness and startup probes on `/readyz`. See [Monitoring]({{< ref "cloud/guides/self-hosted/planning/monitoring.md" >}}).

## Networking

| Key | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `service.type` | `ClusterIP` | Service type. |
| `service.port` | `9876` | Service port for the server. |
| `service.hydraAdminProxyPort` | `9879` | Port of the internal proxy that sits between Kratos and the Hydra admin API. Set `0` to turn the proxy off. |
| `ingress.enabled` | `true` | Creates the Ingress. |
| `ingress.className` | `nginx` | Ingress class. |
| `ingress.annotations` | `{}` | Controller annotations. |
| `ingress.hosts` | One empty host routing `/` to port 9876 | Hosts and paths. You must set the host. Add `/kratos` and `/hydra` paths for the identity services. |
| `ingress.tls` | `[]` | TLS secret and hosts. The chart does not create certificates. |

## Server settings (`env`)

| Key | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `proto` | `""` | `http` or `https`. Used to build redirects to organization custom domains. Set `https` on a TLS deployment. |
| `serverbaseurl` | `http://localhost:9876` | Public base URL of the deployment. Also the base of the OAuth2 callback `<serverbaseurl>/callback`. |
| `serverHost` | `localhost` | Public hostname of the deployment. |
| `port` | `9876` | Port the server listens on. |
| `environment` | `cloud` | Deployment mode. `development` connects to a local database at `127.0.0.1:5432`, tolerates a failed migration, logs rendered email bodies, and skips reCAPTCHA. Use any other value in production. |
| `debug` | `"false"` | Sets the `DEBUG` variable. |
| `loglevel` | `4` | Log level: `4` info, `5` debug, `6` trace. Not in the default values; the server uses `4` when unset. |
| `db`, `hydradb`, `kratosdb` | In-cluster PostgreSQL URLs with `sslmode=disable` | Connection strings for the `meshery`, `hydra`, and `kratos` databases. Change the user, password, host, and `sslmode`. |
| `minmesheryversion` | `v1.0.55` | Lowest Meshery Server version that can complete sign-in. A connecting Meshery Server below it is shown a "Meshery Deployment Incompatible" error. |
| `initConfig` | `""` | Provider initialization document. See [Provider Initialization]({{< ref "cloud/guides/self-hosted/deployment/provider-initialization.md" >}}). |
| `otelConfig` | `""` | OpenTelemetry tracing configuration. See [Monitoring]({{< ref "cloud/guides/self-hosted/planning/monitoring.md#traces" >}}). |
| `anonymousUserSessionsEnabled` | `false` | Lets the deployment serve guest sessions, as used by kanvas.new. Leave off unless you operate that flow. |
| `ghtoken` | `""` | GitHub token the server uses to dispatch workflows. |
| `githubappid` | not set | GitHub App identifier for the GitHub integration. |
| `githubappkeypath` | `key.pem` | Path of the GitHub App private key file inside the chart. |
| `githubAppClientId`, `githubAppClientSecret` | `""` | OAuth client ID and a client secret from the settings page of the GitHub App that `githubappid` names. Layer5 Cloud v1.0.287 and later uses them to confirm which installations of the App the authorizing GitHub account can access. When either is empty, the server logs a warning at startup and no GitHub connection can be created or re-authorized. The App must also meet the [Self-hosted GitHub App requirements]({{< ref "cloud/guides/integrations/github-integration/index.md#self-hosted-github-app-requirements" >}}). |
| `stripeSecretKey`, `stripePublicKey` | not set | Stripe keys for payment processing. |
| `recaptchaSiteKey`, `recaptchaSecretKey` | not set | Google reCAPTCHA keys. Signup verification runs only when both are set. Organizations on a custom domain with a different registrable domain are exempt. |

### Identity connections

| Key | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `kratospublic` | none, required | In-cluster address of the Kratos public service. The chart fails to render without it. May contain `{{ .Release.Namespace }}`. |
| `kratosadmin` | not set | In-cluster address of the Kratos admin service. |
| `kratosbrowser` | not set | Address browsers use for Kratos, such as `https://cloud.example.com/kratos`. |
| `hydrapublic` | `http://hydra-public:4444` | Address of Hydra's public API. |
| `hydrabrowser` | not set | Address browsers use for Hydra, such as `https://cloud.example.com/hydra`. |
| `hydraadmin` | `http://hydra-admin:4445` | Address of Hydra's admin API. |
| `hydrapublicinternal` | `""` | In-cluster address of Hydra's public API for calls the server makes to itself. Falls back to `hydrabrowser` when empty. May contain `{{ .Release.Namespace }}`. |
| `oauthclientid` | `meshery-cloud` | Id of the Hydra OAuth2 client the server uses. |
| `oauthsecret` | `secret1234567890` | Secret of that client. Replace it. |
| `kratosWebhookApiKey` | `""` | Key Kratos sends in the `X-API-Key` header on registration hooks. When empty, the server accepts the placeholder `dev_token`. Set it, and set the same value in the Kratos hooks. |
| `providerOrgGithubKey`, `providerOrgGithubSecret` | `""` | Client id and secret of the default GitHub OAuth application. |
| `providerOrgGoogleKey`, `providerOrgGoogleSecret` | `""` | Client id and secret of the default Google OAuth application. |

### Encryption keys

| Key | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `cloudCredentialEncryptionKey` | not set | Base64 of 32 bytes. Encrypts stored credentials. When empty, encrypting or decrypting a credential fails. |
| `cloudOidcStateHmacKey` | not set | Base64 of 32 bytes. Signs the state of brokered social sign-in. When empty, brokered sign-in fails. |
| `stripeWebhookSecret`, `githubWebhookSecret` | not set | Signing secrets for inbound payment and GitHub webhooks. When empty, those inbound webhooks are rejected. |

### Webhooks

| Key | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `webhookHelpAndSupport` | not set | URL that receives support requests. |
| `webhookKanvasEntitlement` | not set | URL that receives Kanvas entitlement events. |
| `webhookSignupRequest` | not set | URL that receives signup decisions. |

See [Customize Webhooks]({{< ref "cloud/guides/self-hosted/customizing-webhooks.md" >}}).

## Mail (`smtp`)

| Key | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `smtp.smtphost` | `""` | Relay host. Must resolve to a public address. |
| `smtp.smtpport` | `""` | `25`, `465`, `587`, or `2525`. Port `465` uses implicit TLS; the others require STARTTLS. |
| `smtp.smtpusername` | `""` | Mailbox login. Must be a full email address, because it becomes the `From` address. |
| `smtp.smtppassword` | `""` | Mailbox password. |

Set all four or none. A partial configuration stops the server at startup. See [Troubleshoot Email Delivery]({{< ref "cloud/guides/self-hosted/operating/smtp.md" >}}).

## Kratos (`kratos`)

The `kratos.kratos.config` tree is passed to Kratos unchanged. The [Kratos configuration reference](https://www.ory.sh/docs/kratos/reference/configuration) describes every field. The values you must change for a real deployment:

| Key | Default | Change to |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `kratos.enabled` | `true` | Keep `true` unless you bring your own Kratos. |
| `kratos.service.public.port`, `.admin.port` | `9010`, `9011` | Public and admin ports. |
| `kratos.kratos.config.dsn` | In-cluster URL for the `kratos` database | Your connection string. |
| `kratos.kratos.config.secrets.cookie`, `.cipher` | `[""]` | Long random strings. |
| `kratos.kratos.config.serve.public.base_url` | `http://localhost:9010/` | `https://<host>/kratos`. |
| `kratos.kratos.config.serve.public.cors.allowed_origins` | `http://localhost:9010/` | Your public origin. |
| `kratos.kratos.config.selfservice.default_browser_return_url`, `.allowed_return_urls` | `http://localhost:9876` | Your public URL. |
| `kratos.kratos.config.selfservice.flows.*.ui_url` | `http://localhost:9876/...` | Your public URL with the same paths. |
| `kratos.kratos.config.selfservice.flows.registration.after.*.hooks` | `web_hook` to `http://localhost:9876/identity/users`, key `dev_token` | `https://<host>/api/identity/users` and your `kratosWebhookApiKey`. |
| `kratos.kratos.config.selfservice.methods.oidc.config.providers` | GitHub and Google with empty credentials | Your `client_id` and `client_secret`. |
| `kratos.kratos.config.courier` | SMTP courier, empty connection string | Your courier. See [Plan a Deployment]({{< ref "cloud/guides/self-hosted/planning/_index.md#mail" >}}). |

Other defaults you can change: password sign-in is on with a minimum length of 8, breached-password and similarity checks on; login flows last `720m`, registration `24h`, recovery and verification `720h`; verification and recovery use codes; `privileged_session_max_age` is `15m`; the log level is `debug`; automatic migration is on.

A list in a values file replaces the chart's list as a whole. Copy the full `providers` or `hooks` list before you edit it.

## Hydra (`hydra`)

The `hydra.hydra.config` tree is passed to Hydra unchanged. See the [Hydra configuration reference](https://www.ory.sh/docs/hydra/reference/configuration).

| Key | Default | Change to |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `hydraPrefix` | `cloud-hydra` | Name prefix of the Hydra resources. The services become `<prefix>-public` and `<prefix>-admin`. |
| `hydra.hydra.config.dsn` | In-cluster URL for the `hydra` database | Your connection string. |
| `hydra.hydra.config.secrets.system` | `[""]` | A long random string. |
| `hydra.hydra.config.urls.login`, `.consent`, `.error`, `.post_logout_redirect` | `https://public.hydra.localhost/...` | `https://<host>/login`, `/consent`, `/error`, and `/login`. |
| `hydra.hydra.config.urls.self.public`, `.self.issuer` | `https://public.hydra.localhost/hydra/` | `https://<host>/hydra/`. |
| `hydra.hydra.dangerousForceHttp` | `true` | `false` once Hydra is reached over TLS. |
| `hydra.hydra.config.strategies.access_token` | `jwt` | Keep `jwt`. |
| `hydra.hydra.config.ttl.access_token`, `.refresh_token`, `.id_token`, `.auth_code` | `24h`, `1000h`, `1h`, `1h` | Token lifetimes. |

Other defaults: automatic migration is on, the log level is `debug`, and the liveness and readiness probes use `/health/alive` and `/health/ready` on port 4444.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "How Layer5 Cloud Works with Meshery and Kanvas"
url: /cloud/concepts/architecture/index.md
description: How Layer5 Cloud acts as the remote provider for Meshery Server and Kanvas, what it supplies to a connected server, how sign-in is handed off, and what it stores.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Layer5 Cloud is a [Meshery remote provider](https://docs.meshery.io/extensibility/providers). Meshery Server delegates identity, tenancy, and persistence to it, and Kanvas, which runs inside Meshery, reaches it through Meshery Server. Knowing what Cloud supplies, and what it does not touch, explains why some features need an account, why a feature can appear for one user and not another, and why Meshery Server, rather than your browser, is what reaches your clusters.

<figure>
  <img src="images/cloud-meshery-provider-architecture.webp" alt="Architecture diagram titled Meshery Architecture - Providers. On the left, a Remote Provider and a Local Provider connect to Meshery in the center. On the right, Meshery connects to Kubernetes clusters, where Meshery Operator runs MeshSync and Meshery Broker, and to adapters." />
  <figcaption>Read the diagram from left to right. Providers sit on the left: Meshery runs with either a remote provider, which is the role Layer5 Cloud plays, or a local provider. The remote provider handles identity, tenancy, and the storage and sharing of designs. Meshery sits in the middle and mediates every request between the provider and your infrastructure. Your clusters sit on the right, where Meshery Operator runs MeshSync and Meshery Broker to report live state back to Meshery. Meshery, not the provider, is drawn connecting to the clusters and adapters on the right.</figcaption>
</figure>

## What Cloud provides to a connected Meshery Server

When a Meshery Server uses Layer5 Cloud as its provider, Cloud supplies four things:

- **Identity and sign-in.** Cloud authenticates the user and hands Meshery Server a token. Cloud publishes the keys that verify its tokens, as a JSON Web Key Set, at its unauthenticated `/keys` endpoint.
- **Tenancy.** Cloud holds the organizations, teams, workspaces, environments, and roles that decide what a user can see and do. See [Concepts]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/_index.md" >}}) for how these relate.
- **Persistence.** Cloud stores designs and their versions, records who each design is shared with, hosts the [catalog]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/catalog/_index.md" >}}), and keeps the event log.
- **A capabilities document.** Cloud tells Meshery Server which features the provider offers to the current caller, and Meshery and Kanvas enable only those features.

Meshery Server also registers itself with Cloud as a connection owned by the signed-in user. See [Meshery Server Registration]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/meshery-server-registration.md" >}}).

## The sign-in handoff

A Meshery Server, or Kanvas, does not collect credentials itself. It hands the browser to Cloud and waits for a token to come back:

1. The client sends the browser to Cloud's sign-in with a source: the address of its own token callback, encoded in base64url.
2. The user signs in to Cloud. If the browser already holds a live Cloud session, Cloud skips the sign-in page.
3. Cloud returns the browser to the source's token endpoint with a token and the original reference in the query string.

The token callback path is `/api/user/token` or `/api/token`. Older Meshery Servers send `/user/login` or `/login`, and Cloud rewrites those to the current paths, so older servers keep working.

If the user was working anonymously and the handoff carries the anonymous identity, Cloud moves the designs created under that anonymous identity to the signed-in account.

### Which sources Cloud returns a token to

Cloud issues a token only to a source it trusts. A source must use https, name a host, and carry no port and no user information. Its host must then be one of three kinds:

| Source host | Accepted when |
| :--- | :--- |
| Cloud's own host | The source uses the same scheme as Cloud's configured base URL. |
| A custom domain of an organization | The domain is configured on a live organization and the source uses https. |
| A loopback host | The deployment runs in development mode. Outside development mode, loopback sources are refused. |

Every other source is refused with an error and no token is issued. That includes other schemes and any host that is not Cloud's own host or a configured organization domain. There is no built-in list of trusted hosts beyond these rules. If Cloud cannot complete the lookup of an organization's custom domain, it refuses the source rather than accepting it. Cloud never applies the live-session shortcut in step 2 to a source on its own host.

## What a Meshery Server gets from Cloud, by caller

Meshery Server requests the capabilities document with `GET /<meshery-version>/capabilities`, optionally adding `os` and `playground` query parameters. The older unversioned `/capabilities` path is deprecated. The document Cloud returns depends on who is asking:

| Caller | Capabilities returned |
| :--- | :--- |
| Anonymous, or no valid token | Default capabilities only. |
| Signed-in user | Account capabilities: overview, profile, and tokens. |
| Signed-in user with the Kanvas role | Account capabilities, plus the Kanvas extension capabilities and the latest Kanvas extension package version for the connecting Meshery version. |
| Provider Admin | Account capabilities, plus administrative capabilities (user management, statistics, and events) and the Kanvas extension capabilities. |
| Playground (`playground=true`) | Playground capabilities, added to the set the caller would otherwise receive. |

Every new user receives the Kanvas role when their account is created, so a typical signed-in user gets Kanvas in Meshery without any extra setup. A user without that role still signs in but does not receive the Kanvas extension from Cloud.

### The provider name

Meshery shows the provider's name in its interface. When Cloud resolves the caller's organization, the provider name is that organization's name, which is how branded organizations appear under their own name. Otherwise Meshery shows the default provider name.

## What Cloud stores and what stays with you

Cloud and your own deployment hold different things:

| Held by Layer5 Cloud | Held by your Meshery Server and clusters |
| :--- | :--- |
| User accounts, organizations, teams, workspaces, environments, and roles | The live state of each cluster, which MeshSync records in Meshery Server |
| Designs, their versions, and who each is shared with | The workloads and resources a deployed design produces |
| The catalog and the event log | The connections from Meshery Server to your Kubernetes clusters, through Meshery Operator, MeshSync, and Meshery Broker |
| Connection registrations, including each registered Meshery Server and its metadata | |

Meshery Server, not your browser, talks to your Kubernetes clusters, through the components it deploys into each one. Deploying, dry-running, and undeploying a design are operations Meshery Server performs against the contexts you select. When Meshery Server registers a Kubernetes connection with Cloud, Cloud records that connection and its credential.

Real-time collaboration is the one path from the browser straight to Cloud: Cloud hosts the signaling service that introduces collaborators, and edits then synchronize directly between their browsers. See [How Kanvas Works with Meshery and Layer5 Cloud]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/architecture/index.md" >}}) for that path and for the full picture from the Kanvas side.

## Remote provider versus local provider

Meshery runs with either a remote provider or the local provider. In both cases, requests about your connected clusters and their resources stay within Meshery. The difference is what happens to provider-bound requests:

- **With Layer5 Cloud as a remote provider**, Meshery Server forwards provider-bound requests, such as designs, views, the catalog, sharing, and support, to Cloud and relays the answers back.
- **With the local provider**, there is no remote service behind Meshery, so every provider-bound feature returns HTTP 501 Not Implemented.

Choose a remote provider for any feature that depends on accounts, sharing, or stored designs.

## SaaS versus self-hosted

Layer5 Cloud runs as a hosted service and as a self-hosted deployment, and both act as a remote provider in the same way. The trusted-source rules above are relative to each deployment: a self-hosted Cloud trusts its own configured base URL and the custom domains of its own organizations, not those of the hosted service. To run your own deployment, see [Self-Hosted]({{< ref "cloud/guides/self-hosted/_index.md" >}}).


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Identity Services"
url: /cloud/guides/self-hosted/planning/identity-services/index.md
description: Plan the identity services of a self-hosted deployment: Kratos accounts, Hydra tokens, the default Google and GitHub sign-in, and where organizations bring their own.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

A self-hosted deployment is its own identity provider. Ory Kratos owns user accounts and sign-in, Ory Hydra issues OAuth2 tokens, and the Layer5 Cloud server connects the two to organizations, teams, and roles. Users can sign up with an email address and password, or with Google or GitHub. For how identity fits together as a concept, see [Identity and Security]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/_index.md" >}}).

## What the chart configures by default

| Capability | Default |
| --- | --- |
| Password sign-in | On. Minimum 8 characters, checked against known-breached passwords, and rejected when too similar to the account identifier. |
| Email verification | Required before a password sign-in succeeds. Delivered as a code. |
| Account recovery | On, delivered as a code. |
| Social sign-in | Google and GitHub are enabled but have no credentials until you add them. |
| Login flow lifespan | A started sign-in must finish within 12 hours (`720m`). |
| Recovery and verification flow lifespan | A recovery or verification request stays valid for 30 days (`720h`). |
| Registration flow lifespan | A started sign-up must finish within 24 hours. |
| Session lifespan | Not set by the chart. Kratos applies its own default. See [Sessions]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/sessions.md" >}}). |
| Access tokens | JWT, valid 24 hours. Refresh tokens are valid 1000 hours, ID tokens 1 hour, and authorization codes 1 hour. |

Change any of these through the `kratos.kratos.config` and `hydra.hydra.config` values. Both are passed to the Ory services unchanged, so the [Kratos](https://www.ory.sh/docs/kratos/reference/configuration) and [Hydra](https://www.ory.sh/docs/hydra/reference/configuration) configuration references apply.

## Default Google and GitHub sign-in

Every organization signs in through the deployment's default providers until the organization registers its own. You supply those defaults as two OAuth applications, one for Google and one for GitHub, and the deployment uses them in two places:

| Where | Used for | Configured with |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Kratos | Social sign-in and sign-up on the deployment's own hostname, and social sign-up on every hostname | `client_id` and `client_secret` of the `github` and `google` entries under `kratos.kratos.config.selfservice.methods.oidc.config.providers` |
| Layer5 Cloud server | Social sign-in on organization custom domains | `env.providerOrgGithubKey`, `env.providerOrgGithubSecret`, `env.providerOrgGoogleKey`, `env.providerOrgGoogleSecret` |

Use the same OAuth application for both. Register these redirect addresses on it, replacing `<host>` with your deployment hostname:

| Provider | Addresses to register |
| --- | --- |
| Google | `https://<host>/kratos/self-service/methods/oidc/callback/google` and `https://<host>/oidc/callback/google`. Google matches redirect addresses exactly. |
| GitHub | `https://<host>/`. GitHub matches by path prefix, so the host root covers both callbacks. |

You register addresses on your deployment hostname only. A custom-domain organization that uses the default providers completes the exchange on your hostname and returns to its own domain.

### How the defaults are stored

At every start, the server reads the `env.providerOrg*` values and stores each pair it finds, encrypted with `env.cloudCredentialEncryptionKey`, as a credential and connection in an administrative environment of the provider organization. Three behaviors follow:

- **A provider needs both its key and its secret.** A provider with only one set is skipped, and the log says so.
- **The server needs an administrator first.** The seed records which user created the rows, so it waits until the provider organization has a member. On a new deployment, [provider initialization]({{< ref "cloud/guides/self-hosted/deployment/provider-initialization.md" >}}) creates that member on first start, and the seed runs on the same start.
- **Stored credentials are not overwritten.** After the first successful seed, changing `env.providerOrg*` and redeploying does not change what the server uses. There is no self-service rotation of the defaults today: replacing them means replacing the stored credential directly in the database, so plan their lifetime before you go live and ask Layer5 support for guidance when you must rotate.

The seed never blocks startup. When it fails, the server starts and sign-in on custom domains that rely on the defaults fails until a later start succeeds. Search the startup log for `IdP seed` messages.

## Bring your own credentials

An organization can register its own Google or GitHub OAuth application, or an OIDC provider, so that the consent screen carries its own brand and the whole exchange stays on its own domain. The organization's administrators do this themselves; Provider Admins can do it for any organization. See [Configuring Identity Providers]({{< ref "cloud/guides/organizations/org-management/_index.md#configuring-identity-providers-bring-your-own-credentials" >}}).

Bringing your own credentials is always optional. Social sign-in works on every custom domain with the deployment's defaults, including a custom domain on a different registrable domain from your deployment. An organization brings its own credentials for its brand, its own rate limits and audit trail, or a separate authentication boundary, never to make social sign-in available.

| Organization's domain | Default providers | Own credentials |
| --- | --- | --- |
| None, or a subdomain of the deployment's base domain (`team.example.com` on a `cloud.example.com` deployment) | Work out of the box | Optional |
| A different registrable domain (`meshery.yourcompany.com` pointed at your deployment) | Work out of the box | Optional |

For the named combinations and when to choose each, see [Organization Configuration Scenarios]({{< ref "cloud/guides/organizations/configuration-scenarios/index.md" >}}).

## The identity provider is the security boundary

Organizations that sign in through the same identity provider sit inside the same authentication boundary. An organization that brings its own credentials is a distinct boundary. The shape of the host name does not decide this; the identity provider behind it does.

| Host class | Example | Identity provider | Authentication boundary |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Canonical host | `cloud.example.com` | The deployment's default providers | The shared boundary |
| Subdomain of the same base domain | `partner.example.com` | The default providers | The shared boundary |
| Different base domain | `meshery.yourcompany.com` | The default providers, unless the organization brings its own | The shared boundary, unless it brings its own |
| Any host, with own credentials | Any of the above | The organization's own provider | A distinct boundary |

The authentication boundary combines with authorization: each organization context scopes what a user may do through [keys]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/keys.md" >}}), [keychains]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/keychains.md" >}}), and [roles]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/roles/_index.md" >}}). See [Security Boundaries]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/_index.md#security-boundaries" >}}) for the full picture.

## Custom domains

Setting up a custom domain for an organization is a Provider Admin task. See [White-label Layer5 Cloud]({{< ref "cloud/guides/self-hosted/white-labeling/_index.md#configuring-a-subdomain" >}}) for the steps and [Social sign-in on a custom domain]({{< ref "cloud/guides/self-hosted/white-labeling/_index.md#social-sign-in-on-a-custom-domain" >}}) for how sign-in behaves there.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Manage Workspaces"
url: /cloud/guides/workspaces/managing-workspaces/index.md
description: Create, edit, and delete workspaces; give teams access; attach environments; place designs and views; and review workspace activity.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

A workspace is the unit you use to organize designs and to decide which teams can reach an organization's environments and connections. This guide covers every task on a workspace. For what a workspace is and how it relates to teams, environments, and designs, read the [Workspaces concept]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/workspaces.md" >}}).

Each task names the permission it needs. Layer5 Cloud checks the permission in the organization that owns the workspace. A custom role or a team role can hold any of these permissions; the default holders are below.

{{< keys-matrix caption="Workspace permissions" functions="View Workspace|Create Workspace|Edit Workspace|Delete Workspace|Assign team to workspace|Remove team from workspace|Assign environment to workspace|Remove environment from workspace|Assign Designs to Workspaces|Remove Designs from Workspaces|Assign Views to Workspace|Unassign Views from Workspace" >}}

## Find workspaces {#view-workspaces}

**Needs:** View Workspace to see the Workspaces page. The API lists workspaces for any signed-in member of the organization.

Every member of an organization can list every workspace in it. Team membership does not narrow the list. A list request names one organization. A user who holds View All Organizations can ask for every organization at once.

You can search by name or description, order by creation or update time, and page through results.

## Create a workspace

**Needs:** Create Workspace in the organization that will own the workspace.

A workspace takes a name, a description, and an organization. The workspace stays in that organization for its whole life; Layer5 Cloud ignores a later request to change it.

- The Workspaces page requires a name and an organization. The API does not check that the name is non-empty.
- Name and description are each limited to 255 characters. A longer value fails with `Unable to create workspace`.
- Names do not have to be unique. Two workspaces in one organization can share a name, so choose names you can tell apart.
- You become the owner of record. Creating a workspace does not assign any team or environment, and an empty workspace gives nobody access to anything.

## Edit a workspace

**Needs:** Edit Workspace.

You can change the name and the description. An update changes only the fields you send. A request with an empty body fails. A workspace that is not in one of your organizations answers `workspace not found`.

## Give a team access to a workspace {#assign-teams-to-a-workspace}

**Needs:** Assign team to workspace to add a team, Remove team from workspace to take it away.

The team and the workspace must belong to the same organization. A team from another organization is refused with HTTP 403. Assigning a team that is already assigned changes nothing and returns the existing assignment.

What a team assignment grants is narrower than it sounds:

| It grants | It does not grant |
| --- | --- |
| Read-only access to the connections, and their credentials, in every environment attached to the workspace | Access to private designs in the workspace |
| | The ability to see the workspace (all organization members see all workspaces) |
| | Permission to create, edit, or delete anything |

Removing the team ends the access at once. To give a team access to a private design, share the design with the people who need it. See [Share Designs]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/collaborating/sharing-designs/index.md" >}}).

## Attach an environment to a workspace {#link-environments-to-a-workspace}

**Needs:** Assign environment to workspace to attach, Remove environment from workspace to detach.

Attaching an environment makes its connections readable to every member of the workspace's teams. The environment and the workspace must belong to the same organization; a cross-organization attachment is refused with HTTP 403.
