Some environments are provisioned by Layer5 Cloud itself to hold organization configuration such as the mail server or sign-in providers. Layer5 Cloud refuses to attach one to a workspace: `this environment is provisioned by the platform and cannot be added to a workspace`.

Attaching an environment that is already attached returns the existing attachment. Detaching one that was never attached answers `no such environment assignment`. Detaching an environment that was already detached returns the earlier record without error.

The same environment can sit in any number of workspaces. Creating and filling environments is covered in [Manage Environments]({{< ref "cloud/guides/workspaces/managing-environments/index.md" >}}).

## Place designs and views in a workspace {#move-designs-and-views-between-workspaces}

**Needs:** Assign Designs to Workspaces and Remove Designs from Workspaces for designs. Assign Views to Workspace and Unassign Views from Workspace for views.

A design or view belongs to at most one workspace. Placing it in a workspace moves it: Layer5 Cloud removes every earlier workspace assignment, then adds the new one. There is no copy.

- **Ownership does not change.** The user who created a design stays its owner after any move.
- **The workspace decides the organization.** A design is listed under the organization of the workspace that holds it, and the Share Design permission is checked in that organization. Moving a design into a workspace in another organization moves it into that organization.
- **Workspace membership is not design access.** A private design stays private. Only the owner, provider administrators, and users the design was shared with can open it, wherever it sits. Private, public, and published designs can all live in one workspace.
- **Removing a design** from its workspace leaves it with no workspace. The design and its owner are unaffected.

The permission is checked in the destination workspace's organization only. Layer5 Cloud does not check that you own the design or that the design is in your organization.

The unassigned list for a workspace shows only designs you own.

## Review workspace activity {#view-recent-activity}

**Needs:** View Workspace.

Each workspace keeps an event log. It records the creation, update, and deletion of the workspace, and every assignment and unassignment of a team, environment, design, or view, with the email of the person who acted. Failed attempts are recorded as error events. The log is paged and searchable.

## Delete a workspace

**Needs:** Delete Workspace.

Deleting a workspace ends, in one step, every team, environment, design, and view assignment it holds. It deletes none of those resources: the teams, environments, connections, designs, and views all remain. Designs and views that were in the workspace have no workspace afterwards, and team members lose the connection access the workspace gave them.

**An organization must keep at least one workspace.** Layer5 Cloud refuses to delete the last one with `cannot delete workspace: at least one workspace must exist for the organization`. The check holds under concurrent requests, so two simultaneous deletes cannot empty an organization. The refusal arrives as HTTP 500.

Create the replacement workspace first, then delete the other.

## Patterns that work

- **One workspace per project.** Attach the project's team and environments, and keep its designs together.
- **One workspace per stage.** Give a production workspace only the production environment and the platform team. Members of other teams cannot read production connections through it. See [Promote a Design from Staging to Production]({{< ref "cloud/tutorials/promoting-a-design.md" >}}).
- **One workspace per team.** Attach the team and the environments it works with.

## Questions

**Can other workspace members edit or delete my design?** Workspace membership grants no design access. People you shared the design with can read, edit, and clone it. Only the owner or a provider administrator can delete it.

**How do I make a design read-only for everyone?** Publish it. See [Publish Designs]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/designs/publishing-designs/index.md" >}}).

**Does a workspace have size limits?** No. Layer5 Cloud enforces no space or file-count limit on workspaces, and no plan check on workspace actions.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Manage Your Account"
url: /cloud/guides/account/managing-your-account/index.md
description: Edit your profile, change your password, link GitHub or Google sign-in, and delete your account, with what each change does and what it leaves behind.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Your profile belongs to you, not to an organization. A change applies in every organization you belong to. This guide covers the four things you can change about your account: the profile, the password, the linked sign-in providers, and the account itself.

## Before you start

- You need the **View Profile** permission to open the profile. The default user role holds it.
- Changing your password needs **Reset Password**. Deleting the account needs **Delete Account**. The default user role holds both.
- Layer5 Cloud signs you in through an identity service. Password changes and account deletion need a live browser sign-in. A script that holds only an API token cannot do either.
- Changing a password or linking a provider is a privileged action. If your sign-in is older than the privileged-session window, Layer5 Cloud asks you to sign in again first. The window is 24 hours on hosted Layer5 Cloud and 15 minutes by default in the self-hosted chart.
- A user's profile can also be edited by an administrator who holds **Update User Profile** in an organization you share with them. Only a Provider Admin can change another user's email address.

## Edit your profile

The profile form saves itself. About one second after you stop typing, Layer5 Cloud saves the change and confirms it with a short message. There is no Save button, and edits made during a save are queued, not lost.

| Field | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| First Name, Last Name | Free text. An empty value never overwrites the stored name. |
| Username | Read-only. It is the identifier assigned to the account and cannot be edited. |
| E-mail | Must look like an address (`name@host.domain`). An invalid value blocks saving and shows "Please enter a valid email address". |
| Country, Region | Optional. Pick a country, then a region of that country. |
| Avatar URL | Optional. A public URL to a JPEG, PNG, GIF, SVG, or WEBP image. Layer5 Cloud loads the image before it saves. An address that does not load as an image is rejected. |
| Avatar color | The background color shown when you have no avatar image. Saved as a user preference. |
| Tagline | A short public line about you. |
| Social Links | Up to 5 links, each with a type (GitHub, LinkedIn, X, Company or Organization, or Personal Website) and a URL. An empty URL is allowed; a malformed one is rejected. |

Your avatar, tagline, and social links appear on your public profile.

### Change your email address

Changing the email address changes the identifier you sign in with. Layer5 Cloud marks the new address as unverified and sends it a verification message. The confirmation reads "Profile updated. Please check your new email address to verify it." Verify the new address before you rely on it. If the verification message cannot be sent, the change still completes.

Layer5 Cloud writes the change to the identity service first and to your profile second, so a rejected address never leaves the two out of step.

## Change your password

Use the Reset Password control on the profile. Enter the new password twice. The two entries must match, or the form reports "Your new passwords do not match".

The identity service enforces the password policy:

- At least 8 characters.
- Not a password found in known breaches.
- Not too similar to your email address.

A strength bar (Very weak to Strong) shows how guessable the password is. It is advice only and does not block you; the policy above does. A rejected password returns the identity service's reason. A successful change shows "Password updated".

Changing your password does not end your other sessions or revoke your API tokens. To cut off a device or script, end the session or revoke the token yourself with [Review and Sign Out Sessions]({{< ref "cloud/guides/security/sessions.md" >}}) and [Create and Use an API Token]({{< ref "cloud/guides/security/api-tokens.md" >}}).

If you forgot your password, use the recovery flow from the sign-in page instead. It emails a one-time code and link that stay valid for 30 days.

## Link or unlink a sign-in provider

Link GitHub or Google to sign in with whichever you prefer. Either method opens the same account, with the same organizations, designs, and roles. GitHub and Google are the only supported providers.

The profile lists a **Link** option for each provider you have not linked and an **Unlink** option for each provider you have linked. The provider you used to create the account appears in neither list: you cannot unlink it, and it is already linked.

Linking sends you to the provider to approve access, then returns you to Layer5 Cloud. Layer5 Cloud asks GitHub for your profile and email address and Google for your email and profile. Unlinking removes the provider from your account. Your password and the other linked provider keep working.

A provider account can be linked to one Layer5 Cloud account only. Linking depends on the provider reporting a verified email address. For how Layer5 Cloud resolves sign-ins that share an email address, read [Account Consolidation]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/users/account-consolidation.md" >}}) and the [Account Linking]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/users/_index.md#account-linking" >}}) rules.

## Delete your account

Deletion is permanent. Layer5 Cloud asks you to confirm, and then does not offer recovery.

What deletion does:

1. Hands any credential you hold on behalf of an organization to that organization's successor, so the organization keeps working. The successor is the organization's owner, or else its longest-standing Organization Admin.
2. Marks your account as deleted and removes your memberships in every organization and team, which removes your roles with them.
3. Records the deletion in the audit trail.
4. Removes your sign-in identity, including linked GitHub and Google sign-in, and signs you out.

What deletion leaves behind:

- Published content, such as items you published to the catalog, stays public.
- Organizations you own continue to exist. Deleting your account does not delete or transfer them.
- The audit trail keeps its entries.

Re-registering with the same email address does not restore the old account or re-link a provider.

### When deletion is refused

Layer5 Cloud refuses the deletion, and changes nothing, when you are the only owner or Organization Admin of an organization that holds credentials designated to it. The message begins "Refusing to delete your account" and names the organization. Without a successor, those credentials would be orphaned.

Resolve it, then retry:

- Promote another member of that organization to Organization Admin. An organization's ownership cannot be transferred, so a second Organization Admin is the way to give it a successor.
- Or release the credentials from the organization, or delete them.

## See also

- [Users]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/users/_index.md" >}}) explains accounts, memberships, and sign-in methods.
- [Set Notification Preferences]({{< ref "cloud/guides/account/notification-preferences.md" >}}) controls the email you receive.
- [Security]({{< ref "cloud/guides/security/_index.md" >}}) covers sessions and API tokens.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Promote a Design from Staging to Production"
url: /cloud/tutorials/promoting-a-design/index.md
description: Build staging and production workspaces, promote a design between them, deploy it to a production environment, and confirm who did what.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

A pipeline is only as trustworthy as its boundaries. In this tutorial you build two stages of one in a single organization: a staging workspace and a production workspace, each with its own team and its own environment. You put a design in staging, promote it to production, deploy it to the production environment from Kanvas, and read the production workspace's activity log to confirm every change and who made it.

By the end you know what each object controls:

- A **workspace** is a boundary. It decides where a design lives and which teams reach which connections.
- An **environment** is a deploy target: a named group of connections.
- A **team assignment** gives read-only access to connections. It does not give access to designs.

## Before you begin

- You have a Layer5 Cloud account and work in an organization where your role holds the permissions below. Organization Admin and Workspace Admin hold all of them.
- The organization has at least one connection, such as a Kubernetes cluster. Two connections, one per stage, make the separation clearer, but one works: a connection can belong to more than one environment.
- The organization has a team for each stage, or one team you assign to both. To create teams, see [Manage Teams]({{< ref "cloud/guides/organizations/managing-teams/index.md" >}}).
- To complete step 7, you run a Meshery Server that holds the cluster connection. The hosted kanvas.new site does not deploy designs.
- You own a design. If you do not, clone one with [Start from a Catalog Design]({{< ref "cloud/getting-started/creating-a-design-from-template.md" >}}).

Each step needs a specific permission. The table shows which built-in roles hold each one:

{{< keys-matrix caption="Permissions used in this tutorial" functions="Create Workspace|Assign team to workspace|Create Environment|Assign connections to environment|Assign environment to workspace|Assign Designs to Workspaces" >}}

Confirm that the organization switcher shows the organization you intend. Every workspace and environment you create belongs to that organization permanently.

## 1. Create the staging and production workspaces

Create two workspaces in your organization and name them `staging` and `production`. Layer5 Cloud does not require unique names, so check the workspace list first and pick names nobody else in the organization uses.

Each new workspace starts empty: no teams, no environments, no designs. Every member of your organization can already see both workspaces in the list. Visibility is organization-wide; what a workspace grants comes from what you assign to it next.

## 2. Create an environment for each stage

Create two environments named `staging` and `production`. Assign a connection to each: your staging cluster to the staging environment and your production cluster to the production environment. If you have one connection, assign it to both.

An environment is the unit you deploy to. Grouping connections this way means that later, choosing where a design runs is one choice, not a list of clusters.

## 3. Give each workspace its environment

Assign the staging environment to the staging workspace and the production environment to the production workspace.

A workspace never holds connections directly. It holds environments, and the environments hold connections. This step makes each stage's connections reachable from its workspace.

## 4. Assign a team to each workspace

Assign your staging team to the staging workspace and your production team to the production workspace. Each team must belong to the same organization as the workspace.

Assigning a team completes a chain: team member, to team, to workspace, to environment, to connection. Every member of the production team can now read the production connection and its credential. That access is read-only; only the connection's owner can modify or delete it. Remove any link in the chain and the access ends.

## 5. Put your design in staging

Assign your design to the staging workspace. When you look for designs to add, the list offers only designs you own that are not already in the workspace.

The design is now listed under your organization through the staging workspace. The staging team cannot open it, though. A team assignment grants connection access, not design access, so a private design stays private. Keep that in mind for step 8.

## 6. Promote the design to production

Assign the same design to the production workspace.

Now look at the staging workspace: the design is gone. A design lives in at most one workspace, so assigning it to production moved it there. Promotion is a move, not a copy, which means there is exactly one current version and one place to find it.

Layer5 Cloud checks one permission for this move: Assign Designs to Workspaces in the production workspace's organization. Anyone who holds it can promote, so grant it only to the people who should decide what reaches production.

## 7. Deploy to the production environment

Open the design in Kanvas and deploy it. The deploy action offers environments from your organization's whole list at the moment you deploy. It does not limit the list to the design's workspace, so select the production environment yourself. For the deploy options, see [Deploy a Design]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/deploying/deploying-designs/index.md" >}}).

The workspace decided where the design lives. The environment you choose now decides where it runs. Those are two separate decisions, and keeping them separate is what lets one design move through stages.

## 8. Let the production team read the design

The production team can reach the production connection but still cannot read your private design. To give them access, share the design with the people who need it. See [Share a Design]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/collaborating/sharing-designs/index.md" >}}).

## 9. Confirm who did what

Open the production workspace's recent activity. It lists each change recorded against the workspace, including the environment assignment, the team assignment, and the design assignment from this tutorial, each with the email address of the person who made it. Reading the activity log requires the View Workspace permission.

Use this log whenever you need to answer who promoted a design and when.

## Roll back

To roll back, assign the design to the staging workspace again. It leaves production the same way it left staging, and the staging workspace's activity log records the assignment.

## What you built

| Object | Staging | Production |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Workspace | `staging` | `production` |
| Environment (deploy target) | `staging`, with the staging connection | `production`, with the production connection |
| Team access | Read-only access to the staging connection | Read-only access to the production connection |
| Design | Lived here first | Lives here now, deployed to the production environment |

## Next steps

- [Workspaces]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/workspaces.md" >}}) explains the full access chain and lifecycle rules.
- [Environments]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/environments.md" >}}) explains deploy targets and connection access.
- [Manage Workspaces]({{< ref "cloud/guides/workspaces/managing-workspaces/index.md" >}}) covers editing, removing members, and deleting workspaces.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Build a Challenge"
url: /cloud/academy/creating-content/building-challenges/index.md
description: A step-by-step guide to building a hands-on challenge in the Academy, and to monitoring how learners get on with it.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

In [Layer5 Academy](https://cloud.layer5.io/academy/), a **Challenge** is a hands-on, scenario-based task. Where a Learning Path teaches a subject from the ground up and a Certification tests knowledge a learner already has, a Challenge gives them a concrete problem and asks them to solve it.

## When to use a challenge

Choose a challenge when the learner should build, break, or fix something real and is scored on the result. Compare the content types in [Create Academy Content]({{< ref "cloud/academy/creating-content/_index.md#choose-a-content-type" >}}).

{{< alert type="info" title="Challenge: Focus on Doing, Not Reading" >}}
Choose a Challenge when the point is for the learner to build, break, or fix something real. If most of your material is explanation, it belongs in a [Learning Path]({{< ref "cloud/academy/creating-content/creating-your-learning-path/index.md" >}}) instead.
{{< /alert >}}

## How to Create Your Challenge

Challenges are authored the same way as every other Academy content type: as Markdown in your organization's Academy content repository, published through a Git-native workflow. If you have not set that repository up yet, start with [Creating Content for the Academy]({{< ref "cloud/academy/creating-content/creating-your-learning-path/index.md" >}}), which covers the repository setup once for all three content types.

### Get your identifiers

Register the challenge in the Instructor Console and choose **Challenge** as the content type. The console generates the challenge `id` and a ready-to-paste front matter block. Use your organization's ID in the directory path. See [Create Academy Content]({{< ref "cloud/academy/creating-content/_index.md#register-content-in-the-console" >}}).

### 1. Set Up the Directory Structure

All challenges live under `content/challenges/<your-organization-uuid>`, each in its own folder named with a descriptive, URL-friendly slug. The final URL follows this pattern:

`https://cloud.layer5.io/academy/content/challenges/<your-organization-uuid>/<challenge-folder-name>/`

A challenge is typically one scenario broken into a few sections:

```text
content/challenges/<your-organization-uuid>
└── keda-autoscaling-challenge/     <-- The <challenge-name> directory
    ├── _index.md                   <-- Defines the challenge's metadata
    ├── keda-icon.svg               <-- Banner image, referenced from the front matter
    └── autoscaling-with-keda/      <-- The task itself
        ├── _index.md               <-- The objective and prerequisites
        └── content/
            ├── description/        <-- What the challenge is about, and the steps
            ├── getting-started/    <-- How to set up and begin
            └── faq/                <-- Common questions
```

A challenge that ships an interactive lab and a graded exam adds them as their own sections alongside the task:

```text
content/challenges/<your-organization-uuid>
└── heal-the-mesh/
    ├── _index.md
    ├── lab/
    │   └── _index.md               <-- The hands-on lab
    └── exam/
        └── _index.md               <-- The assessment that closes the challenge
```

{{< alert type="info" title="Sections Are Yours to Name" >}}
`description`, `getting-started` and `faq` are a convention, not a fixed structure - the folder hierarchy you create is what the Academy renders as the challenge's navigation. Use the sections your scenario actually needs.
{{< /alert >}}

### 2. Define the Challenge with Front Matter

The `_index.md` at the root of the challenge folder carries its metadata. Here is a complete example, taken from a published challenge:

```yaml
---
title: "CNCF Autoscaling Challenge"
description: "Learn event-driven autoscaling in Kubernetes. Work with scaled objects in KEDA, monitoring with Prometheus, OpenTelemetry & CloudEvents and advanced KEDA configurations."
banner: "keda-icon.svg"
id: "<your-challenge-uuid>"
weight: 1
tags: [meshery, keda, open source]
level: "advanced"
categories: [platform]

prerequisite_knowledge:
  - title: "Access to Meshery"
    children:
      - title: "Self-hosted Meshery"
        link: "https://docs.meshery.io/installation"
      - title: "Meshery Playground"
        link: "https://play.meshery.io"

additional_attributes:
  - title: "Retake Policy"
    value: "3"
    description: "Up to three retakes allowed per exam"
---
```

#### Front Matter Fields Reference

> Fields marked ✅ are required; those marked - are optional.

| Field | Required | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `id` | ✅ | **Crucial.** A stable UUID used to track learner progress. **Do not change it** once learners have enrolled. |
| `title` | ✅ | The human-readable title shown to learners. |
| `description` | ✅ | A summary of the scenario. This is the text learners read on the catalog card. |
| `weight` | - | Controls display order (lower numbers appear first). Items are sorted alphabetically by title if not specified. |
| `banner` | - | Path to a banner image in the same folder (Page Bundle). |
| `tags` | - | Keywords for discovery. Learners can browse by tag. |
| `level` | - | Intended difficulty: `beginner`, `intermediate` or `advanced`. Default: `beginner`. |
| `categories` | - | Assigns the challenge to a category. |
| `badge` | - | Defines the digital badge awarded on completion. Its `png` and `svg` fields accept a full remote URL or a local file path in the same folder. |
| `prerequisite_knowledge` | - | What a learner needs before starting, rendered as a list with optional links. |
| `additional_attributes` | - | Free-form title/value/description rows, used for things like retake policy and scoring. |

{{< alert type="info" title="Where `type` Comes From" >}}
You do not set `type: "challenge"` on every file. The `content/challenges/_index.md` at the top of the section declares it once and cascades it to everything beneath, so each challenge inherits the right type - and therefore the right template - automatically.
{{< /alert >}}

### 3. Write the Scenario

The task's own `_index.md` is where you state the objective and the prerequisites, and the sections beneath it carry the detail:

- **Description** - what the challenge is about, and the numbered steps a learner must follow to complete it.
- **Getting Started** - how to get an environment ready, including any Meshery access the scenario needs.
- **FAQ** - the questions learners predictably ask.

Write the steps so that success is unambiguous. A challenge is scored, so a learner needs to know exactly what "done" looks like before they start.

### 4. Add the Assessment

Most challenges close with an exam that validates the learner's work. Exams in a challenge follow the same unified Academy assessment standard as every other content type.

{{< alert type="info" title="How to Create and Configure Exams" >}}
For question types, scoring, passing percentages, question pools and retry settings, see the [Integrating Assessments in the Academy]({{< ref "cloud/academy/creating-content/integrating-assessments-in-the-academy.md" >}}) guide.
{{< /alert >}}

### 5. Publish

Publishing a challenge is the same two-stage release process as the rest of your Academy content: a GitHub Release on your content repository, followed by a Layer5 Cloud release. Until both have happened, your changes will not be live. See [Publishing Your Content]({{< ref "cloud/academy/creating-content/creating-your-learning-path/index.md#publish" >}}).

## Monitor your challenge

The [Instructor Console]({{< ref "cloud/academy/instructor-console-guide/index.md" >}}) reports on challenges alongside your other content:

- **Learners** lists registrations. Filter by content type `Challenge` and by status to follow who is Registered, In Progress, Completed, Failed, or Withdrawn.
- **Curricula** shows registrations, completion rate, and pass rate for each published challenge.
- **Overview** shows pass rates per assessment. A low pass rate separates a hard challenge from unclear instructions only when the attempt count is high enough to mean something.

{{< feature-tiers categories="Academy" >}}

## Learner outcomes

Completing all the required components of a challenge earns the learner a digital badge - a verifiable credential they can share on their professional profiles. Unlike a Certification, a Challenge does not issue a paid Certificate of Completion; its outcome is the score, the rank, and the badge.

The badge is awarded when the learner passes the final test of the challenge. See the [Learner Guide]({{< ref "cloud/academy/using-the-academy/index.md" >}}) for the learner's side of this.

## Frequently Asked Questions

<details>
<summary>Can a challenge have more than one task?</summary>

Yes. The folder hierarchy beneath the challenge's `_index.md` is what defines its structure, so a challenge can hold several sections. Most challenges are a single scenario because that keeps the objective sharp, but nothing prevents a longer one.
</details>

<details>
<summary>Does a challenge have to include an exam?</summary>

No. An exam is the usual way to validate that the learner solved the problem, but a challenge whose completion is judged by a lab does not need one.
</details>

<details>
<summary>Can I change a challenge after learners have started it?</summary>

You can edit its content freely - but never change its `id`. That UUID is what learner progress is recorded against, and changing it orphans every registration made against the old value.
</details>

<details>
<summary>How do learners find my challenge?</summary>

Through the Academy catalog, filtered by **Content Type** → **Challenge**. See [Exploring the Content Catalog]({{< ref "cloud/academy/using-the-academy/index.md" >}}).
</details>


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Child Organizations"
url: /cloud/guides/organizations/org-management/child-organizations/index.md
description: Create organizations inside an organization, see who can view and administer them, and understand what a parent administrator can and cannot do in a child.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

A **child organization** is an organization created inside another organization, called its **parent**. A child is otherwise an ordinary organization: it has its own members, teams, workspaces, invitations, domain, and credentials. The parent relationship adds one thing, which is that administrators of the parent can manage the child's settings and membership from the parent.

{{< alert title="Permissions Required" type="info" >}}
Creating a child organization requires the **Create Organization** permission in the parent. Seeing the list of a parent's children requires **View Organizations** in the parent. Editing, deleting, or adding members to a child from the parent requires the Organization Administrator or Owner role in the parent. To understand the specific roles needed for each action, please refer to the [Roles and Permissions reference]({{< ref "cloud/reference/default-permissions.md" >}}).
{{< /alert >}}

## How Organizations Nest

- An organization can have any number of child organizations.
- A child can have child organizations of its own, and those can have children of their own. There is no limit on depth.
- Every top-level organization sits directly under the **provider organization** of your Layer5 Cloud deployment. The provider organization is never itself a child, and it does not appear in the child organizations section.
- A child belongs to exactly one parent. A child cannot be moved to another parent after it is created.

A parent administers its **direct** children only. An administrator of a grandparent does not administer a grandchild by virtue of that role; the administrator of the intermediate organization does.

## Creating a Child Organization

Any member holding the **Create Organization** permission in the parent can create a child. The creator becomes an Organization Administrator of the new child.

Select the parent organization, then create the child from the **Child organizations** section of the Organizations page. The form asks for the same details as any organization: name (required), country, region, and description.

The parent is always the organization you have selected, so there is no parent field to fill in. If you do not see a create control, your role in the parent does not include **Create Organization**.

## Viewing Child Organizations

The **Child organizations** section on the Organizations page lists the direct children of the selected organization, showing each child's **name**, **description**, and **domain**. It appears for anyone holding **View Organizations** in the selected organization, and it does not appear when you have the provider organization or all organizations selected.

{{< alert title="Seeing a Child Is Not Joining It" type="info" >}}
Being able to see the list of children does not make you a member of any child. You do not see a child's members, invitations, or other settings from the list, and the child does not appear in your organization switcher unless you are a member of it.
{{< /alert >}}

## What a Parent Administrator Can Do

An Organization Administrator or Owner of the parent can manage a direct child from the parent, without joining the child. From the parent, they can:

-   **Edit the child's settings**, using the edit action on the child's row.
-   **Add members to the child.** The **Child organizations** section has no add-member control, so this is done through the existing add-member API for the child.
-   **Search the child's members.**
-   **Delete the child**, using the delete action on the child's row, provided the child has no child organizations of its own (see [Deleting Organizations That Have Children](#deleting-organizations-that-have-children)).

This access is read from the parent administrator's role in the parent on every request. Removing someone as an Organization Administrator of the parent ends their access to the settings of every child at once, with nothing to clean up in the children.

## What a Parent Administrator Cannot Do

Governing a child does not make the parent administrator a member of it. Anything inside the child still requires membership in the child and the usual role there, including:

-   workspaces, environments, connections, and credentials,
-   teams,
-   identity providers,
-   the mail server.

To work inside a child, a parent administrator must be added to it as a member like anyone else. Holding a permission such as Edit Organization in the parent does not grant that permission in the child.

## Switching into a Child

The organization switcher lists only the organizations you are a member of. A parent administrator who is not a member of a child can edit that child's settings from the parent but cannot switch into it. The creator of a child is a member of it from the start, so the creator can switch into it right away. Other members of the parent do not appear in the child until someone adds them to it. See [Switching Between Organizations](../#switching-between-organizations) for how the switcher and the active organization work.

## Deleting Organizations That Have Children

An organization that still has child organizations cannot be deleted. The request is refused and nothing is deleted. Delete the children first, starting with the deepest, and then delete the parent. Children are never deleted along with their parent and are never moved to another parent.

Deleting a child removes it as described in [Deleting Your Organization](../#deleting-your-organization).


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Organization Configuration Scenarios"
url: /cloud/guides/organizations/configuration-scenarios/index.md
description: Choose how an organization is reached and who authenticates its users, then set up a custom domain. Covers the Hosted, Branded, and White-Label scenarios.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Every organization in Layer5 Cloud is configured by two choices: **where your users sign in** (the front door) and **whose identity provider authenticates them**. The combinations form five named scenarios. This guide helps you pick one and then walks through the settings that implement it, including who is allowed to change each setting.

For the mechanics behind the choices, see [White-labeling]({{< ref "cloud/guides/self-hosted/white-labeling/_index.md" >}}) (themes, logos, custom domains) and [Identity Services]({{< ref "cloud/guides/self-hosted/planning/identity-services/index.md" >}}) (bring-your-own-credentials and authentication boundaries).

## Provider and tenant organizations {#first-the-two-organization-types}

These scenarios configure a **tenant organization**, which is every organization except one.

- **Provider organization.** The single top-level organization that operates the deployment. On the hosted service it is Layer5. On a self-hosted deployment it is your platform team. It owns the deployment's default identity providers, the Google and GitHub applications every other organization falls back to. A Provider Admin manages platform-wide settings.
- **Tenant organization.** Every other organization: a customer, partner, or business unit. A tenant is what you configure into one of the scenarios below.

The provider organization always signs in on the deployment's canonical address with the default identity providers.

## The two choices

| Choice | Options |
| --- | --- |
| **Front door**: where users sign in | **Shared**: the deployment's own address, such as `cloud.layer5.io`. **Branded subdomain**: a subdomain of the deployment's base domain, such as `acme.layer5.io`. **Custom domain**: your own domain, such as `cloud.acme.com`. |
| **Identity provider**: who runs sign-in | **Shared**: the deployment's Google and GitHub applications. **Your own (BYOC)**: your own Google, GitHub, or OIDC single sign-on. |

Email-and-password sign-in and the Google and GitHub buttons work in every scenario, including on a custom domain that uses the default identity providers. The scenarios differ in whose identity provider authenticates users and whose brand appears on the consent screen, not in whether social sign-in is available.

## The scenarios at a glance

| Scenario | Front door | Identity provider | Branded sign-in pages | Consent screen shows | Setting needed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Hosted** | Shared | Shared | No (shared page) | Platform name | None. This is the default. |
| **Branded** | Branded subdomain | Shared | Yes | Platform name | Domain (Provider Admin) |
| **Branded + BYOC** | Branded subdomain | Your own | Yes | Your brand | Domain (Provider Admin) and identity providers |
| **White-Label** | Custom domain | Shared | Yes | Platform name | Domain (Provider Admin) |
| **White-Label + BYOC** | Custom domain | Your own | Yes | Your brand | Domain (Provider Admin) and identity providers |

One combination does not exist: the shared front door always uses the shared identity provider, so there is no "Shared + your own identity provider". To use your own identity provider, give the organization a branded subdomain or a custom domain first.

## Choose a scenario {#how-to-choose}

1. **Do you need a branded address?**
   - No: use **Hosted**. Nothing to configure.
   - A subdomain of the platform is fine: continue with **Branded**.
   - It must be your own domain: continue with **White-Label**.
2. **Do you need your own identity provider?** You need one for your own consent-screen branding, your own OAuth rate limits and audit trail, corporate single sign-on, or a distinct authentication boundary.
   - On a subdomain: no means **Branded**, yes means **Branded + BYOC**.
   - On your own domain: no means **White-Label**, yes means **White-Label + BYOC**.

Bringing your own identity provider is always optional, whatever the domain.

## What each scenario means for your users {#the-scenarios-in-detail}

### Hosted

Users sign in at the deployment's address and pick your organization in the organization switcher. Theme colors and logo appear inside the app. The sign-in page itself is the platform's, shared by every organization on that address. This is the default and needs no configuration.

### Branded

The organization has its own subdomain of the deployment's base domain. Sign-in, sign-up, and error pages carry your colors, logo, and links. Social buttons use the platform's applications, so the consent screen shows the platform's name.

### Branded + BYOC

A branded subdomain plus your own OAuth clients or OIDC provider. The consent screen shows your brand, and the organization becomes a distinct authentication boundary. See [The identity provider is the security boundary]({{< ref "cloud/guides/self-hosted/planning/identity-services/index.md#the-identity-provider-is-the-security-boundary" >}}).

### White-Label

The organization runs on your own domain, on a different base domain from the deployment, with the platform's identity providers. Social sign-in works without extra setup and shows the platform's name on the consent screen.

### White-Label + BYOC

Your domain and your identity provider. The organization is branded end to end. This is the usual choice for a partner or reseller that offers the platform under its own name.

## Set up a custom domain

A domain routes users who arrive at that address into your organization. The scenarios other than Hosted all depend on it.

### Who can set it

Only a **Provider Admin** can set a domain to a new value. An Organization Admin sees the domain field in the organization settings, but the save fails with a 403 error that says the domain requires a Provider Admin. Organization administrators can keep the stored value and can clear it. Ask the provider to set the domain, and tell them the exact hostname.

### What a valid domain looks like

Layer5 Cloud checks the domain when it changes:

| Rule | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Length | 3 to 253 characters. |
| Labels | Dot-separated, each 1 to 63 ASCII letters, digits, or hyphens, not starting or ending with a hyphen. |
| Format | A hostname. Email-shaped input with `@` is rejected. The value cannot start with `http`, `https`, or `www`. |
| Internationalized names | Write them in Punycode (`xn--`). |
| Reserved hosts | The provider's own hosts, including the canonical Layer5 Cloud address and the Layer5 marketing and documentation hosts, are rejected. |
| Uniqueness | One organization per domain. Deleted organizations keep their domain, so clear the domain before you delete an organization if the address must be reused. |

The check is syntactic. Layer5 Cloud does not resolve the name when you save, so a valid hostname whose DNS is not ready yet is accepted. Point the domain's DNS at your Layer5 Cloud deployment, as described in [White-labeling]({{< ref "cloud/guides/self-hosted/white-labeling/_index.md" >}}).

### How the domain is used

- **Exact match.** Layer5 Cloud compares the host of each request, with the protocol and port removed, to organization domains. The match is exact, so `cloud.acme.com` and `www.cloud.acme.com` are different hosts.
- **The domain wins.** A request that arrives on an organization's domain runs in that organization, ahead of the request header, the saved preference, and the browser session. See [Switching Between Organizations]({{< ref "cloud/guides/organizations/org-management/_index.md#switching-between-organizations" >}}).
- **Never custom.** The deployment's own address, IP addresses, and reserved hosts are never treated as custom domains.
- **Cache.** Lookups, including misses, are cached for five minutes. Creating, updating, or deleting an organization clears the affected entry on the server that handled the change, so the change is visible there immediately and everywhere within the cache window.
- **Clearing.** Emptying the field removes the assignment. Users who arrive on the old address no longer land in the organization.
- **Open invitation.** When an organization has an [open invitation]({{< ref "cloud/guides/organizations/org-management/_index.md#using-the-open-organization-invitation-link" >}}), a non-member who signs in on its domain joins through it.

Changing a domain that users already rely on can break their routing and bookmarks. Announce the change first.

### Verify the assignment

The by-domain lookup is public and needs no credentials. It returns the organization record when the domain is assigned and `null` with a 200 status when it is not:

```bash
curl "https://cloud.layer5.io/api/identity/orgs/by-domain?domain=cloud.acme.com"
```

Substitute your deployment's address and your hostname. A `null` result means the domain is unassigned, mistyped, or still inside the cache window for a recent change.

## Add your own identity provider

Organization Admins and Owners add, rotate, and remove identity providers without the provider's help. The procedure is in [Configuring Identity Providers]({{< ref "cloud/guides/organizations/org-management/_index.md#configuring-identity-providers-bring-your-own-credentials" >}}). The first provider you save switches the organization to its own identity providers. Removing the last one returns it to the platform's defaults.

## Membership policy is independent {#these-choices-are-independent-of-who-can-join}

The scenario controls where and how users sign in. It does not control who may join. Membership is governed by invitations, open sign-up, and the roles and teams an invitation grants. Any scenario pairs with any membership policy. See [Using the Open Organization Invitation Link]({{< ref "cloud/guides/organizations/org-management/_index.md#using-the-open-organization-invitation-link" >}}) and [User Invitations]({{< ref "cloud/guides/organizations/inviting-users/index.md" >}}).


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Manage Environments"
url: /cloud/guides/workspaces/managing-environments/index.md
description: Create environments, assign and remove connections, edit and delete environments, and know which environments you cannot change.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

An environment groups connections into a deploy target and is the means by which a workspace exposes those connections to its teams. This guide covers every task on an environment. For the model behind it, read the [Environments concept]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/environments.md" >}}).

Each task names the permission it needs. Layer5 Cloud checks the permission in the organization that owns the environment.

{{< keys-matrix caption="Environment permissions" functions="View Environment|Create Environment|Edit Environment|Delete Environment|Assign connections to environment|Remove connections from environment|View Connections" >}}

The feature matrix lists environments under the Enterprise plan. Layer5 Cloud does not refuse environment actions because of the plan.

## Find environments {#view-environments}

**Needs:** View Environment to see the Environments page. The API lists environments for any signed-in member of the organization.

Every member of an organization can list every environment in it, whether or not the environment is attached to a workspace they belong to. A list request names one organization; View All Organizations widens it to every organization. You can search by name or description, order by creation or update time, and page through results.

Environments that Layer5 Cloud provisions for itself appear in the list too. See [Environments you cannot change](#environments-you-cannot-change).

## Create an environment

**Needs:** Create Environment in the organization that will own the environment.

An environment takes a name, a description, and an organization. The organization is required; without it the request fails with `organizationId is required`. The environment stays in that organization for its whole life.

- The Environments page requires a name and an organization. The API does not check that the name is non-empty or unique.
- Name and description are each limited to 255 characters.
- A new environment is empty and attached to no workspace. It is an ordinary environment, which means you can edit and delete it and manage its connections.

## Edit an environment

**Needs:** Edit Environment.

An update replaces both the name and the description with the values you send. A field you leave out becomes empty, so send both every time. Editing never changes the organization and never changes the connections.

## Assign connections to an environment

**Needs:** Assign connections to environment.

Assigning a connection places it in the environment, whether the connection is managed or discovered. One connection can be in any number of environments, and an environment can hold any number of connections.

Assigning a connection also makes its credentials reachable. Who can use it follows the [access rules for connections]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/environments.md#access-to-connections-and-credentials" >}}): the owner, members of teams assigned to a workspace that holds the environment, and holders of View All Organizations.

Layer5 Cloud answers an assignment this way:

| Condition | Result |
| --- | --- |
| The environment exists and is ordinary | The connection is assigned |
| No live environment has that identifier | HTTP 404, `no environment with the requested id` |
| The environment is provisioned by the platform | HTTP 403, `this connection cannot be assigned to this environment` |

Layer5 Cloud checks the permission in the environment's organization. It does not compare the connection's organization with the environment's, and it does not check who owns the connection.

## View the connections in an environment

**Needs:** View Environment.

The connection list of an environment defaults to the connections assigned to it. Switch the filter to see the connections not yet in it, which is the pick list for an assignment. You can search, order by creation time, update time, or name, and page through results.

## Remove connections from an environment

**Needs:** Remove connections from environment.

Removing a connection takes it out of this environment only. The connection and its credential remain, and so does its membership in any other environment. Team members who reached the connection only through this environment lose that access.

| Condition | Result |
| --- | --- |
| The connection is in the environment | It is removed |
| The connection was never assigned | HTTP 404, `no such connection assignment` |
| The environment is provisioned by the platform | HTTP 403, `this connection cannot be detached from this environment` |

## See the environments in a workspace {#see-the-environments-in-a-workspace}

The environments attached to a workspace default to the list of its environments. Switch the filter to list the organization's environments not yet attached, which is the pick list for an attachment. Attaching and detaching are workspace tasks. See [Attach an environment to a workspace]({{< ref "cloud/guides/workspaces/managing-workspaces/index.md#link-environments-to-a-workspace" >}}).

## Delete an environment

**Needs:** Delete Environment.

Deleting an environment ends every connection assignment and every workspace attachment it holds. It deletes no connection, credential, or workspace. Connections that also belong to other environments stay in those. Team members lose the access the environment gave them through workspaces.

| Condition | Result |
| --- | --- |
| The environment is ordinary and live | It is deleted |
| No live environment has that identifier | HTTP 404, `no environment with the requested id` |
| The environment is provisioned by the platform | HTTP 403, `this environment is provisioned by the platform and cannot be deleted here` |
| Any other failure | HTTP 400, `unable to delete environment` |

## Environments you cannot change

Layer5 Cloud provisions some environments itself to hold organization configuration, such as the mail server or sign-in providers. They show in the environment list like any other. The controls on this page refuse them:

- You cannot delete one.
- You cannot assign connections to one or remove connections from one.
- You cannot attach one to a workspace.

An existing attachment of one to a workspace can still be removed. Manage the configuration they hold through the organization guides: [Bring Your Own Mail Server]({{< ref "cloud/guides/organizations/org-management/bring-your-own-mail-server.md" >}}) and [Organization Configuration Scenarios]({{< ref "cloud/guides/organizations/configuration-scenarios/index.md" >}}).


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Meshery Server Registration"
url: /cloud/concepts/meshery-server-registration/index.md
description: How a Meshery Server registers itself with Layer5 Cloud, how Cloud recognizes the same server on every later registration, and what each failure means.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Layer5 Cloud is a [Meshery remote provider](https://docs.meshery.io/extensibility/providers). When a Meshery Server uses Layer5 Cloud, hosted or self-hosted, the server registers itself with Cloud on behalf of the signed-in user. Registration is what makes that Meshery Server known to Cloud: it appears as a `meshery` connection owned by that user. This page explains what the server sends, how Cloud tells a new server from one it already knows, what survives re-registration, and what each failure means.

For where registration fits in the overall relationship between Cloud and Meshery, see [How Layer5 Cloud Works with Meshery and Kanvas]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/architecture/index.md" >}}).

## Why registration exists

Registration answers two questions for Cloud:

1. **Which Meshery Server is calling?** Many Meshery deployments can work with the same Cloud deployment, and Cloud must keep them apart.
2. **Who owns it?** Every registration is owned by exactly one user, the user whose session made the request.

A registration record answers both. It ties a stable server identifier to an owner and survives Meshery Server restarts.

## How Cloud identifies a Meshery Server

A Meshery Server generates a stable server identifier on its first start and keeps it locally. It sends that identifier as `serverId` inside the connection's `metadata`.

Cloud recognizes an existing registration by three values together:

- the connection kind, `meshery`
- the owner, which is the authenticated user
- `metadata.serverId`

Each owner and `serverId` pair maps to exactly one connection. Cloud places no limit on either side of that pair: one user can register any number of Meshery Servers, and one Meshery Server can be registered by any number of users, with one connection per user.

Connections are owned by a user, not by an organization. Each user sees their own connections, including the Meshery Servers they registered.

## The registration request

A Meshery Server registers by sending a connection to:

```
POST /api/integrations/connections
```

The request must be authenticated with a Cloud session or a bearer token. Cloud takes the owner from that authentication, never from the request body.

| Field | Required | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `kind` | Yes | The connection kind. Case-insensitive. Accepted values are `meshery`, `kubernetes`, `prometheus`, and `grafana`. A Meshery Server registers itself with `meshery`. |
| `metadata.serverId` | Yes, for `meshery` | The stable identifier the Meshery Server generated. The key is camelCase. |
| `name` | No | A display name. When omitted, Cloud names the connection `<kind>-<random>`, for example `meshery-` followed by a random suffix. |
| `metadata` (other keys) | No | Additional details about the server, such as its version. Cloud refreshes them on every registration. |

On success, Cloud responds with HTTP 201 and a one-item page of connections containing the registered connection. Every registration call, first or repeat, records a "registered" event for the connection in the account's event log.

## First registration

When no connection matches the owner and `serverId`, Cloud creates a new `meshery` connection owned by the authenticated user.

## Re-registration

A re-registration is any later call from the same Meshery Server, carrying the same `serverId`, for the same user. It typically follows a Meshery Server restart, a new sign-in, or a reconnect.

Cloud updates the existing connection in place:

| Kept from the stored connection | Refreshed from the request |
| :--- | :--- |
| ID, name, kind, type, sub-type, status, owner, and creation time | Metadata and the last-updated time |

Two consequences follow:

- **Re-registering never renames a server.** A request that omits `name`, and would otherwise get a random name, cannot replace the name the connection already has.
- **Re-registering never resets status.** A Meshery Server you disconnected or ignored stays disconnected or ignored when it registers again.

{{< alert type="info" title="Status changes through connection lifecycle actions" >}}
Connection status changes through the dedicated connection lifecycle actions, such as connect, disconnect, ignore, and delete, not through registration. Registration carries the stored status forward, so a restarting server cannot undo a status you set.
{{< /alert >}}

## Other connection kinds

The same endpoint registers the other accepted kinds, with their own identity rules:

- **Kubernetes.** Cloud derives the connection's ID from the cluster and the owner, so registering the same cluster again updates the existing connection instead of creating another. Cloud stores the cluster's credential once and keeps the stored status.
- **Prometheus and Grafana.** Cloud creates the connection or updates the existing one in place.

## Validation and errors

| Condition | Result |
| :--- | :--- |
| The request carries no Cloud session or bearer token | Rejected. The endpoint requires authentication. |
| The authentication does not resolve to a user | Rejected before anything is stored, with the error "cannot register meshery connection: missing owner in authenticated session". |
| `kind` is not one of the accepted values | HTTP 500 with the error "connection kind: `<kind>`, not implemented yet". |
| `metadata.serverId` is missing or empty on a `meshery` registration | HTTP 500 with the error "empty server id; cannot check for existence". No connection is created. |

## Operator guidance

If you operate a self-hosted Layer5 Cloud, these symptoms map to the most common causes:

- **Registration fails with "missing owner in authenticated session".** The request reached Cloud with authentication that does not resolve to a user. Look at the request in your logs and confirm that it carries a valid session or bearer token for an existing account.
- **Registration fails with "empty server id; cannot check for existence".** The client did not send `serverId` in `metadata`. Cloud does not fall back to creating an unidentified connection. Confirm that the client sends the identifier under the camelCase key `serverId`.
- **Registration fails with "not implemented yet".** The client sent a `kind` other than `meshery`, `kubernetes`, `prometheus`, or `grafana`.
- **A Meshery Server appears under the wrong user.** The owner comes from the session, not from the request body. The server was registered while a different account was signed in.
- **The same Meshery Server appears more than once.** Each owner and `serverId` pair is a separate connection, so a server registered by two users appears once for each of them. If one user sees the same server twice, the server presented a different `serverId`, which happens when it loses the identifier it stored locally and generates a new one.
- **A Meshery Server's name or status in Cloud does not change when it reconnects.** This is intended. Re-registration preserves the stored name and status; change them through the connection's own actions.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Networking"
url: /cloud/guides/self-hosted/planning/peer-to-peer-communication/index.md
description: The network paths a self-hosted Layer5 Cloud deployment needs, including how real-time co-editing connects browsers and what the signaling endpoint can see.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Plan these network paths before you deploy. Most are ordinary HTTPS traffic through your ingress. Real-time co-editing is the exception: it connects browsers directly to each other, and the deployment only introduces them.

## Required network paths

| From | To | Protocol | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Browsers, Meshery Servers, API clients | Ingress, public hostname | HTTPS | UI, API, sign-in (`/kratos`), and OAuth2 (`/hydra`) |
| Browsers | Ingress, `/collaboration` | WebSocket over HTTPS | Co-editing signaling |
| Layer5 Cloud server | Kratos and Hydra services | HTTP, in cluster | Account and token operations. Default ports: Kratos public 9010 and admin 9011, Hydra public 4444 and admin 4445 |
| Kratos | Layer5 Cloud server | HTTP, in cluster | Registration hooks, and identity mail when the HTTP courier is selected |
| Layer5 Cloud server, Kratos, Hydra | PostgreSQL | TCP 5432 | Databases `meshery`, `kratos`, `hydra` |
| Layer5 Cloud server | SMTP relay | SMTP on 25, 465, 587, or 2525 | Mail. The relay must resolve to a public address |
| Layer5 Cloud server | Webhook receivers | HTTPS | Optional webhooks |
| Layer5 Cloud server | OpenTelemetry collector | OTLP gRPC | Optional traces |
| Browsers | Public STUN and TURN hosts | UDP and TCP | Direct connections between co-editing browsers |

The ingress must support WebSocket upgrades. A controller or load balancer that closes idle connections shorter than the signaling keep-alive (below) disconnects users from their co-editing session.

## How co-editing connects people

When two people open the same design, their browsers exchange edits directly over WebRTC. Layer5 Cloud takes part only at the start and for presence:

1. Each browser opens a WebSocket to `/collaboration` on the provider that signed the user in and joins a room named after the design.
2. The server tells each browser who else is in the room.
3. The browsers ask public STUN servers how to reach each other, and fall back to a public TURN relay when a direct path is blocked.
4. Edits then travel browser to browser. They do not pass through Layer5 Cloud or Meshery Server.

A self-hosted provider is its own signaling host. Users connected to your deployment never signal through Layer5's hosted service.

In short: the WebSocket carries introductions and presence, WebRTC carries the work, and STUN and TURN help the browsers find each other.

### What the signaling endpoint does and enforces

- **Authentication.** A connection must present the user's access token. The server answers an unauthenticated connection with `401`.
- **Rooms.** The endpoint creates a room when someone joins and tracks who is in it. It accepts any room name from a signed-in user and does not check that the user may open the design the room belongs to. Design identifiers are random, and the content of a design stays on the peers, so treat the identifier as the secret that gates a room.
- **Messages.** The server relays join, leave, and broadcast messages, and pushes the member list of each room to its members, with each person's name and avatar.
- **Keep-alive.** The server pings each connection every 27 seconds. A client that does not answer within 30 seconds is dropped.
- **Persistence.** The server stores nothing from a session. The person who made an edit saves it through the normal design save; a person who opens the design later loads the last saved version.
- **Origins.** The endpoint accepts WebSocket connections from any origin.

### What peers see

Each participant is shown to the others with their name, avatar, cursor, and selected component. Presence colors are random per session, so two people can share a color. A second browser tab with the same account appears as another collaborator.

## Sizing and limits

Layer5 Cloud enforces no cap on the number of people in a room, on document size, or on session length. Because every browser connects to every other browser, connection count grows with the square of the room's size, and a very large room degrades before the server does. Plan for design reviews and pairing, not broadcast to large audiences.

## When co-editing cannot connect

Kanvas keeps working as a single-user editor and writes the reason to the browser console. There is no on-screen indicator and no automatic retry. Check these in order:

| Symptom | Likely cause |
| --- | --- |
| The WebSocket to `/collaboration` fails with `401` | The user's session has expired. Signing in again fixes it. |
| The WebSocket never upgrades | The ingress or an intermediate proxy does not pass WebSocket upgrades on `/collaboration`. |
| The WebSocket connects, but people do not see each other's changes | Browsers cannot reach the public STUN and TURN hosts, or a firewall blocks WebRTC. The STUN and TURN hosts are set by the Kanvas client and are not configurable in the deployment. |
| People see each other's presence but not edits | The same cause: signaling works and the peer connection does not. |


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Set Notification Preferences"
url: /cloud/guides/account/notification-preferences/index.md
description: Choose which Layer5 Cloud events send you email, and know which preferences are live today.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Layer5 Cloud sends email when something happens that involves you: you earn a badge, your role changes, someone comments on your design. Notification preferences decide which of those emails reach you. Preferences belong to your account, so they apply in every organization you belong to.

Email is the only channel. Layer5 Cloud has no per-event choice between email and another channel.

## Before you start

You need the **View Profile** permission, which the default user role holds. The preferences are on your own account, and you cannot set them for anyone else.

## How preferences work

- **Everything is on until you turn it off.** A new account receives every notification. You opt out of the ones you do not want, and a notification added later is on for you until you turn it off.
- **Preferences save themselves.** About one second after your last change, Layer5 Cloud saves it and confirms with "Notification preferences updated". There is no Save button.
- **Preferences are grouped.** The preferences appear under categories and sub-categories. Each category has a switch that turns every preference in it on or off at once. To opt out of all email, turn every category off.
- **A preference suppresses email, not the event.** The event still happens and still appears in the audit trail. Only the email is skipped.

## Preferences you can set

The categories below are the ones the account page lists. Layer5 Cloud reads the list of available preferences from its own configuration, so a deployment can list more or fewer.

| Category | Preference | Emails you when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Acknowledgment | Badge assignment and updates | A badge is awarded to you or changed. |
| Organization Activity | Organization update | An organization you belong to is updated. |
| Workspace Activity | Team, user, and organization management | A team you belong to is updated, or you are added to a team. |
| Workspace Activity | Role assignment and updates | Your roles change. |
| Workspace Activity | Comments on your designs | Someone comments on a design you own. Turning this off silences email about comments on your designs. |
| Workspace Activity | Participating and @mentions in comments | You are mentioned in a comment, or a thread you took part in gets a reply. |

To stop email from one thread without turning the preference off, mute that thread. See [Mute a thread]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/collaborating/reviewing-designs/index.md#mute-comment-notifications" >}}).

### Preferences that do nothing yet

Three preferences appear greyed out and unchecked, and cannot be changed: **Changes to designs**, **Deployments in environments**, and **Weekly summary**. Layer5 Cloud does not send those emails today. Do not rely on them.

## Edge cases

- Anonymous accounts never receive organization update email.
- Layer5 Cloud checks the preference when it is about to send the email. Turning a preference back on does not resend email that was skipped while it was off.
- If saving fails, the page shows the reason, and your previous setting stays in force.

## See also

- [Review and collaborate on designs]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/collaborating/reviewing-designs/index.md" >}}) describes who receives comment email.
- [Manage Your Account]({{< ref "cloud/guides/account/managing-your-account.md" >}}) covers your profile and sign-in.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Provider Initialization"
url: /cloud/guides/self-hosted/deployment/provider-initialization/index.md
description: Reference for INIT_CONFIG, the setting that creates the provider organization and the first Provider Admin when a self-hosted deployment starts: format, fields, behavior, and failure modes.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

A new deployment has no users, so nobody can sign in to administer it. Provider initialization solves that: when the server starts with `INIT_CONFIG` set, it creates the **provider organization** and its first **Provider Admin**. From that account, you create organizations, assign roles, and manage the deployment. See [Roles and Permissions]({{< ref "cloud/reference/default-permissions.md" >}}) for what a Provider Admin can do.

## Format

`INIT_CONFIG` holds a YAML document. In Helm, set it as a multiline string in `env.initConfig`, or load it from a file with `--set-file env.initConfig=provider-init.yaml`.

```yaml
organization:
  name: "Example Corp"
  description: "The provider organization for Example Corp."
  country: "United States"
  region: "North America"

user:
  first_name: "Ada"
  last_name: "Admin"
  email: "admin@example.com"
  username: "admin@example.com"
  password: "<initial password>"
```

| Field | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `organization.name` | Yes | Name of the provider organization. |
| `organization.description` | No | Description. |
| `organization.country` | No | Country. |
| `organization.region` | No | Region. |
| `user.first_name` | Yes | First name of the administrator. |
| `user.last_name` | Yes | Last name of the administrator. |
| `user.email` | Yes | Email address. It is the sign-in identifier. |
| `user.username` | No | Defaults to the email address. |
| `user.password` | Yes | Initial password. |

The provider organization always has the fixed identifier `11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111`. Every deployment uses the same one.

## What happens at startup

The server evaluates `INIT_CONFIG` on every start, after database migrations and before it reports ready.

1. **Not set.** Initialization is skipped.
2. **Set but invalid.** A missing required field or YAML that does not parse is logged as an error. The server keeps starting, with no provider administrator.
3. **The provider organization already exists.** Initialization is skipped, and any change to `INIT_CONFIG` is ignored.
4. **The provider organization does not exist.** The server runs these steps in order:
   1. Creates a Kratos identity with the password and the email marked verified.
   2. Creates the user and marks the account active.
   3. Grants the user the Provider Admin role and the Kanvas role.
   4. Creates the provider organization with the fixed identifier, owned by that user.
   5. Adds the user to the organization with the Organization Admin role.

The first administrator can sign in as soon as the server is ready. They never see an email verification step, because the address is created verified.

After the organization exists, the server also seeds the deployment's default Google and GitHub sign-in credentials from `env.providerOrg*`. See [Identity Services]({{< ref "cloud/guides/self-hosted/planning/identity-services/index.md#how-the-defaults-are-stored" >}}).

## Failure modes

| Condition | Result |
| --- | --- |
| A step fails after earlier steps succeeded | The server logs the error and keeps starting. The steps are not wrapped in one transaction, so rows from earlier steps remain. Fix the cause and restart. A restart repeats the whole sequence for as long as the provider organization does not exist. |
| Kratos rejects the identity (for example, the password is too weak or the identity exists) | The server logs a warning and continues with the remaining steps. |
| `INIT_CONFIG` removed after the first successful start | No effect. The organization exists. |
| `INIT_CONFIG` changed after the first successful start | No effect. Change the administrator through the product. |

## Handling the password

The initial password is stored in the Helm release, in the pod environment, and in the server log, because the server logs the configuration it reads. Treat all three as secret. After you have signed in and changed the password, remove `env.initConfig` and run `helm upgrade`. The administrator account is unaffected.

## When to use it

Use `INIT_CONFIG` for every new self-hosted deployment, and keep the file in your secret manager next to the other values. It makes a deployment reproducible: a rebuilt cluster with the same values and a restored database comes up with the same administrator, and a rebuilt cluster with an empty database creates it again.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Roles and Permissions"
url: /cloud/reference/default-permissions/index.md
description: Which permissions each default Layer5 Cloud role holds, who assigns each role, and which default keychains group the permissions.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

This page tells you which permissions each default Layer5 Cloud role holds. Use it to find out why an action is missing for a user and which role grants it. For how roles, keychains, and permissions fit together, see [Roles]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/roles/_index.md" >}}).

## How permission checks work

A permission is a named key that allows one action, such as Create Team. A keychain groups keys, and a role groups keychains. Layer5 Cloud checks the key, never the role name. Before it runs a guarded action, Cloud resolves the organization the request names, then checks whether the user holds the key through a role in that organization. A user's permissions are the union of the keys from every role the user holds there.

When a user lacks the key, Cloud refuses the request with HTTP 403 and the message "You do not hold the permission this action requires in this organization". The response body is JSON with an `error` message and a `code`.

Provider Admin passes every permission check, in every organization.

## Default roles

| Role | Scope | Assigned by |
|---|---|---|
| Provider Admin | Provider | Provider Admin |
| Kanvas | Provider | Provider Admin. Every new account receives it automatically. |
| Curator | Provider | Provider Admin |
| Organization Admin | Organization | Organization Admin or Provider Admin |
| User | Organization | Organization Admin or Provider Admin |
| Workspace Admin | Organization | Organization Admin or Provider Admin |
| Workspace Manager | Organization | Organization Admin or Provider Admin |
| Academy Admin | Organization | Organization Admin or Provider Admin |
| Academy Learner | Organization | Organization Admin or Provider Admin |
| Team Admin | Team | Team Admin or Provider Admin |

An anonymous user, someone using Kanvas without signing in, receives an internal Anonymous User role. It is not listed and cannot be assigned. See [Permissions by Role]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/permissions.md" >}}) for what anonymous users can do in Kanvas.

The Kanvas role holds no keychains. It makes the Kanvas extension available when a Meshery Server connects to Layer5 Cloud.

## Reading the matrices

The matrices below are refreshed automatically from the Layer5 permission list.

- A check mark means the role holds the permission.
- A check mark with an asterisk means the role holds the permission only on resources the user owns.
- A dash means the role does not hold the permission.

The columns show the roles that hold permissions in the list. "Org Admin" is the Organization Admin role. Workspace Manager, Curator, Kanvas, and the Academy roles have no column; see [Roles outside the matrices](#roles-outside-the-matrices).

### Designs and catalog

{{< keys-matrix caption="Catalog" functions="View Catalog|Share Design|Clone Design|View Catalog Requests|Approve Catalog Request|Deny Catalog Request" >}}

### Teams

{{< keys-matrix caption="Teams" functions="View Team|View Teams|View All Teams|Create Team|Edit Team|Delete Team|Add User to Team|Invite User to Team|Remove User from Team|Assign Roles to Team members|Remove Roles from Team members|Open Team Invite|Leave Team" >}}

### Organizations and roles

{{< keys-matrix caption="Organizations" functions="View Org|View Organizations|View All Organizations|Create Organization|Edit Organization|Add User to Organization|Invite User to Organization|Remove User from Organization|Promote or Demote User to Org Admin|Assign Roles to Organization members|Remove Roles from Organization members" >}}

{{< keys-matrix caption="Roles" functions="Assign User Roles" >}}

### Workspaces, environments, and connections

{{< keys-matrix caption="Settings and extensions" functions="View Settings|View Metrics|View Registry|Connect Metrics|Connect adapter|View Extensions|Install extension" >}}

## Roles outside the matrices

| Role | What it holds by default |
|---|---|
| Workspace Manager | The permissions of Workspace Admin for workspaces, environments, teams, and lifecycle actions, plus management of the designs, environments, and connections inside the workspaces where the user holds the role. It does not hold the catalog curation permissions. |
| Curator | No keychains in a default install. Organization Admin and Workspace Admin hold the catalog curation permissions, including approving and denying publish requests. |
| Kanvas | No keychains. See [Default roles](#default-roles). |
| Academy Admin | The Academy management permissions, plus team management and workspace management. |
| Academy Learner | Access to Academy content and registration. |
| Anonymous User | The Kanvas design permissions for people who are not signed in. |

## Default keychains

Each default keychain groups the permissions for one area. Roles hold keychains, so granting a keychain to a role grants every permission in it.

| Keychain | What it groups |
|---|---|
| User View | Permissions for individual users. |
| User Management | Managing users and their roles. |
| Team View | Viewing teams and their members. |
| Team Management | Managing teams and team membership. |
